Title: The Marprelate Tracts, 1588, 1589, edited with notes historical and explanatory
Creator: Martin Marprelate (pseudonym; the authorship is argued in the editor's notes, with John Penry and Job Throkmorton the principal candidates) (William Pierce, editor)
Publisher: London: James Clarke and Co., 13 and 14 Fleet Street
Publication Date: 1911 (title page: 1911)
Rights: Public Domain (published London 1911, more than 95 years ago, so public domain in the United States by date; the archive.org item carries no possible-copyright-status field, so the determination rests on the printed date)
Source: Internet Archive item marprelatetracts0000will, file marprelatetracts0000will_djvu.txt (University of Arizona Library copy, internetarchivebooks collection, not access-restricted), fetched directly by the library/source-research thread (Era VII session, second pass, English and Scottish worlds agent), 2026-10-23; host rights statement: none given on the item (possible-copyright-status field absent)
Provenance note: Header prepended; the OCR text follows unchanged (no long-s glyphs were present). Nothing retyped, dropped or corrected. Rights basis restated: this printing's own date, 1911, is more than 95 years before 2026, so the text is public domain in the United States by date.
Content note: Pierce's edition of the seven tracts in modernised spelling, with his introduction (from about file line 407) and heavy explanatory notes beneath the text, which are the editor's and not Martin's. The Contents at the head gives the order and printed pages: The Epistle (Oh read over D. John Bridges, 1588; the tract's own title page at about file line 2525), The Epitome (1588; running heads from about line 12746), The Minerals (1589), Hay any Work for Cooper (1589; from about line 21605), Theses Martinianae or Martin Junior (1589; from about line 28587), The Just Censure or Martin Senior (1589), The Protestation (1589), and the Index (from line 41471). CAVEAT on the OCR: the text pages are clean at the 10 and 70 per cent sample points, but the scan OCR'd several blank versos and the facsimile title pages as mirrored garbage (the 30 and 90 per cent samples fell on such pages, and similar runs occur between tracts); a reader should expect stretches of nonsense characters between the tracts and treat them as scan noise, not text. The 50 per cent sample fell in the editor's index-like notes and was readable.

PREFACE 


THe present volume is the completion of a task which 
has occupied my leisure for some years, the earlier part 
of which I have presented to the public in the Historical 
Introduction to the Marprelate Tracts. I now present an 
annotated edition of the Tracts themselves. The text is 
given as if stands in the originals, except that the spelling 
and punctuation have been modernised. Any other liberties 
taken with the text have been precisely noted as they 
occur. The pagination or the signatures of the originals 
are given in the margins. All references to the pages of 
the Tracts are to the pages in the present volume. 

As before, I desire to express my thanks to the keepers 
of the great public libraries, who have afforded me every 
facility in my studies. The greater part of my work has 
been done in the British Museum, to the expert knowledge 
of whose learned assistants, treasured in the great catalogue 
and otherwise available in case of need, I am under 
great obligation. To the Archbishop of Canterbury I 

am particularly obliged by his permission to transcribe the 
text of the unique Lambeth copy of the third Tract; the 
seventh Tract also has been by permission copied from the 
same collection. Iam also under further special obligation 
to his Grace, and to his learned librarian, the Rev. Claude 
Jenkins, M.A., for pormission to photograph the title pages |

of all the Tracts, and also to reproduce the excellent

| As regards the history of the period and the particular 
history of the production of the Tracts, and of the con- 

troversy which immediately ensued upon their publication, 

| I have to refer my readers to the Historical Introduction. 

There they will also find all that I have to say in regard 

to the authorship of these writings. In the present volume 

I have contented myself with a brief historic note prefacing 

each Tract. As this edition may be used as a book of 

reference, I have duplicated some of the explanatory notes 
for the convenience of the reader. 

The references in the notes to contemporary literature 
are, unless otherwise indicated, to the original editions, and 
for the convenience of the reader in the case of the frequent 
references to Bishop Cooper’s Admonition, the page is 
generally given in Dr. Arber’s useful reprint. Neal’s 
History of the Puritans is referred to in the edition of 1822 
in 5 vols. 8vo; Foxe’s Acts and Monuments, in the edition 
of Stoughton and Pratt; and Strype’s Works in the Oxford 
8vo edition, 1822—1828. In references to other works, 
particulars where needed are given ag they occur. The 
letter At in the foot-notes indicates the original text of the 

Marprelate Tracts. 

I have only to add that I have been greatly helped in 

| various ways by many friends, who have placed their stores 

| of learning and their practical wisdom at my disposal.

1. In the year 1584, the year after the elevation of John 
Whitgift to the archbishopric of Canterbury, there was 
published anonymously, but bearing the imprint and device 
of Robert Waldegrave, a small 8vo of 154 pages of long 
primer, under the title of A Briefe and Plaine declaration 
concerning the desires of all those faithfull Mimsters, that have 
and do feeke for the Discipline and reformation of the Church 
of Englande; but its popular name was given to it by 
Waldegrave, who added the running headline ‘A Learned 
Discourse of Ecclesiastical Governement.’ Tradition, with

XIV INTRODUCTION 


what basis of authority lam unable to say, has long attri- 
buted its authorship to Dr. William Fulke, Master of 
Pembroke Hall, as then it was, a famous anti-papal contro- 
versialist in his day, and chiefly known by his defence of 
the Hinglish translations of the Bible against the Rhemists. 
If Fulke be indeed the author of the Learned Discourse, 
then we can readily understand why he chose to publish it 
anonymously; and if the ecclesiastical authorities suspected 
him of being the author we can also understand why so 
capable a man should not be promoted to high office, in a 
day when John Bullingham, Marmaduke Middleton, John 
Scory, Hugh Curwen and the like were esteemed eligible 
for the episcopate. 

The Learned Discourse became popular because of its 
merits. It set forth the arguments of the ‘seekers after 
discipline and reformation’ with admirable lucidity and 
conciseness. ‘he common folk could understand the 
‘writer’s contention that the Church of Christ being a 
‘household’ needed not prelates but household officers, 
They felt the cogency of the warning against following 
the example of ‘the kings of the Gentiles,’ and of Dio- 
trephes, whose special sin was that ‘he was Philoproteuon, 
one that desired the primacie in the Church.’ The ambition 
of the sons of Zebedee was cited as an example of how men 
imperilled their place in the ‘household of the faith’ by 
lusting for power and preéminence. When men, with the 
New Testament in their hands, were directed to the litle 
child placed in the midst of the jealous aspirants for the 
apostolic headship, and to the sacred example of Christ 
washing His disciples’ feet, they easily passed judgment 
on those who unceasingly wrote obsequious letters to all 
supposed to have the ear of the Queen, beseeching their 
help to gain preferment ; and on such ecclesiastical princes 
as Archbishop Whitgift riding at the head of his gorgeous 
cavalcade of palace officers and retainers. What if the 
little child had been placed in the great hall at Lambeth

INTRODUCTION XV 


when the Primate was being served ‘on the knee’? The 
writer of the Learned Discourse could remind the prelates 
how they had reproved the swollen pride of the Papacy by 
hurling against it the great utterance ‘You have but one 
Master which is Christ, and all you are brethren.’ But it 
was now they who were claiming prelatical superiority over 
their ministerial brethren. In like manner the writer urges 
the elementary right of a Christian congregation to choose 
its own pastor; the right of the Church as against the 
bishops to exercise discipline over its members, as is assumed 
in the admonition ‘Tell it to the Church’; and also to 
check the action of its officers by insisting that no decision 
can have valid authority until it be confirmed by the 
Church. 

2. Its onslaught on the established order was thought to 
be so effective that Dean Bridges of Salisbury was appointed 
to reply to the Learned Discourse. This he did first in a 
sermon delivered at Paul’s Cross, and next by expanding 
and elaborating the sermon into a large volume of over 
fourteen hundred pages quarto, divided into sixteen books, 
one of which was directed against The Judgment of a most 
Reverend and Learned Man from beyond the Seas—the 
English translation of a letter written by Theodore Beza, 
Calvin’s successor at Geneva. The rest of the volume was 
more or less concerned with the Learned Discourse. Bridges’ 
volume was answered after the usual grave manner by 
Dudley Fenner and also presumably by John Penry (sce 
-p. 402, note (2)). But something more was wanted in this 
unequal warfare. The ‘seekers after reformation’ had no 
pulpit open to them, the Press was strictly censored against 
them, their chief men were in gaol, and most of them 
reduced to poverty. 

8. Then it was in the great year 1588 that Martin 
Marprelate came forth to attack the oflicial champion of the 
bishops, with new weapons, and compelled the attention of 
ali classes of the community. There was a piquancy no

XVi _ INTRODUCTION 


doubt in the spectacle of a satirical humourist of the first 
order undertaking the defence of men who for the most 
part were innocent of all joking, whose demeanour was of 
the gravest, whose religious life was habitually solemn and 
at this time was the more austere by reason of the sorrows 
they were called upon to endure. And the fact is that 
large numbers of them repudiated their voluntary champion. 
They preferred the gravity and dulness of their persecutors 
as exemplified in Dean Bridges’ Defence and Bishop Cooper’s 
Admonition, to the pungent wit and the satirical invective 
of Martin Marprelate. It was only men like quaint Giles 
Wigginton, the life-long victim of Whitgift’s vindictive hate, 
men themselves endowed with some natural humour, who 
heartily approved of the unknown champion’s philippic 
against the bishops. 

4. Jt is unnecessary to repeat the history of the Mar- 
prelate Tracts, but it will help us rightly to estimate their 
value and their place in the religious controversies of the 
age in which they appeared, if we enquire on what grounds, 
expressed or implied, Martin Marprelate entered into the 
fray; for the most superficial reader will see that beneath 
his humour and his mischievous gossip he is fiercely in 
earnest, indeed the substratum of his righteous anger not 
infrequently outcrops to the surface. 

(i) It is necessary in the first place to remember that 
the men represented by Marprelate’s serious contention 
were not conscious Separatists. They had not the daring 
and commanding logic of Robert Browne, the father of 
Separatism, who must claim with Richard Hooker to be 
one of the two English ecclesiologists whose writings are 
of permanent significance for our Church history. It was 
their failure that made Marprelate’s clients in a later 
generation Separatists. For the time, though they felt that 
a cruel Mother had driven them from their natural home, 
they cherished the thought that it was theirhome. Though 
they refused to attend their parish churches, when and

INTRODUCTION xvii 


because that which they esteemed to be Popery was 
introduced into their worship; though they surreptitiously 
held their classes and indulged in the secret and dangerous 
luxury of Presbyterian worship and fellowship, yet they 
were not conscious that the Church of England could be 
otherwise than their Church. The assumption of their 
persecutors, as a matter of fact, was identical. with their 
own instinctive view. They were to be compelled by law, 
and by bitter ecclesiastical ordinances, which were not 
English law, to belong to the established system, whether 
they would or not. The representation of Anglican critics 
that these ‘seekers after discipline and reformation’ were 
officiously endeavouring to change the character of some- 
body else’s Church entirely obscures the issue. 

(ii) Moreover the Puritans were encouraged in their 
propaganda by what they considered to be the tentative 
character of the reforms already effected. This belief was 
fostered in the commencement of Elizabeth’s reign. Such 
was the hope of the returning exiles. So they wrote confiden- 
tially when the Queen insisted on the proviso that, though 
the conference appointed should choose the later and more 
Protestant of Edward’s two Prayer Books, the ‘ ornaments ’ 
authorised in the earlier book should be retained, ‘ until it 
please the Queen to take other order for them’ (x). In the 
Preface to the Advertisements issued at the Queen’s 
command by Archbishop Parker in 1565, after disavowing 
that the rules prescribed therein are ‘ equivalent with the 
Eternal Word of God,’ we have the assurance that they 
are merely ‘rules in some part of Discipline concerning 
decency distinction and order for the time.’ It was only 
when that hope, revived on the accession of James J. and 
expressed in the Millenary Petition presented to him, 
utterly expired, that the Puritans in increasing numbers felt 
that the logic of their position led them to Separatism. 

(iii) The Puritans were conscious that for high political

XVill INTRODUCTION 


reasons, good or bad, a certain restraint was put on those 
who would reform the Church. ‘Those Roman Catholics 
who held resolutely to their faith were not in themselves 
a dangerous element in the community. Their attempts in 
Norwich, in the west, and in the northern parts to raise a 
rebellion were contemptible exhibitions. But in conjunction 
with the designs of the Catholic powers of France and Spain, 
and the intrigues of the Vatican, they might add consider- 
ably to the national peril. But there was a general expecta- 
tion among the reformers that when the country was strong 
enough to defy the Armada it was time to doff the habits of 
the enemy and, careless of consequences, to weed out the 
remaining superstitions surviving from the Roman dominion 
—the interrogations and the sign of the Cross in baptism, 
kneeling at Communion, and the like, as well as the 
distinetive vestments of Rome. 

(iv) In their contention they were strongly of opinion 
that the mass of the nation was with them. They even 
cherished the belief that the Queen was in her heart 
favourable to the anti-papal protest. They did not forget 
that she was the daughter of Henry and Anne Boleyn, 
whose very birth symbolised the breach with the Papacy. 
They realised that already she had given substantial proof 
that, although she was prepared to walk circumspectly, neither 
she nor her realm were again to be subject to the Roman 
obedience. It is true that a seasoned old dissimulator like 
Guzman, the Spanish Ambassador, who had reduced diplo- 
matic lying to a very fine art, was hoodwinked atrociously ~ 
when Elizabeth put her hand upon her heart and vowed 
that if the Holy Father could but look into her secret mind 
he would see that she was a true Catholic. In furtherance 
of her diplomacy she could introduce the little silver cross 
into her private chapel and show a greater severity towards 
recalcitrant Protestant Nonconformists. But the fact 
remained that the nation was moving away from, and not 
towards, Rome. So in all the Puritan writings we find

INTRODUCTION xX 


the statement that if the Queen but knew how her loyal 
Protestant subjects were being mishandled by the Bishops, 
she would graciously interfere for their protection. I do 
not gather from their writings that they founded their 
judgment upon any known evidence of her evangelical 
views, except so far.as they assumed their own position was 
the logical consequence of her opposition to the doctrine 
and dominion of Rome. They rather rested upon the 
conviction of her womanly, or rather: motherly, compassion 
and her solicitude for all her subjects. 

(v) Whether they were right in holding as Marprelate 
also held, that the bulk of the nation desired with them 
a more complete purification of the ceremonial of the 
Church from all vestiges of the Roman ritual is a question 
which needs to be freshly examined. The interested con- 
jectures of Catholic recusants who divided the country into 
three parts and claimed two for the Pope seem to be 
eminently unreliable data upon which to base a sound’ 
judgment. The great unpopularity of Mary and of Bonner, 
the chief agent in her barbarous policy of persecution, is a 
fact which cannot be doubted. Mary the people regarded 
with cold and sullen aversion. Bonner, equally notorious 
for his luxurious life and his inhuman cruelty, was to them 
the embodiment of Romanism; and him they openly 
execrated. I'he demand for a change in the national religion 
was too fierce to be denied, even had Elizabeth been inclined 
to follow her sister. And as an indication of the sentiments 
of the people at large, the sympathy of Elizabeth’s parliaments 


with the reformers cannot be overlooked. Moreover the 


testimony of the martyrdoms to the wide prevalence of 
Protestant convictions has not, as it would seem to me, been 
properly estimated. A man must hold what he believes to 
be the truth with a deep conviction to be willing to be burnt 
alive rather than deny it. And for one who went to the 
stake there would be a score recanting through fear, and a 
still greater number who were not called upon to recant

because they kept their heretical views secret. If, in the 
ruthless years of the Marian persecution, Kent had fifty- 
four Protestant witnesses who suffered at the stake—that 
number embracing men and women, and rich and poor—it 
seems fair to assume that at the death of Edward, Kent 
must have been substantially a Protestant county. But to 
this we must add the influence of the martyrdoms upon 
public opinion. So careful and authoritative a writer as 
Prof. A. E. Pollard can say that they ‘stamped on the 
English mind a hatred, unthinking, ferocious and almost 
indelible, of Rome and all its belongings.” We cannot 
therefore be far wrong in supposing that at the death 
of Mary the county of Kent contained very little Catholicism. 
And though the martyrdoms were almost confined to London 
and the nearer division of the Midlands, together with the 
country lying immediately to the east and south of the 
metropolis, their testimony to the extent of Protestantism 
at the death of Edward is very weighty, and their influence 
in extending Protestant views during the reign of Mary was 
very great. It is by no means improbable that the reformers 
wére right in their assumption that the bulk of the nation 
desired that the worship of the Church as well as its doctrine 
should be freed from all taint of Romanism. 

(vi) The Puritans were no doubt incited to attack the 
bishops because they judged them to be grossly inconsistent. 
They were all of them pronounced anti-papalists. It may 
be alleged that men lke Kitchin and Curwen could have 
had no convictions worth regarding, they had professedly 
changed their views so often; but even they outwardly 
united with rest of the bishops in regarding the Pope as 
antichrist. ‘he earlier of the Elizabethan bishops would 
gladly have abolished the papal vestments and the ceremonies 
which savoured of Popery. The most commanding figure 
among them, John Jewel, Bishop of Salisbury and author 
of the Apology, has described the contention for the

(vii) In connection with the great controversy to which 
the Marprelate Tracts are related, two volumes were 
issued by the bishops, expressing their common views, 
written and supervised by the chief of them, including the 
Archbishop of Canterbury. There can be no question, 
judged by these officially endorsed works, as to the 
definitely anti-Roman, and most positively Protestant, 
character of the Church established by Elizabeth. The first 
of these volumes is the Defence of Dean Bridges of 
Salisbury. A quotation from its pages distinguishing the 
two classes of opponents assailing the established order, the 
Papists and the Puritans, will sufficiently illustrate the case. 


‘The controuersies between the common adversaries [the 
Papists] and vs, are pro Arts et focis; for matters, 
and that capitall matters, of the substance and life 
of our Christian religion ; not trifles, as some newtrals 
would beare the people in hande. And _ therefore 
our aduersaries, in matters of religion, are incensed 
against vs with mortall, or rather, with immortall 
hatred. Whereas the controversies betwixt vs and 
our Brethren [the Puritans] are matters, or rather 
(as they call them) but manners, and formes of the 
Churches regiment [rule]... ... the Papists from 
whose grosse errors in doctrine we both dissent, and 
against whome, in the vynitie and substance of Gods 
truth we both agree’ (Preface, 48, rect et vers). 


And the very definite view of the Prelates about the Mass 
may be given from the same work. Dean Bridges after 
speaking of the devil tempting Hive, proceeds—

diuelish Ministers and instruments; so did he by the 
Masse, which is of some called well the Horse of 
Troy, that had so many fierce and bloody captaines

The second official volume is Bishop Cooper’s Admonition, 
an even more carefully considered statement of the doctrine 
of the Elizabethan Church, given thirty years after its 
establishment, written by Cooper, in conference with Arch- 
bishop Whitgift and several other bishops and containing 
the personal statements of Whitgift, Aylmer, Young and 
Cooper himself in reply to Marprelate, besides a general 
exposition of the doctrine and ceremonies of the Church as 
established. The Admonition, like the Defence, declares that 
the Puritans ‘in doctrine agree with the present state’ 
(p. 80; Arber, p. 27). And Whitgift in his special defence, 
replying (in the third person) to the allegation that ‘ there 
was no great jarre betvveene the Papistes and the Arch- 
bishop in matters of Religion,’ says ‘I think Martin him 
selfe doubteth not of the Archbishops soundnesse in such 
matters of Religion, as are in controuersie betwixt the 
Papists and vs’ (p. 48; Arber, p. 35). In regard to the 
‘external government and other outward orders’ Cooper 
claims for the Church of England the liberty enjoyed 
by the foreign Reformed Churches, to choose such as 
they thought ‘in wisedome and godlinesse to bee most con- 
uenient for the state of the countrey, and disposition 
of the people.’ There is no claim on behalf of ‘an 
historic episcopate’; episcopacy is only defended as an 
expedient system (p. 76 ; Arber, pp. 64, 65). The priests 
of the Church of England are, he declares, ‘ Priestes of Gods 
holy, blessed, and true Church, and yet tbat they are not 
such sacrificing Priests of God as are mentioned’ in the 
laws of Moses (p. 166; Arber, 124). Equally definite is“the

preaching is contrary ’ (p. 186; Arber, 187). Cooper claims, 
in the name of its bishops, that the Church represents the 
views of the Marian Martyrs, and that its doctrines are set 
forth authoritatively in Nowell’s Catechism and Jewel’s 
Apology. 

(viii) All this was present to the mind of the Puritans; 
they admitted the bishops’ claim that their doctrine 
was in the main irreproachable from tbe Evangelical 
standpoint. They also saw that the same essential theology 
was contained in the Book of Homilies reissued by 
Elizabeth. Even more significant was the formal state- 
ments of the creed of the Church as set forth in the 
Thirty-Nine Articles of 1562. It lay beyond the com- 
prehension of Conformist or Reformer that, against 
the overwhelming testimony of those engaged in estab- 
lishing the reformed Church, its early authoritative 
preachers and apologists, and its formal declarations, there 
should be posed a rubric which ambiguously directed what 
clothes the clergy should wear. They had too great a 
sense of the dignity of a Christian Church to suppose it 
could be founded upon a sartorial direction—a proviso 
added to the definitely Protestant service-book of 1552, by 
personal command of the Queen, who cared nothing for 
doctrine, but much for a pompous and richly-coloured 
ceremonial. The strong contention of the Puritan, and also 
of Bishop Jewel, was, that the Church, so definitely 
Evangelical in doctrine, should be made consistent. Having 
discarded the Mass, the nation should not perpetuate the 
Pope in the person of Whitgift, nor dress their ministers 
in the garments of the Church that burnt the martyrs 
and excommunicated the Queen. It was notorious that 
Klizabeth’s early bishops were strongly averse to the ‘ relics 
of the Amorites.’ Strype says that— 

‘The first bishops that were made, and who were but 

newly returned out of their exiles, as Cox, Grindal,

Horne, Sandys, Jewel, Parkhurst, Bentham, upon their 
first returns, before they entered upon their ministry, 
laboured all they could against receiving into the 
Church the papistical habits, and that all the ceremonies 
should be clean laid aside.’—Annals, I., i., 263. 


The seekers after reformation did but continue at great 
self-sacrifice that protest. 

5. In so unequal a battle the foibles and public incon- 
sistencies, and in some cases the notorious faults of the 
persecuting bishops, and the unfitness of many of the 
clergy ordained by them, were considered a fair mark for 
Martin’s satire and his contemptuous exposure. Much hard 
writing has been expended on this feature of the Marprelate 
Tracts. No doubt it is difficult to be just in writing of 
these matters, difficult not only for the inheritors of Non- 


‘conformist traditions to measure their aversion from the 


harsh and illegal proceedings of persecutors such as Whitgift 
and Aylmer, but difficult also for the apologists of the 
prelates to pay allegiance to the common instincts of 
humanity, and to revere the paramount authority of 
conscience amidst the dust and heat and the provocations 
of ecclesiastical strife. . 

Mr. W. H. Frere, of the Mirfield Community of Anglican 
monks, who was given my earlier volume to examine 
in the critical pages of the Lnglish Historical Review 
complains that I have taken for granted all the unfavourable 
stories about the bishops. He professes to give me a better 
example by dubbing them all in the lump slanders(x). I 
have taken some years, as a matter of fact, to examine 
these charges and to make myself better acquainted with 
the Elizabethan bishops. I may say, after Martin’s manner, 
that their worst enemies would not accuse them of being a 
very high-minded body of men. But the chief persons 
accused have themselyes examined the charges alleged

unclerical in his treatment of the subject if we set aside the 
uncharitable opinion that it 1s unclerical to tell the truth 
about these prelates, eminent or otherwise, both when it 
favours them and also whenit condemns. And in the same 
just spirit Mr. White deals with the masterful and fateful 
interference of Elizabeth in ecclesiastical affairs.

XXVill INTRODUCTION 


suffering for conscience’ sake leads to intellectual liberty. and 
toleration. It exhibits the folly of attempting to coerce the 
conscience, the regal rights of which it at the same time 
proclaims. John Rogers, the Marian protomartyr, learnt 
the lesson of religious liberty in the shadow of the stake. 
John Penry learnt the same truth in the same hard way. 
The Marprelate Tracts mark a stage in the Whitgiftian 
persecution, when the victims could testify that ‘fire and 
faggot,’ the chief arguments of the bishops, were not 
adequate to persuade men against their convictions. J am 
only too well aware from the reviews of the first section of 
my work how all the crimes against humanity are condoned 
on the immoral principle that every act is to be judged 
according to the fluctuating moral standard of the age in 
which it occurs; the moral standard being fixed by a 
consensus of the crimes actully perpetrated in that age. 
Good men and women when Elizabeth came to the throne 
branded Bouner with the name of ‘butcher.’ But they 
forsooth were wrong, since the moral standard operative 
a few months earlier palliated the roasting alive of 
ecclesiastical opponents. No one in the past is to be 
condemned for the inhumanities of religious persecution. 
Indeed the only persons to blame are the Elizabethan 
Puritans, who, it is true, did not actually persecute, but, we 
are assured, would have done so had they had the chance. 
Yet I recognise a difference between the rule of Mary and 
the rule of Elizabeth. I have contended in these pages that 
the Church on the aceession of Elizabeth went through a 
fundamental change. What argument could so conclusively 
prove that the new Church was not the old Catholic Church 
as it is proved by the simple fact that the unspeakable 
Bonner was allowed to die in bed ?

1. Tue Episrte is a small quarto of 52 pages, in a 
handsome Black Letter, called at the time a ‘ Dutch Letter.’ 

It was secretly printed at the house of Mrs. Crane, at 
East Molesey, on the Thames, a couple of miles above . 
Kingston. Mrs. Crane’s principal residence was in 
Aldermanbury, where she provided a refuge for the perse- 
cuted and needy Puritans of that time. To Aldermanbury 
Robert Waldegrave, the Puritan printer, fled with a couple 
of boxes of type when his house was raided in April, 1588. 
About midsummer of that year Waldegrave occupied the house 
at Hast Molesey, and was busily engaged during the subse- 
quent months in printing controversial pamphlets by Udall 
and Penry, and also the first Marprelate Tract known as 
Tue Epistie. The director of the secret press was John 
Penry, who acted as proof reader of Tue Epistun. The tract 
came into circulation about the middle of October. The 
press was removed from Molesey before November Ist, its 
next resting place being Fawsley House, in Northampton- 
shire, the residence of Sir Richard Knightley. 

2. The particular controversy to which THe Epistre was 
a contribution began with the publication of A briefe and 
plaine declaration—not to be confounded, as has been so 
generally done, with Walter Travers’ tract A full and plaine 
declaration-—a small 8yo. pamphlet of 154 pages, known 
commonly as the Learned Discourse, issued in support of 
the Puritan reform movement in 1584. So popular was 
the Learned Discourse that the ecclesiastical authorities 
appointed Dr. John Bridges, Dean of Salisbury, to preach 
against it at Paul’s Cross during Whitsuntide, 1585. 
During the next two years Bridges expanded his sermon into

4 INTRODUCTORY NOTE 


a large quarto volume of 1400 pages and more. It was pub- 
lished in 1587 under the title of A Defence of the govern- 
ment established in the Church of Englande for ecclesiastical 
matters. An answer appeared the same year from the pen 
of the well-known reforming minister Dudley Fenner, 
though his name did not appear upon the title-page. It was 
entitled A Defence of the Godlie Ministers. It was included 
in Waldegrave’s collection A Parte of a Register under 
Fenner’s name. The next year, 1688, appeared a second 
reply, also anonymous, entitled 4 Defence of the Ecclesticall 
Discipline, which Marprelate seems to suggest was written 
by John Penry (see Tue Prorysratyon, supra, 402, n.*), 

3. The memorable response to Dean Bridges’ work, how- 
ever, is Martin Marprelate’s series of Tracts, and especially 
the two first, Tse Eprrsrue and Tur Errroms, which are in 
form a single work, with almost identical title-pages. No 
book or pamphlet of that age ever appeared without its 
introductory ‘ epistle’ addressed to the reader—impartial, 
courteous, Christian, or otherwise. Martin sets out to write 
an ‘ Epitome’ of the First Book of Bridges’ voluminous 
Defence. As there was a delay in completing his task, he 
issues his introductory Hpistle separately. It is the present 
Tract. When later he issues his promised Epitome, it could 
not appear nakedly without an accompanying introductory 
chapter, notwithstanding that the Epistle proper had already 
been published: He, however, calls this further preface in 
his descriptive headline, ‘ The Second Epistle to the Terrible 
Priests.’ ‘The reader need only to be warned that, although 
thus formally distinguished, and separately published, 
Epistte and Errrome are continuous answers to Bridges’ 
work. 

The external history of this and the subsequent writings 
of Martin Marprelate, and the effect they had on the course 
of religious controversy and ecclesiastical adininistration, 
have been fully dealt with in the Author’s earher volume, An 
Historical Introduction to the Marprelate Tracts (Constable 


& Co., 1908).

AN EPISTLE TO THE TERRIBLE 
PRIESTS 


To the right puissant and terrible Priests, my clergy masters 1 
of the Confocation-house, whether Fickers-General, 
worshipful Paltripolitans, or any other of the Holy 
League of Subscription: this work I recommend unto — 
them with all my heart, with a desire to see them all so 
provided for one day, as I would wish, which I promise 
them shall not be at all to their hurt. 

Right poison’d (x), persecuting and terrible priests: The 
theme of mine Epistle unto your venerable mssterdoms is 
of two parts (and the Epitome of our Brother Bridges’ book 
shall come out speedily). 

First, Most pitifully complaining, Martin, Marprelate 
&e. 
Secondly, May it please your good Worskips, &c. (2). 

‘Most pitifully complaining,’ therefore, you are to under- 
stand that Dean Bridges hath written in your defence, a 
most senseless book, and I cannot very often at one breath 
come to a full point, when I read the same (3). 

Again, ‘May it please you’ to give me leave to play the 
dunce (4) for the nonce, as well as he; otherwise dealing 
with Master Doctor’s book, I cannot keep decorum persone (5). 

And, May it please you, if I be too absurd in any place 
(either in this Epistle, or that Epitome), to ride to Sarum, 
and thank his Deanship for it. Because, I could not deal 
with his book commendably, according to order, unless I 
should be sometimes tediously duncical (6) and absurd. 


(1) This is thought to be a passable pun on the word ‘ puissant.’ 

(2) These two phrases were the conventional opening words of the peti- 
tions, which, in days when legal justice was scarce, were continually being 
presented to those in authority praying for relief or redress. 

(3) Bridges indulges on occasion in interminably long sentences. 

(4) Always printed ‘ Duns’ in these Tracts, indicating its derivation from 
the name of the schoolman Duns Scotus; himself, it need hardly be said, by 
no means a dunce. 

(5) Martin must play the fool, so as to be in keeping with the Doctor’s 

ok, 

(6) @t. ‘dunsticall’ ‘It is made a great difference among dunsticall 
dcctors between noster magister and magister noster.—-Fulke, Def. of the Eng. 
Bible. Parker Soc. 568.

For I have heard some clergymen gay that Master Bridges 
was a very patch (z) and a dunce when he was in Cambridge. 
And some say, saving your reverence that are bishops, that 
he ig as very a knaye and enemy unto the sincerity of 
religion, as any Popish prelate in Rome. But the patch 
can do the cause of sincerity no hurt. Nay, he hath in this © 
book wonderfully graced the same by writing against it. 
For I have heard some say that whosoever will read his 
book shall as evidently see the goodness of the cause of 
Reformation, and the poor, poor, poor naked | ness of your 
[church] government, as almost in reading all Master 
Cartwright’s works (2). This was a very great oversight in 
his Grace of Cant[lerbury] (3) to suffer such a book to come 
out. For besides that an archbishop is very weakly defended 
by Mass Dean, he hath also by this means provoked many to 
write against his gracious F’athorhood, who perhaps, never 
meant to take pen in hand. And, Brother Bridges, mark 
what Martin tells you. You will shortly, I hope, have twenty 
fists about your ears more than your own (4). ‘Take heed of 
writing against the Puritans, while you live! Yet they say 
that his Grace would not have the book to be published; 
and, if you mark, you shall not find ‘Seen and allowed’ in 
the title of his book. 

Well fare, old Mother Experience, yet! The burnt child 
dreads the fire. His Grace will carry to his grave, I 
warrant you, the blows which Master Cartwright gave him 
in this cause; and therefore no marvel though he was loth

(2) For the controversy between Cartwright and Whitgift, see Historical 
Introduction, chap. I., sec. II., §§ 4,5; pp, 40—51. 

(3) Martin always implies a satirical pun in using the abbreviation 
‘Cant.,’ especially when addressing Whitgift as John of Cant. 

(4) The Bishops insisted upon interpreting this phrase perversely, ‘Sothe 
Ansbaptists, yvithin our memory, after slaunderous and opprobious calum- 
niations against the godly preachers and magistrates then liuing, fell to 
blovves and open violence. The libeller in this booke hath performed the one 
and threatned the other..—Bp. Cooper's Admonition, p. 51. The literary 
hacks employed by the Bishops later were instructed to employ the same 
tactics. See Martin’s protest in Hay ANY Woxkg, Introd, Epistle, p. 217; 
also p. 246.

Others say that John Cant. oversaw every ‘proof.’ If he

(1) The Puritans never doubted that Whitgift relinquished the controversy 
over the Admonition to Parliament, because Cartwright was too learned and 
dexterous an opponent for him. This, Martin suggests, might explain the 
Archbishop’s reluctance to have Bridges’ book published, if the ramour to 
that effect were true. Others, as Martin goes on to say, alleged, and it 
would appear with truth, that Whitgift revised the printer’s proofs. Of 
course, the reluctance to license and the proof-reading might both be true. 
Whitgift replied on both points as follows: ‘God be thanked, he neuer felt 
blowe giuen by him or any other in that cause, except the blovves of their 
despitefull and malitious tongues, vvhich notvvithstanding hee contemneth, 
remembring how true it is that Hierome saith, ste machine hereticorum 
sunt, ct eonvicti de perfidia ad maledicta se conferant. When heretikes are 
conuinced of falsehood and vntrueths, their shift is to flee to railing and 
slandering. . . . He did indeed peruse Doctur Bridges booke before it went 
to the Presse, and hee knovveth that the sufliciencie thereof causeth these 
men to storme, as not being able otherwise to answere it: which maketh 
them so bitterly to inueigh against his person. .. . The desire of disputation 
is but a vaine brag: they haue bene disputed and conferred with oftener 
then [than] either the worthiness of their persons or cause did require. 
Wherin their inability to defend such a cause hath manifestlie appeared.’— 
Bp. Cooper’s Admonition, pp. 38, 39. 

The conferences referred to by Whitgift must have been those held before 
himself sitting on the High Commission, or in the Star Chamber; or by his 
deputies who visited the unbending Puritans filling the London prisons at 
this time. It was one long complaint of the Puritans that they never could 
get a Conference with their ecclesiastical oppenents, Once only Whitgift 
yielded to the clamorous demand when he held a Conference at Lambeth 
which lasted two days, Dec, 10th and 12th, 1584. On the first day the 
Archbisbop had with him the Bishop of Winchester, and there were present 
the Earl of Leicester, Lord Gray, and Sir Francis Walsingham ; the Arch- 
bishop of York and the Lord Treasurer Burghley were added on the second 
day. The Puritan controversialists were Dr. Thomas Sparke and Walter 
Travers. The latter had recently been rejected from the mastership of the 
Temple, though chosen by the benchers and commended by Burghley, through 
the strenuous efforts of Whitgift, who represented to the Queen that 
Travers, among other things, ‘contemned the Book of Common Prayer.’ 
The need of revising the Book of Common Prayer was the stated subject of 
the Conference. he discussion was chiefly notable on the first day by 
Whitgift’s reckless assertion that the Apocrypha was part of the Holy 
Scripture and contained no error; and on the second day by his receiving 
at the hands of Sparke what Martin calls the non plus, which is more 
particularly referred to in the present Tract, p. 87, where in a note 
Whitgift’s defence is quoted from Cooper’s Admonition. Whitgift had 
evidently no mind for any further conferences with the reforming party. 

(2) There is no ground for believing that Bridges and Cosins had their 
licence to preach in Flanders ; though several of the leading Puritans, Walter 
Travers among the number, received their ordination at the hands of the

(1) The invariable policy of the Bishops was to identify conformity to 
their ecclesiastical policy with loyalty to the Queen. See this set forth and 
illustrated more at length in the Hist. Intro. pp. 255, 256, section (a). 

(2) We come here upon one of the famous controversial series of this 
period. The ground-work was entitled An Abstracte of Certain Acts of 
parlement : of Certaine of her Maiesties Iniunctions, of certaine Canons, 
Constitutions and Synodalles Prouinciall: established and in force for the 
peaceable government of the Church, within her Maiesties Dominions and 
Countries, for the most part heretofore enknowen and vnpractized. [B. M,. 
697, {.2.] This was apparently published early in 1584. In the same year 
Doctor Cosins, Dean of Arches, one of Whitgift’s Ecclesiastical Commis- 
sioners, and later the official chronicler of the iniquities of the notorious 
Hacket affair, came forward, as a civil lawyer chiefly engaged in church 
afiairs, with a reply, entitled An Answer to the two first and principall 
Treatises of a certeine factious libell, put foorth latelie, without name of 
Author or Printer, and without approbation by authoritie ender the title of, 
An Abstract, §¢—a small 4to, pp. 12 + 350. [B. M. 697, f.2.] (The 
Abstracte and the Answer, as the press mark indicates, are bound together 
in the British Museum volume. The copy of the Adbstracte consists only of 
‘the two first and principall Treatises’ referred to in Cosins? title; but 
whether this is only a section of the actual work [ have not ascertained ; 
apparently it is all that was published.) The discussion was now taken up 
by Dudley Fenner, sometime a tutor at Cambridge along with Cartwright 
and Travers. As vicar of Cranbrook in Kent, Fenner had come into collision 
with Whitgift over subscription to his ‘three articles,’ in January of this 
same year, 1584. He now published  Counter-Poyson modestlie written 
for the Time, to make Answere to the Objections and Reproches, wherewith 
the Answerer to the Abstract, would disgrace the Holy Discipline of Christ. 
To defend the oflicial view Dr. Jobn Copcot next came forward. He 
also was a Cambridge man, already a University preacher, and destined 
for further promotion. While yet only a Fellow of Trinity he became 
Vice-Chancellor, and in 1587, on Burghley’s recommendation, he was elected

Crosse in 1584, wherein answeare ts made unto the autor of the Counter-poyson 
touching the sense of the 17. verse of the fifte chapter of the firsie to Timothye, 
Also an answere to the defense of the reasons of the Counter-Poyson for the 
maintenaunce of the Lidership, Printing, for the ‘Seekers of Reformation,’ 
had now become both difficult and dangerous, so that we do not hear of 
Fenner until 1586, when he succeeded in publishing 4 Defence of the Reasons 
of the Counter-Poysen, for maintenaunce of the Lldershippe against an

given in Waldegrave’s Rochelle reprint, ‘A Parte of a Register, and Copcot’s 
sermon is also in MS. at Lambeth—MS. 374,f. 115.) Here the discussion 
ceases, and hence Martin’s enquiry, which follows. 

(1) Martin refers to ‘books,’ because the ‘Second Replie’ of Cartwright, 
which remained unanswered by Whitgift, was divided into two sections. 
The first part was published in 1575, and the ‘ Rest of the second replie’ 
in 1577; that is, 13 and 11 years earlier, respectively, than the date at which 
Martin is now writing. He evidently reckons from the date of the second 
volume in saying ‘a dozen years almost’ had elapsed since Cartwright had 
published his reply. The Archbishop’s answer to this taunt is given in the 
Bishop of Winchester’s official reply to TaE HpisTnLn. ‘ Hee neuer thought 
them so necessarie to be answered, as the factious authors of the libel 
pretend. And of that opinion are not a fevve wise and learned men, that 
beare good will ynto the party [of the Bishops], and with all their hearts 
wishe that God woulde direct him to vse his good giftes to the peace and 
quietnesse of the Church. There is sufticient written already to satisfie an 
indifferent [impartial] reader, Hee that with indifferent minde shall read 
the ‘“ Answere” of the one, and the ‘ Replie” of the other, shall see great 
difference in learning betweene them.’—-Bp. Cooper’s Admonition, pp. 38, 39. 
This last sentence amuses the reader, secing that it was dictated by the 
Archbishop himself. Cooper, introducing the defence of Whitgift against 
Martin’s accusations, says, ‘I baue in these matters vsed the instruction of 
them, whom no honest mav may in Christian duetie suspect of vntrueth’ 
[that is, the accused prelates].—JZdid., p. 37. I scareely think that the 
impartial reader of to-day would regard Cartwright, Beza’s ‘most learned 
man in the world,’ to be inferior to Whilwift in scholarship; and certainly 
be was not his inferior in dialectics. See HAY ANY WORKE, p. 266.

Now, most pitifully complaineth Master Marprelate; 
desireth you either to answer what hath been written against 
the gracelessness of your archbishopric, or to give over the 
same, and to be a means that no bishop in the land shall be 
a lord any more. I hope one day her Majesty will either see 
that the Lord Bishops prove their calling lawful by the 
Word, or, as John of London prophesied, saying, ‘Come 
down, you Bishops from your thousands, and content you 
with your hundreds; let your dict be priestlike and not 
princelike, &c.’ quoth John Aylmer in the Harborowe 
[Harbour] of Faithful Subjects (x). But, I pray you, Brother 
John, dissolve this one question to your brother Martin. 
If this prophecy of yours come to pass in your days, who 
shall be Bishop of London? And will you not swear, as 
commonly you do, like a lewd swag, and say, ‘By my faith !’ 
‘ By my faith, my masters, this gear goeth hard with us’ (2). 

Now may it please your Grace, with the rest of your 
Worships, to procure that the Puritans may one day have a 
free disputation with you about the controversies of the 
Church, and if you be not set at a fiat non plus and quite

(2) The Bishop’s reply is at least amusing. ‘It is omitted [that is earlier

not diuine: but as all the rest is lewd, so surely herein he hath a lewde 
meaning. It is to be thought, that the Bishop wil take profite hereby, 
being a man that hath diligently read Plutarhe, De vtilitate capienda. ab 
inimico. If it bee an othe, as this gentleman hath censured it, itis not to be 
doubted, but that he wil amend it: but if it were lawful, as it may bee for

whether it be an othe: then in his wicked and malicious wishes for the

(x) Petherarn observes that a new edition of Zhe Harmony bad recently, 

at the time of his writing, issued from the press, edited by the Rev. Peter 

Hall. The substance of his interesting note on Thomas Thomas may be 

here quoted. He was, says Petheram, a fellow and M.A. of King’s College, 

Cambridge ; the author of a dictionary published under his name in 1588. 

On May 3rd, 1582, he was licensed printer to the University. The Stationers’ 

Company seized his press early in 1584-5; but on Feb, 11th of that year 

another licence was granted him. In 1586 The flarmony, translated out of 

the Latin, was printing there [at Cambridge], which for some reasons was 

{ not allowed to be printed in London. Whitgift sent his letter to the 

Vice-Chancellor ‘and Heads, to cause the book to be stayed in the printing.’ 

(Baker's MSS. Camb., Mm. i. 40 (27); Strype, Anmals, 3, 442.) It was, 

however, published the same year; perbaps, as Strype says, ‘after some 

teview or correction of it.? It has ‘alowed by publique authoritie’ on the 

title-page. That the ‘Bishops called them in’ may be collected from the 

following entry in the Stationers’ Register, A, quoted by Herbert, p, 1417, 
under the year 1589-90. 

‘Whereas all the seiz’d books were sold to Mr Byshop, be it 
remembered that 40 of them being Harmonies of the Churches rated 
at iis. le piece, were had from him by warrant of my Ld. of Cant. and 
remain at Lambeth, with Mr Doctor Cosins.’

beene from exacting the extremity, that offer hath bene made to the Dyars

And further to restore all, or to make sufficient recompence therefore, if by 
law it ought to be so, vpon the examination of the trueth of the case, And 
as for Martin's erronious iudgement, that this is theft, becing taken and 
claymed by right and lawe, as aforesayd, because the true owners are 
defeated (as hee saith) surely, hee might knowe if it were matter for his 
humor, that the Lavve vvorketh this in other cases, as in strayes proclaymed. 
and kept a yeere and a daye, according to the law, the propertie is altered, 
and transferred to the Lord from the true ovvner : so is it for stolen cattell, 
brought bona fide to the ouert [open] market : The first ovyners propertie is 
gone, and the buyer hath it: And so is it for waiued goods, as was this 
cloth. And to shewe that the sayde Bishop had not so great a desire to 
detaine the cloth as the Libeller hath presumed, hee often times asked an 
officer of his, howe it happened that the Dyars came not for it: for hee was 
ener ready, and yet is, to deliuer it to them, or the value thereof, if it 
prooue to be theirs. And thus much is to be answered to that matter,’— 
Bp. Cooper’s Admonition, 51—53. 

Martin’s comment on this tissue of legal quiddities and of damaging 
admissions is brief and to the point. The Bishop admits he has had the 
cloth, Martin gladly notes. Let him make restitution—Hay ANY WORKE, 
p. 278. Knowing the Bishop’s character, in the absence of information to 
the contrary, it is safe to conjecture that he never gave up possession. 

(2) The Bishops took the gossip about Dame Lawson.seriously. Whitgift 
Genies having threatened to send her to Bridewell. He says: 

‘This is a notorious yntrueth. For neither did hee, nor D, Perne euer 
heare (but of this libeller) that shee spake anie such wordes of him. But in 
trueth, as vvell for the immodestie of her tongue, vvherein she excelleth 
beyond the seemelinesse of an honest woman, as also for her vynwomanlie and 
skittish gadding yp, and downe to Lambehith, and from thence in company 
vnfit for her, without her owne husband, he threatened to send her to 
Bridewell, if she reformed not the same: which he meaneth to performe, if 
she continue her lightnesse. And yet Dame Lawson, so notorious 
for the vilenesse of her tongue, and other vnwomanly behauiour, 
is one of Afartin’s canonized saints: Quia quod volumus sanctum est, 
as Augustine said of their predecessors the Dunatists. It is likewise an 
yntruth, vvhich is reported in that page of her words spoken by [about] 
M. Shaller. Yor surely if she had yttered them, hee would haue sent her 
thither without faile. But Dame Lawsvn glorieth in her owne shame, 
and so do her teachers.—-Bp. Cooper’s Admonition, 39. See earlier, p. 38° 
HAY ANY WORKE, p. 268, note (2). 

(2) Dr. Andrew Perne, Master of St. Peter’s, Cambridge, and Vice- 
Chancellor, the ‘old turncoat,’ is referred to in the Mist. Jntro., p. 113, in 
connection with Whitgift. He was a special friend of the Archbishop’s and 
frequently visited Lambeth. He was a guest at Lambeth the following 
year, 1589, when he died. A Protestant controversalist under Edward VL., 
he became a zealous Papist under Mary, taking a foremost part, under the 
direction of Cardinal Pole, in the council which first condemned Bucer as a 
heretic and then ordered the exhumation and the incineration of his bones, 
For the proceedings in 7 Bucer, see Foxe’s Acts and Monuments (Pratt and 
Stoughton), 4th ed., vol, vill, pp, 258 ff.

(1) It will be noticed that Martin refers to ‘uncle Shory’; Whiteift calls 
him ‘ M, Shaller.” In that age it wag no uncommon thing for a man to 
have an alias. Mrs. Shaller was Whitgift’s aunt. Shaller was a verger at 
St, Panl’s. 

(2) Dr. Edward Stanhope was a civil lawyer who enjoyed a number of 
ecclesiastical preferments as well as valuabie civil appointments. He was 
Canon of York, 1572-91 ; advocate at Doctors’ Commons, 1576; Master in 
Chancery, 1577 ; Chancellor of the diocese of London, and Vicar-General of 
the province of Canterbury, 1583 ; Master of the commissioners of the Fine 
Office, 1589 ; rector of Terrington, Norfolk, 1589 ; Canon and Chancellor of 
St. Paul’s, 1591. He was M.P. for Marlborough, 1584-5, 1586-7. He was 
knighted in 1603, and died 16 March, 1607-8. See Foster’s Alumni O2on- 
densis, 1600-1714, ed. 1892, p, 1408. We are not surprised that a man, who 
secured from the ecclesiastical authorities such a liberal share of their 
patronage was a zealous persecutor of the Puritans, His name occurs in the 
various petitions sent during this period by imprisoned Nonconformists to 
the authorities. In the list of these prisoners preserved in the Harleian MS., 
6848 (reprinted by Arber in his Sketch, pp. 38 ff, where he wrongly names 
him Richard Stanhope), we have the entry, ‘ Quyntin Smythe taken from his 
labours, cast into the Dungeon with Irons, his bible taken firom him by 
Stanhoop.’ His name also occurs in the ‘ Brownist Petition,’ given * word 
for word’ in Wall’s A/ore Work for the Dean (London, 1681), p. 17; and 
reprinted in Hanbnry’s Memorials, I. 88. There he is included with Aylmer 
and Justice Young in ‘the persecuting and blood thirsty faculty.’ See 
below, p. 51. 

(3) Martin Marprelate is taken to task by the defenders of the hierarchy 
for treating the Dean as a teamster treats his horse. The truth, however, is 
that he is imitating the style of the Dean, who begins a sentence with 
‘ Sohow !’ or ‘Wo (who he writes) there!’ See his Defence, p. 76. 

(4) This work first appeared without the. author’s name, but in Walde- 
graye’s collection of reprints ‘A parte of a Register’ it is ascribed to Dudley 
Fenner. The title of the work will serve as a brief account of its contents. 
A Defence of the Godlie Ministers against the Slaunders of D{octor| Bridges, 
contayned in his answere to the Preface before the [ Learned] Discourse of 
Ecelesiasticall gouernement, with a Declaration of the Bishops proceeding 
against them. Wherein chieflie 1. The lawfull authoritie of her Maiestie ts 
defended by the Scriptures, her Lawes, and authorised interpretation of them, 
ta be the same which we haue affirmed against his cauilles and slaunders to the 
contrarie. 2. The lawfull refusinge also of the Ministers to subscribe is 
maintayned by euident groundes of Gods worde, and her Maiesties lawes,

(1) Bridges’ ponderous work bears the imprint ‘ Printed by John Windet 
for Thomas Chard.’ Jt would seem that the Dean supplied Chard with the 
‘copy,’ which he undertook to print and publish and gain what profit he 
could out of the sale. We can well understand that the dull, amorphous 
folio of fourteen hundred pages did not find a ready sale, and that to ease 
Chard of his loss a ‘protection’ had to be granted him. Whitgift takes 
notice of Martin’s hint that a second was necessary. ‘That which he calleth 
a Protection, Chard had from the Lords of her Maiesties Priuie Counsell, 
vpou charitable and good causes mouing their Lordships. —Bishop Cooper’s 
Admonition, 40. See HAY ANY WORK, p. 269. 

(2) For the Adstracte see note to the present Tract, supra, p. 20, note (2). 
The reference to the use of waste paper for stopping mustard-pots is not 
infrequent in the literature of the time. ‘Should we (as you) borrowe all 
out of others, and gather nothing of ourselues, our names should be baffuld 
[despised] on euerie Book-sellers Stall, and not a Chandlers Mustard-pot, 
but would wipe his mouthe with our wast paper.’—Pierce Penilesse, 
McKerrow’s Vash, I. 192. 

(3) There is a humorous reference to this old play in the EPIrome, p. 167 ; 
besides an earlier passing allusion on p. 140. Its full title is A Ryght 
Pithy, Pleasaunt, and Merie Comedie: Intytuled Gammer Gurtons Nedle: 
Piayed on Stage, not longe ago in Christes Colledge in Cambridge Made by 
Mr. S. Mr, of Art. It has been recently edited by Mr. Henry Bradley in a 
volume of Representative English Comedies (Macmillan, 1903), under the 
general editorship of Prof. C. M. Gayley, of the University of California, Most 
modern writers have followed one another in ascribing its authorship to 
Bishop John Still. But all we know of Bishop Still makes the ascription 
one of great improbability, and it is not surprising to find that the name of 
the bishop was not associated with the play earlier than Isaac HKeed’s 
edition of Baker's Dict. of the Stage (first published as Biographia 
Dramatica) in 1782. All the evidence that Reed had upon which to base 
his conjecture that Still was the author was an entry in the Bursar’s books 
at Christ’s College, Cambridge, that a play was acted in the house in 
1566-7, and that the only M.A. about that time whose name began with 
S was John Still. But Mr. Bradley in his Introduction to the play makes

The qualities of this book are many. Master Dean showeth 
himself to be very skilful in the learning of ob and sol. If

an excellent case for William Stevenson astheauthor. Allnsionsin the play 
itself indicate that it was written in the days of King Edward VI., and there is 
evidence that a play by Stevenson was acted at Christ’s in the year 1553-4. 
An extended article on the authorship from the pen of Dr. C. H. Ross (of 
Alabama College, Auburn, Ala., U.S.A.) appears in Anglia (Neue Folge, 
Band vii. Halle a. S., 1897), a German periodical devoted to English 
philology and literature. In this article Dr. Ross takes seriously the 
suggestion by Martin that Bridges was the author, and seeks to maintain it, 
accounting the ‘Mr. S.’ in the title to be a mere blind. This, he says, was 
the opinion. of Joseph Hunter, from whose MS. ‘Chorus Vatum Angli- 
canorum’ [Brit. Mus., MS. Addit. 24, 487] Dr. Noss quotes: ‘(The play) 
was however attributed by a contemporary [Martin Marprelate] to a quite 
different person. This was Dr. John Bridges. ... This is a testimony 
not to be despised. . . . It. is supported by the circumstance that Dr. Bridges 
did write in verse, another piece being attributed to him, namely, a sheet 
in rime of all the names attributed to the Lord in the Bible” There are 
few persons, surely, who would regard Bridges’ rhyming list of our Lord’s 
names in Scripture as a circumstance supporting the attribition to him of 
the authorship of Gammer G'urton’s Needle. It is true that Martin, who 
seemed to know all that there was to be known about the clergy concerned 
in the persecution of nonconforming Evangelicals, recorded this rumour 
tbat Dean Bridges was the author of the very unclerical comedy. But it is 
not correct to say that Martin gave credence to the rumour. His critical 
acumen was too keen not to see that the author of the Defence and of 
sundry other things is not to be eredited with writing a comedy, whose 
writer must have been a man of ‘wit and invention. Apart from Mr. 
Bradley’s strong case for Stevenson, no one, on the evidence of his known 
writings, could believe that Dean Bridges wrote the eelebrated drinking 
song in Gammer Gurton’s Needle, at the beginning of the second act. 
The verve of that old Bacchanalian stave lies entirely beyond Dean Bridges’ 
prosy gift.

those ‘whom otherwise in Christe, I] humbly acknowledge to be our own 
deare Brethren. And much gladlier, he continues, ‘the Lord knowes, 
would J be, to haue wholly objected my selfe (as before to my mediocritie 
I have endeuoured) against the publike aduersaries of Gods truth 
[i.e. the Papists].’

(1) The official reply to this accusation is instructive. ‘ Among other 
their reproches, they attirme of the bishop of Stochester, that hee presented

(as they call it), it is by lawe allowed, and hath bene done by other[s].’— 
Cooper's Admon., p. 63. It would have been better to offer no defence 
than to say implicitly that the charge may be true, save only in name. 
He did present himself to Wouldham in 1592 (D. WV. B.). Dr. John 
Young, Bishop of Rochester, was one of those who most completely 
sympathised with Whitgift’s ecclesiastical views and methods. He was 
what was called a ‘strong Churchman,’ and ‘had a noted antipathy to all 
Nonconformists.’ The see of Roehester being poor, he was allowed to keep 
some of his benefices in commendam. He was offered richer bishopriecs, but 
preferred to hold ou to Rochester and bis ‘commendams,’ especially when 
he could on occasion add to the number of the latter. 

(2) A Learned Discourse of Lcclesiasticall Government is the running 
headline of A Briefe and Plaine Declaration, concerning the desires of alt 
those faithfull Ministers that haue and do seeke for the Discipline and 
reformation of the Church of Ienglande. It was printed in London by 
Robert Waldecrave in 1584, and is to be distinguished from A Full and 
Plaine Declaration, published in 1674. See below, p. 61, note (x); Hist. 
Introd., 135 ff. ‘

sentence in the EPITOME, p. 161. ;

Take your spectacles then, and spell your own words, and

points. For, you affirm that a priest may have a lawful 
superior authority over the universal body of the Church. 
And you dare not deny her Majesty to be contained within 
the universal body of the Church. Therefore, to help you 
to spell your conclusion, you have written treason, if you 
will be as good as your writing. Your learned friend

(1) This interpretation was first suggested by Ireneus (Wer., v. 30, i.), 
and, although he did not formally adopt it, it had additional weight from 
the fact that Irenwus was an auditor of Polycarp, the disciple of the 
Apostle John. The numerical value of the Greek letters Aare:vos—in 
which the diphthong e represents the primitive method of writing 7 ong) 
—equals 666. It was an interpretation which naturally attracted the 
Protestant reformers (see Foxe, 4. J AL IV., 106), and continued to hold 
the chief place until the portentous name of Napoleon came to disturb the 
horoscopy and the arithmetic of students of the Apocalypse, who discovered 
that the name of the great Corsican could be made to produce the requisite 
666, But so respectable an authority as Dean Alford reverts to the earlier 
suggestion of Ireneus. ‘The Latin Empire, the Latin Church, Latin 
Christianity have ever been its [the Papal organization’s] commonly current 
appellations : its language civil and ecclesiastical has ever been Latin, its 
public services, in detiance of the most obvious requisite for public worship 
have ever been throughout the world conducted in Latin : there is no one 
word which could so completely describe its character and at the same time 
write the ancient and modern attributes of the two beasts, as this.—Comm. 
Rey. 1318. In the original the key-word is misprinted Latenivs.

(1) For Tarleton the comedian, sce brief reference in HAY ANY WORKE, 
p. 280, note (3). The cellar in the Bishop of London’s palace was a prison. 

(2) This is one of the most scandalous of the accusations made by Martin 
against Aylmer, the Bishop of London. And as the Bishop has taken pains 
to defend himself we had better give his reply at length. He says, ‘The 
Libeller obiecteth against the Bishop as a heinous fault, that of his Porter 
he made a Minister: which, al things considered, he thinketh that doing 
to be iustifiable and lawfully done, and not to Jacke example of many such 
that haue bene after that sort admitted, both since her Majesties comming 
to the Crown, by many good Bishops, and by sound histories Ecclesiastical, 
that vvhere the Church by reason of persecution or multitude of Hamlets and 
free Chapels which haue commonly very small stipends for the Minister, 
honest godly men, yppon the discretion of the Gouernors of the Church, hane 
and might be brought in to serue in the want of learned men, in prayer, 
administration of Sacraments, good example of life, and in some sort of 
exhortation. And this man ,therefore, when the Bishop founde him by good 
and long experience to be one that feared God, to be conuersant in the 
scriptures, and of very honest life and conuersation [conduct] : he allowed 
of him to serue in a small congregation at Padinglon, where commonly 
for the meannesse of the stipeud, no preacher coulde be had, as in many 
places it commeth to passe where the Parsonage is impropriat, and the 
prouision for the Vicar or Curat is very smal. And how this poore man 
behaued himselfe there, time and tryall proved him: for he continued in 
that place with good liking of the people 8. or 9. yeres, till he grew dull of 
sight for age, and thereby vnable for to serue any longer. [The examples 
of what the churches of Spain and Africa did in a time of distress are then 
quoted.] But Martin and his complices, hauing a desire to throwe out of 
the Church, the booke of common prayer, would rather haue the Churches 
serued by none, then by such as by prayer and administration of Sacraments 
should keepe the people together in godly assemblies. ... For most trué 
it is, that the said B. admitteth none to orders, but such as he himself doth 
examine in his owne person in poynts of Diuinitie, and that in the latin 
tongue, in the hearing of many: whereby it commeth to passe, that none 
lightly come at him, but such as be Graduats, and of the vniuersities.’—Bishop 
Cooper’s Admonition, pp. 58—55. It needed much assurance to pen this 
defence when multitudes of learned and pious ministers were being deprived, 
many because they could not take an unreasonable oath concerning the 
total contents of the book of Common Prayer, which neyertheless they were 
willing to use, and others because they ‘scrupled the garments’ as many of 
the Bishops secretly did. It added nothing to the episcopal defence that 
because the parochial income of the Church at Paddington was given away 
to some non-resident laymau, the living was only good enough to pension off 
Aylmer’s purblind gate porter. Martin’s remark on the Bishop’s defence is 
seen in HAy ANY WORKE, p. 278. ‘The circumstance was cited by the 
learned author of A Petition directed to her Majestie ameng the proofs that 
the Church needed further reformation (p. 6, § 4).

(1) The charge against Aylmer that he greedily cut down the timber on 
his episcopal estate assumed a more serious aspect than would be gathered 
from his defence. After denying that Madox [see p. 49] had called him 
Mar-elm, he says: ‘Here might be noted how Doctor Perne being at no 
meane mans table, and hearing of such slanderous rayling of felling of the 
Elmes at Fulham, he asked one of the company being an ancient lawyer, 
howe long the Elmes of Fulham had been felled. Said the Lawyer, some 
halfe yere past. Now truly saide Doctor Perne, they are marucilouslie 
growen in that time, for ] assure I vvas there vvithin these foure daies. and 
they seeme to be tvvo hundred yeares old. And maister Vicechamberlaine 
at her Maiesties being at Fulham, tolde the Bishop that her Maiestie 
misliked nothing, but that her Highnesse lodging was kept from all good 
prospects by the thicknesse of the trees. Lo, you may see hereby, that the 
Libeller to set out his Pasguill (lampoon], raketh all things by all reportes 
from all the Sycophants (?) in the world, and maketh no choice of man or 
matter, so ithat-it may serue his turne.—-Bishop Cooper’s Admonition, p. 56. 
The case against the Bishop came first before the Council in May, 1579. 
He was charged with felling and selling ‘three hundred timber trees at one 
time, and ai hundred at another, and some more besides at another, besides 
disposing of ‘a great number of acres of wood at divers times.’ There 
appeared sufficient truth in the accusation to justify the Lord Treasurer 
in openly blaming him and bluntly reminding him ‘that there was a bishop 
once displaced for such a deed.’ Aylmer did not rest easily under this 
reprimand and persisted that he had only felled ‘pollards, doated and 
decayed at the top,’ and of them not so many as reported. He acknowledged 
that in the three preceding years he had sold one hundred and twenty acres 
of wood, though not deriving so much money from the transaction as was 
alleged. The matter dragged on for the next six months, when further 
letters from the Queen were directed to the Bishop, making inquiries into 
‘the felling of those woods.’ ‘This ended at length with a restraint from 
her Majesty, that the Bishop hereafter should take down no more of his 
woods.’—Strype’s Aylmer, pp. 46—48. Much to his annoyance the charge 
was renewed in the year 1585 ‘by one Litchfield, a Court musician.’ The 
Lord Treasurer in this case ‘shewed himself . .. his greatest friend.’ 
Aylmer protested that he had not felled a single tree since the Queen’s 
injunction, but that the timber was being plundered by his woodwards. 
Litchfield soon after died and the matter dropped.-—/did., pp. 66, 67. But 
when Bancroft entered upon the see of London he roundly alleged ‘that 
Bishop Aylmer made £6,000 of his woods [say £30,000 of our money J, and 
left scarce enough to find the present Bishop yearly fuel. Zdid,, p. 128.

I will for this time leave this figure, and tell your Vener- 
able Masterdoms a tale worth the hearing. I had it at the 
second hand; if he that told it me added anything, I do 
not commend him, but I forgive him. The matter is 
this. A man dying in Fulham, made one of the Bishop of 
London’s men his executor. The man had bequeathed 
certain legacies unto a poor shepherd in the town. The 
shepherd could get nothing of the Bishop’s man, and there- 
fore made his moan unto a gentleman of Fulham, that 
belongeth to the Court of Requests. The gentleman’s 
name is Master Madox. ‘The poor man’s case came to be 
tried in the Court of Requests. The Bishop’s man desired 
his master’s help. Dumb John wrote to the Masters of 
Requests to this effect, and I think these were his words: 


‘My Masters of Requests, the bearer hereof, being my man, bath 
a cause before you. Inasmuch as I understand how the matter 
standeth, I pray you let my man be discharged the Court, and I 
will see an agreement made. Fare you well.’ 


The letter came to Master Doctor Dale. He answered 
it in this sort: 


‘My lord of London, this man delivered your letter. I pray 
you give him his dinner on Christmas day for his labour. And 
fare you well.’ 


Sabboth, which is Christ, hath saide, that the Sabboth was made for man,

The full force of the accusation of playing bowls on the Sabbath will be 
better understood, if we call to mind that the Book of Sports, the reading of 
which was such an offence to the puritan conscience, while regulating the 
recreations which the people might indulge in after tbe early service on 
Sunday was over, although it permitted ‘witson ales’ and ‘morris dances,’ 
rowdy and drunken affairs though they were, yet excluded bowls. ‘Withal 
probibiting all unlawful gaives to be used on Sundays only ; as bear-baiting, 
interludes, and at all times (in the meaner sort of people prohibited) 
bowling. Book of Sports, published May 24, 1618; quoted by Neal, 
History, 11., 105.

| Dumb John not speeding this way, sent for the said 
Master Madox. He came; some rough words passed on 
both sides. Presbyter John said Master Madox was very 
| saucy, especially seeing he knew before whom he spake; 
| namely, the Lord of Fulham. Whereunto the gentleman 
answered that he had been a poor freeholder in Fulham 
before Don John came to be Lord there, hoping also to be 
so when he and all his brood, my Lady his daughter and all, 
should be gone. At the hearing of this specch, the wasp got 
my Brother by the nose, which made him in his rage to affirm 
that he would be Lord of Fulham as long as he lived, in 
| despite of all England. ‘Nay, soft there,’ quoth Master 
| Madox, ‘Except her Majesty, I pray you.’ ‘That is my 
meaning,’ quoth (1) Dumb John. ‘ And I tell thee, Madox, 
thou art but a Jack to use me so.’ Master Madox replying 
said that indeed his name was John, and if every John were 
a Jack he was content to be a Jack. (There he hit my Lord 
over the thumbs.) ‘The Bishop growing in choler said 
that Master Madox’s name did show what he was; ‘ for,’ 
saith he, ‘thy name is Mad-ox, which declareth thee to be 
an unruly and mad beast.’ Master Madox answered again

most significantly show his qualities. ‘ For,’ said he, ‘you

twoo paire of cases, with certaine Pica Romane and Pica Italian letters with

aucthority, and contrary to the said Decrees had printed the said book. Yt

Letters in the Charterhouse (which presse JValdgraue himselfe soulde to one

of Sathan, the author of lyes. Charge them, O shamlesse man, with this 
matter, who are able to answere thee, and not the Archbishop, whome it

Admonition, p. 42. The point in the reference to the Warl of Arundel is

very honest and poore man, hauing maried also the vvidowe of a Printer: 
and hee did vvery vvell like and allovve of his placing by such as haue 
interest therein. Neither did hee ever heare, (but by this Libeller vvho hath 
no conscience in lying) that hee euer printed any such bookes. This I

oath denied, that he euer printed, either Zesus Psalter or Our Lady Psalter, 
or that he euer was any worker about them, or about any the like bookes. 
But the poisoned serpent careth not whome hee stingeth.—-Bishop Cooper's

(1) The brothers William and John Reynolds are noted for the fact that, 
one being a Papist and the other a Protestant, and being engaged in a 
controversy, they succeeded each in converting the other. William, once a 
Protestant, became a Catholic and settled at the English seminary at Rheims, 
Whitaker (Bellarmine’s ‘most learned heretic’) carried on a series of contro- 
versies with the champions of the Papacy. Among them he attacked Nicolas 
Saunders’ Forty Demonstrative Arguments to prove that the Pope was not 
Antichrist. W. Reynolds intervened in this discussion, and Martin asserts 
that in his book he spoke favourably of Whitgift. See Brook’s Lives, sub 
nom. W. Whitaker ; also THE MINERALLS, § 26, p. 191. 

(2) Whitgift replies, ‘It is no disparagement to receiue testimonie of a 
mans eduersarie: and therefore if Master feinolds haue given that com- 
mendation to his booke in comparison of others, it is no impeachment to the 
trueth thereof. I haue not seene Reinolds his booke: the Libel is so full of 
lies, that an honest man can not beleeue any thing conteined in it.’—Bishop 
Cooperx’s Admonition, pp. 43, 44. 

| (3) The Archbishop was wanting in a sense of humour when he permitted 
himself to reply gravely and with some heat to this piece of banter. He 
says, ‘That of the Spaniards stealing him away, Se. is foolish and ridiculons. 
I would the best Martinist in Ingland durst say it to his face before 
witnesse.—Jvid. He would evidently summon up all the power and dignity 
appertaining to his office to break this fly upon the wheel; provided only 
there be witnesses present. Pie

Amen. Ifyou are of God, then he is of the devil, as we 
think him to be. And so he being of the devil, will not you 
deprive him? Why should you suffer such a one to trouble 
the Church? Now, if he be of God, why is your course so 
contrary to his; and, rather, why do not you follow him,

we will think him to be of God, and go home with him, with 
gentler good will towards him than we came hither with - 
hatred ; and look you for a fall.’ His Grace, hearing this 
northern logic, was moved on a sudden, you must think, 
[and] promised to deprive Wigginton. And so he did, 
This Atkinson this winter, 1587, came up to London,
