(@) Giles Wigginton occupies a somewhat prominent place in the Marpre- 
late controversy, as is shownin the /Zist. Intro. He gave particular offence 
to the Archbishop by his personal demeanour towards him at his trial. 
Wigginton was something of what we commonly call a ‘character,’ and 
certainly destitute of all fear of the little Archbishop, as may be seen in his 
racy and sharp replies to him when under examination. Whitgift charges 
him with being ‘ malapert,’ a ‘langhing stocke’ as a youth, and increasingly 
foolish as man, ‘ridiculous euen to his owne faction.’ It was the best of 
the parishioners that witnessed against him. Whitsift calls his faults 
‘enormities,’ but it must be remembered that they were ecclesiastical and 
not moral faults. He also says that ‘the tale of Atkinson is a lowde, notori- 
ous, and knoven lie.’—Bishop Cooper’s Admonition, pp. 45, 46. Wigginton 
was one of those whom rumour suspected of being ‘Martin’ ; even Nicholas 
Tomkins, the servant in Mrs. Crane’s notorious Puritan household, where 
Wigginton was a welcome guest, gives him as one of the men charged with 
being the ‘great unknown.’ He was one of the first to receive copies of the 
Tracts, and if anyone knew their true author it was he. This question has, 
however, been sufficiently discussed ; here we have only to indicate his 
relations with Whitgift. He went to Cambridge under the patronage of 
Sir Walter Mildmay, the founder of Emmanuel College, a privy councillor, 
and under-treasurer to the Hxchequer. Wigginton'was chosen a fellow of 
Trinity, his own college, ‘though much opposed by Dr. Whitgift, then head 
of the House. And the opposition continued throughout Wigginton's 
career ; for it must be admitted that Whitgift showed something like genius 
in his alertness and unwearied persistence in hunting down all who opposed 
his ecclesiastical policy. Appointed to Sedbergh in the North Riding, 
Wigginton soon roused the opposition of the anti-Puritan party, so that 
Sandys, Archbishop of York, advises the Bishop of Chester not to allow him 
to preach in his diocese ; Sedbergh at the time was in the see of Chester. 
Three years Jater, in 1584, he is in London, being appointed, despite his 
Puritanism, to preach at St. Dunstan’s before the Judges. Hearing of the 
appointment on the day previous Whitgift sent his pursuivants, who only 
reached Wigginton’s lodgings in the middie of the night, to prohibit him 
from preaching ; and next day had him over to Lambeth to give an account 
of himself. Refusing the oath ex officio mero, by which he would be 
required to answer any question upon any subject in regard to any person, 
there being meanwhile no definite charge and no witnesses, Wigginton chose 
rather to go to prison. Fle was sent with much reviling from the Archbishop 
to the Gatehouse at Westminster, where he remained ‘nine weeks but a day.’ 
Whitgift did not long lose sight of him. Upon the information of one 
Hdward Middleton, ‘a man of profane character and a suspected Papist,’ 
Whitgift ordered Sandys to proceed to his deprivation. His living was then 
given to aman of immoral character pained Colecloth, and himself sent, under

May it please you to yield unto a suit that I have to your 
Worships. I pray you send Wigginton home unto his charge 
again. I can tell you it was a foul oversight [want of sight] 
in his Grace to send for him out of the north to London, 
that he might outface him at his own door. He would do 
his Canterburyness less hurt if he were at his charge, than 
now he doth. 

Let the Templars have Master Travers their preacher 
restored again unto them. He is now at | leisure to work 
your priesthood a woe, I hope. If such another book as the 
Heclesiastical Discipline was, drop out of his budget, it 
were as good for the Bishops to lie a day and a night in 
‘Little Ease’ in the Counter (z). He is an odd fellow in 


harsh circurostances, to Lancaster Gaol. One hundred and forty of his 
narishioners at Sedbergh, for hearing him preach and receiving the eucharist 
at his hands, after his deprivation, were excommunicated ; the harshness of 
the sentence being intensified by their having to travel from sixty to eighty 
riiles to attend their trial, The next year, 1586, Wigginton is again before 
the Archbishop, and, refusing the oath ex officio, and to accuse himself, he 
is sent to the White Lion in Southwark and there treated with great barbavity. 
Writing to Sir Walter Mildmay, his constant friend, he says the keeper ‘ by 
the archbishop’s strict charge so loaded me with irons, confined me in close 
prison, and deprived me of necessary food, that in about five weeks I was 
nearly dead.’ He further intreats Justice—he wants not mercy. ‘My old 
adversary the archbishop hath treated me more like a Z'urk or a dog than a 
roan or « Christian minister.’ He was released and again imprisoned in the 
Compter; released and again summoned to Lambeth (Dee. 6th, 1588) and 
sent to the Gatehouse, and is supposcd to have remained there till about the 
time he was restored to his benefice at Sedburgh in 1592. A letter is extant 
addressed by him to Burghley and dated April 4th, 1597, and is referred to 
in the article on Wigginton in the D. V. G. It is included in the Lansd. 
MSS. (vol. $4, art. 105). Its purport is to commend to the favourable judg- 
ment of the Lord Treasurer the proposal to found a seminary where young 
men could be trained to meet Roman Catholic priests in controversy. He 


“accompanies the letter by a MS. of his own entitled ‘A Paire of Ridles 


against the Philistynes of Rome.’ This is the last date we have in connec- 
tion with bis life. The date of his death is not known. He wrote in prison 
s work on Predestination, and also ‘Giles Wigginton his Catechisme’ 
(London, 1589, 8°). Strype also says he wrote The fool's bolt, also entitled 
A father’s Exhortation toa young Courtier, which he describes as a ‘halting 
yhyme, roaring lewdly’ both at Church and State. He also informs us that 
reatly influenced ‘the madman Hacket.’ But all Strype’s references are 
strongly biased by the misrepresentations of Cosins’ work on the Hacket 
Sonspiracy. See especially Brook’s Lives, 1. 418, Cooper's Ath. Cuntab., ti. 

G Neal’s Hist. of the Puritans (1822), i. 377, Platt’s fist. of Sedburgh 
(4876), p. 17, and art. in the D. M. B, already cited.

following an argument; and you know he hath a smooth

(1) Walter Travers was a leading figure in the ecclesiastical controversies 
of the day. Owing to the rigorous terms of subscription imposed upon 
candidates, Travers was ordained at Antwerp, after the manner of the foreign 
Reformed Churches. He gained some notoriety by his opposition to Hooker, 
then Master of the Temple, on which foundation also Travers was Lecturer, 
one of the few posts he could fill conscientiously, as it demanded no subscrip- 
tion to Whitgiit’s intolerant Articles. The benchers, strongly supported by 
Burghley and others, would have elected Travers to the mastership ; but 
Whitgift, with unfailing alertness, had the Queen apprised of Travers’ various 
disqualifications. The fact was, however, that Travers had already shown 
his friends the impossibility of his accepting the position. ‘I declined the 
place, because I could not subscribe to my lord of Canterbury’s late articles, 
which I would not do for the mastership of the Temple, or any other place in 
the church,’—Travers’ Supplication (1612), quoted by Brook, Lives, ii. 326, 
See Hooker’s Leeles. Pol, (Oxford, 1850), vol. L1., pp. 654—695 ; Strype’s 
Whitgift,i. 340 ff. ; and the article inthe D. V, B. with the reff. there given. 
Travers made an important contribution to the religious controversy of his 
age by writing (anonymously) Jeclesiastice Discipline et Anglicane 
Heclesie ab illa aberrationis, printed at Rochelle, cir, 1574. This gave 
literary form and order to the scattered and unco-ordinated ideas of a large 
section of the Puritans; the discipline advocated being that of presbyter 
(elder), deacon, and teacher, with a rigorous moral supervision of the life of 
the church—a work which was not attempted by Field and Wilcox’s 
Admonition to Parliament, nor by Cartwright in the extended controversy 
with Whitgift arising out of its publication ; and still proceeding in 1574. 
The plan and perspective of the contributions of Cartwright and Whitgift to 
that memorable controversy were too entirely determined by the exigencies 
of debate. An English translation, furnished with a brief preface, both 
generally ascribed to Cartwright, of Travers’ Latin treatise appeared imme- 
diately, under the title—a,literal translation of the original—A yull and plaine 
declaration of Leclesiasticall Discipline, &c., the book referred to by Martin 
as the Leclesiastical Discipline and ascribed by him to Travers as a matter 
of course ; a foreign quarto in black letter (? secretary type) printed, so the 
British Museum catalogue conjectures, at Middleburg in Zeeland ; pp. xii. 
+ 194. This is the volume, as already stated (see above, p. 36), which, owing 
to the mistake, originally, of Petheram, has been mistaken by all subsequent 
writers for A Briefe and plaine declaration, the little tract which by its 
popularity called forth Dean Bridges’ ponderous reply, and, consequentially, 
the Marprelate Tracts. See fist. Zntrv., 135 et seq. Travers, being silenced 
by Whitgift, was for some years provost of Trinity College, Dublin. He 
died, after 1624, in obseurity and poverty. A full account of him is given 
in Brook’s Lives, ii, 314-330. In his bibliography Brook gives the Latin 
title of Travers’ work under the shortened form of De disciplina Keclesiastica 
ex Dei verbo descripta, the form under which the same volume is described 
in the XX XI. Articles exhibited against Cartwright before the High Com- 
mission (Sept. Ist, 1690) and there ascribed to him as author, “Brook falls 
into error in identifying the volume he thus describes with the Directory, 
said to have been found in Cartwright’s study after his decease, which came

Will you not send Master Wyburn to Northampton, that 
he may see some fruits of the seed he sowed there sixteen or 
eighteen years ago. Thatold man Wyburn hath more good 
learning in him, and more fit gifts for the ministry in his 
little toe, than many braces of our Lord Bishops. Restore 
him to preaching again ; for shame ! (rz) 

Master Paget shall be welcome to Devonshire. He is 
more fit to teach men than boys. JI marvel with what face 
a man that had done so much good inthe Church, as he. did 
among a rude people, could be deprived (2). 


into use when the authoritative use of the Book of Common Prayer was 
abolished under the Commonwealth. He could not have realised that the 
Directory was only an affair of 24 pp. 4to, printed in large type. 

(1) It is almost certain that Martin is here guilty of a confusion of names, 
or else Waldegrave misread Martin’s ‘ copy’ and the error escaped his reader, 
Penry. ‘Oldman Wyburn,’ the deprived Northampton minister, I cannot 
doubt should be ‘Old man Merbury,’ whose history fits Martin’s allusions 
exactly. He was one of those at first suspected of being Martin himself; 
but the above reference would not favour that supposition [see Hist. Lntro., 
p- 281}. On the other hand, there is a well-known Puritan leader, Dr. 
Percival Wyburn, a prebendary of Westminster, and vicar of St. Sepulchre’s, 
Holborn, who was sequestered by Parker in 1564. He was esteemed ‘a 
peaceable Nonconformist,’ and had some liberty accorded him of preaching. 
Conyented again in 1571, he made great efforts to satisfy the prelates, but 
was obliged,to ‘scruple the vestments.’ Later he was a preacher at 
Rochester, and in 1581 was nominated one of the divines who were to dispute 
with the Papists. He was subsequently suspended, but towards the close of 
his life was a preacher at Battersea. In the fairly full record we have of 
the main incidents of his ministry he does not appear to have had any con- 
nection with Northampton. Penry, acting as Martin’s press reader, would 
not know the ecclesiastical history of the town sixteen years before he first 
came to reside in it. See Brook’s ives, ii. 169. A letter defending the 
position held by his school, contained in A Parte of a Register, is ascribed to 
DL [ector] W[yburn]. 

(2) Eusebius Paget (or Pagit) was a singularly unfortunate member of the 
Puritan party. He has already been referred to as one of those suspected of 
havinga hand in thejTracts. //ist. Intro. p. 283. Suspended, not for the first 
time, by Bishop Scambler in 1574, he got into further trouble, and into 
prison eventually, for taking part in Presbyterian worship. He, however, 
on obtaining his release, obtained the living of Kilkhampton in Devon on 
the understanding that certain details of the Book of Common Prayer, which 
he was willing to use generally, should not be urged against him. After 
doing good work among the ‘rude people,’ he excited the envy of one 
Farmer, a curate of Barnstaple, who laid information against him.— Second 
Part of a Register, pp. 570, 574. Paget was in due course deprived ; vainly 
complaining that he was promised by his ‘ordinary’ not to be pressed in 
regard to certain ceremonies ; that the Bishops and others used greater 
liberties in altering and omitting the Prayer Book order; adding, which was 
certainly pertinent to the oceasion, that the church was not provided with a 
copy of the Prayer Book. The irregularity of the proceedings of the High 
Commission was a more serious matter and is referred to elsewhere, Mean-

Briefly, may it please you to let the Gospel have a free’ 


course, and restore unto their former liberty in preaching 
all the preachers that you have put to silence. And this far 
is my first suit. 

My second suit is a more earnest request unto you, that 
are hinderers of the publishing of [it, that] the Confuta- 
tion of the Rhemish Testament by Master Cartwright may 
be published. A reasonable request, the granting whereof, 
I dare assure you, would be most acceptable unto ali that 
fear God, and news of woeful sequel to the Papists. For 
shall I tell you what I heard once from the mouth of a man 
of great learning and deep judgment, who saw some part of 
Master Cartwright’s answer to the said Rhemish and 
traitorous raffody (x)? His judgment was this: that Master 
Cartwright had dealt so sooundly against the Papists, that 
for the answering and confuting of the adversary (that) one 


work would be sufficient alone. He | farther added that 2 


the adversary was confuted by strange and unknown reasons, 


while, having a wife and numerous family, Paget set up a school, only to 
be driven presently from this last resource by an order demanding subscrip- 
tion from schoolmasters. His illustrious kinsman Admiral Sir John Hawkins, 
who throughout sympathised with him, saved the family from starvation. 
After Whitcift’s death Paget obtaincd the living of St. Anne and St. Agnes, 
in Aldersgate, London, which he retained to the close of his life in 1617. 
While a youth at Oxford he broke his arm—it is said in carrying the pyx in 
a religious procession—and ever after signed himself ‘Lame Euseb. Paget.’ 
Many writers have inferred that he was halt. But the maimed in arms and 
legs were alike called lame. Stowe in his Survey of London, describing 
sridewell, speaks of machines which could be worked by prisoners: ‘lame in 
the arms.’ It indicates how little acquainted with the facts were the literary 
hacks hired by the Bishops to write down Martin, that they describe Paget 
as ‘polt-foot... Thomas Nash, whom we assume to have written Zhe Returne 
of the renowned Caraliero Pusquill, states that ‘Paget marshalleth the way 
with a couple of great clubbes, one in his foote, another in his head.’ Sig. 
B. iii. vers. The author of dn Almond for a Parrat (cd. Petheram, pp. 12, 
34) improves the occasion to describe how Paget with ‘one [leg] and a 
stump’ ran away from Houns[{low] on the publication of a gross scandal 
against him. But the limp and the scandal are the inventions of the scribe. 
See Neal’s (ist. of the Puritans, i. 354 ; Brook’s Lives, ii. 253 ; aud the article 
in the D. V. B. Greenfield (see margin) may be Martin’s substitute for 
Farmer. Strype (Annals, II., App. ii. 617) refers to a ‘Mr. Greenfield of 
Deyon’ who was denounced by a notorious coiner as one of his clients. 
Paget is mentioned in THE JUST CENSURE, p. 584.

(1) The publication of the Reims New Testament with its bold scholar- 
like opening treatise and its controversial notes seemed a standing challenge 
to the evangelical reformers. The chief mover in its production was William 
Allen, afterwards a Cardinal, who in Mary’s time was principal of St. Mary’s 
Hall, Oxford and Canon of York. He fled to Douay, and being made a 
Canon at Reims, he had the English college moved for the time to that 
city. Therein conjunction with Gregory Martin and Richard Bristow (or 
Bristol) he produced in 1582 an English translation of the Vulgate New 
Testament. (The whole Bible, bearing the imprint ‘ Doway’ was published 
twenty-seven years Jater.) Queen Elizabeth is said to have invited Beza to 
confute it, who referred her to one of her own subjects better fitted for the 
task—Thomas Cartwright. Walsinghain, who forwarded £100 towards the 
cost, and other eminent persons urged Cartwright to undertake the work ; so 
also did a number of Cambridge scholare. In,1590 he writes that ‘he had 
received commaundment from the Archbishop to deale no further in it’ 
He completed the work, but it was not printed until after his death in 1618. 
Permission to print Thomas Cartwright’s reply was one of the Conditions of 
Peace stipulated by Martin. See below, par. 2, p. 80.

(1) Dr. Arber has calculated this date to be Feb. 20th, 1588. If this 
were correct it would be a puzzle to know what work of Penry’s, issued at or 
about this date, could be described as ‘a supplication and a book to the 
Parliament.’ The only books at all answering to this description which 
might be considered in this connection are The Aquity of an Humble 
Sup plication, and the tract commonly calied the Supplication [A View of some 
part of such publike wants fc.| The first of these must have been published 
in March, 1587 (see the interesting note by the Rey. Principal A. Gordon, 
Cong]. Hist. Socy’s Z’ransactions, May, 1905); and the second we know 
definitely to have been published early in March, 1589. The one date is too 
early and the other too late to suit Dr. Arber’s calculation. It seems clear 
to me, however, on carefully examitiing the facts, that he is mistaken. In 
the year 1587 Easter Day fell as late as April 16th, so that any one speaking 
of the Lent of that year, though generally following the Old Style, would 
mean the year 1536-7 and not the year 1587-8. The‘ begianing of Lent’ is 
nota precise statement of date, and ina year in which Easter Sunday fellafter 
the middle of April we need not seek a difference between the Old Btyle 
and the New. The book was doubtless the quity.

(2) The examination, here referred to, confirms the lastnoie. For Penry’s 
first appearance before Whitgift was in consequence of the publication of his 
first book, The dguity of an Mumble Supplieation. The circumstauces are 
given by Penry himself, in 7h’ Appelation, where he tells us that the 
equity, which ‘was ajlowed to be printed by publike authority, and had 
been presented to Parliament (before March 23rd 1587), was called in by 
order of the Archbishop. The wardens of the Stationers’ Company, Bishop 
and Denham, seized Penry himself and 500 copies of his book. And here 
we may profit by Arber’s careful research showing that the wardens’ year of 
office expired July 10th, 1587. See Penry’s Appelation, pp. 3 {%, which is 
helpfully quoted and the dates elucidated by Arber in his Introductory 
Sketch, p. 68; Brook’s Lives, ii. 49; D. N. B. Mr. Sidney Lee’s article on 
‘Penry,’ in which there are one or two conjectural dates to be amended. It 
may be convenient to the reader to quote the texts above referred to. 
Rom. 10!4—‘How then shall they call on bim in whom they have not 
believed ? and how shall they believe in him whom they have not heard? and 
how shall they hear without a preacher?’ 1 Cor. 17,—‘It was God’s good 
pleasure through the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.’ 
Ephes. 13, ‘Tu whom ye also, having heard the word of truth ..... having 
believed, ye were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise.’

Evans. An honourable personage, Ambrose Dudley, now 
Exar] of Warwick—-and long may he be so, to the glory of

in the singular love he bare to the town of Warwick, would

he offered the subscription which the Statute requireth ; 
Wwhereunto men may subscribe with a good conscience. The 
Earl sent him with his letter to his Gracelessness of Cant.,

am sure if he be [that] Ambrose Dudley, the noble Earl of . 
Warwick, whose famous exploits both in peace and war this 0, monstrous

true John Canterbury, if I were a nobleman, and a Councillor

Leicester, was all that Martin claimed on his behalf. After the suspicion 
that fell upon him in connection with the affair of Lady Jane Grey had 
subsided, he rose steadily into favour. He marricd a daughter of the Karl of 
Bedford, with the smiles of Elizabeth upon his nuptials. He was a Privy 
Jouncior and a Knight of the Garter, and filled various offices of dignity 
in the State. Nevertheless he could not appoint Master Evans to the 
vicarage of Warwick. But he consistently favoured the ‘reformers.’ Itwas 
by his countenance that Cartwright became Master of the Hospital at 
Warwick. The Archbishop contended that he was‘ maliciously reported.’ 
‘Tle rejected [Evans] for lacke of conformitic to the orders of the Church. 
Tf hee haue done him any wrong thereby, the lawe is open, hee might haue 
had his remedy. That honourable person mentioned by the Libeller, I am 
sure, accepted of his answer. And I knowe that according to his honourable 
disposition, hee thinketh himselfe greatly abused by the libeller in this point.’ 
—Bishop Cooper’s Admonition, pp. 47, 48. Thelaw to which Whitgift invited 
his victims to have recourse was not so open as he assumes for the sake of his 
defence. And the question of subscription, as is shown elsewhere, was com- 
plicated by a demand that it should include articles framed by Whitgift him- 
self. The civil lawyers were convinced of the gross illegality of his position, 
contending that the High Commission could only deal with cases where the 
ecclesiastical laws as constitutionally enacted were alleyed to be broken and 
disregarded. Whitgift hid himself behind the Queen’s prerogative. ‘The 
acts of the ‘Commission for Ecclesiastical purposes’ as provided by the 
terms of its appointment were the Queen’s acts. So that the invitation to 
seek a remedy at law was something of a cruel mockery.

(rt) It is no wonder that John Bullingham, Bishop of Gloucester, is the 
object of Martin’s aversion. Avaricious and infcrior men as most of the 
Elizabethan bishops were, yet one wonders how even in such an age John 
Bullingham could have become a bishop in a Protestant Church, Parker’s 
judgement of him, and also Ayliner’s, leads us to believe that the extraordinary 
storics told of him by Martin Marprelate were substantially true. The 
‘massmonger’ went into exile during Udward’s reign, but returned at the 
accession of Mary, and was duly furnished with a nuinber of benefices. At 
the accession of Klizabeth he chose at first to refuse to subscribe and lost 
them. But in a year or two he thought better of it, and soon managed vo 
recoup himself, chiefly by the gift of lucrative offices by his kinsman Bishop 
Nicholas Bullingham. In 1581 he became Bishop of Gloucester. He was 
an ignorant and incapable man. Further references to him will be found in 
the present Tract, pp. 90f. 97; Hay ANY WORKE, pp. 217, 230.

as showing that he had the second Marprelate Tract in his possession when 
writing his Admonition. The words appear in THE HPrromy, p. 150, where 
they are rightly ascribed to the Bishop of London. They cecur in Aylmer’s 
notorious Harborowe for Iaithfull Subiectes, where he divides the English 
bishops of Mary’s reign into two sorts—one, prudent (like Harpagus, who, 
having an eye tothe future, spared the child of Mandanc), not appearing to 
clamour against the martyrs ; the other, ‘desperate Dicks’ that went for- 
ward sparing none. See Sigg. i 2 vers. E 3 Gvhich Martin notes as pp. 28, 
29). 

For the faith of the English Church Cooper can refer with pride to Dean 
Nowell’s Cutechism, also to Bishop Jewel’s Apology, with Peter Martyr’s 
Kpistle prefixed, where he also speaks ‘for many other learned men in the 
Church of Tygure { Zurich], and other places.’ Bishop Jewel in his Apolegy 
condemns the corruptions of Rome, or such as have been brought in by 
heretics ancient and modern. Cooper also shows that the Uneglish Con- 
fession is based upon an interpretation of Seripture which has the witness 
and consent of ‘all the learned antiquity ... for certaine hundred years,’ 
Thus the Councils noted support the ‘foure principal Articles’ concerning 
Q) ‘the person of Christ in his Godhead and manhood ; (2) ‘the grace and 
benvefite of Christ, the beginning whercof riseth from the eternal loue of God 


- toward vs, and from the free election to redemption’ through ‘the dispensa- 


tion of Christ once offered vpon the crosse, by effectual calling wrought by 
the holy ghost in preaching of the gospell, by our justification, sanctification 
and the gift of perseverence and continuance in the faith, thereby in the 
end to obtain resurrection and eternall life’ ; (8) ‘the true Catholique Church 
(a matter of great importance even at this day)’; (4) ‘the Sacrament of the 
Lordes Supper.’ Cooper contends that in these articles, chosen as chief 
examples, the Church’s Confession had ‘the testimonie and consent of the 
Primitine Church and the ancient learned Fathers. From which Consent 
they should not depart, either in doctrine or other matter of weight, vnlesse 
it so fal out in them, that we be forced thereto, either by the plaine wordes 
of the Scriptures, or by cuident and necessary conclusions following upon 
the same, or the Analogie of our faith.”—Bishop Cooper’s Admonition, 64--68 
[printed 69 in error]. 

The latter part of this note is given at this length that the evangelical 
character of the Elizabethan Church as defined by its Confession may be 
seen. And the above is an authoritative statement made by representative 
men. It is out of these materials, and the like, that the modern Anglican 
has to construct the continuity of his Catholic Church.

Jingland should have these wretches for the eyes thereof, 
that would have the people content themselves with bare 
reading only, and hold that they may be saved thereby 
ordinarily. But this is true of our Bishops; and they are 
afraid that anything should be published abroad, whereby 
the common people should learn that the only way to 
salvation is by the word preached. 

There was the last summer, a little Catechism made by 
Master Davison(1) and printed by Waldegrave. But 
before he could print it, it must be authorised by the 
Bishops, either Canterbury or London. He went to 
Canterbury to have it licensed. His Grace committed it to 
Doctor Neverbegood (Wood) (2); he read it over in half a 
year. The book is a great one of two sheets of paper. In 
one place of the book the means of salvation was attributed 
to the Word preached; and what did he, think you? He 
blotted out the word ‘preached’ and would not have that 
word printed, so ascribing the way to work men’s salvation 
to the Word read. ‘Thus they do to suppress the truth and 
to keep men in ignorance. John Cant. was the first father 
of this horrible error in our Church; for he hath defended 
it in print, and now, ss you have heard, accounteth the

Whitgift, i. 587, 588. In reply to the accusation Whitgift writes, ‘How 
Danisons Catechisme was allowed, or bow long in perusing, I know not: 
some paultrie pamphlet belike it is, like to that busie an vniearned Scot, now 
termed to be the author thereof. D. Wood is better able to judge of such 
matters, then either Dawison, or any Martinist that dare be knowen.’— 
Bishop Cooper’s Admonition, 49. 

(2) This Doctor Wood is no doubt the same person as the Doctor Wood 
of All Souls’ referred to in Tuk PRorEsTAtyon, p. 12, note (4). 

(3) Gabriel Goodman, a native of Ruthin, N. Wales, He graduated at 
St. John’s, Cambridge, received in 1560 a prebend at Westminster, and 
the following year, Sept. 23rd, was elected Dean. He was sometime 
chaplain to Sir William Cecil; he was also the translator of 1st Corinthians in 
the Bishops’ Bible. He served on the High Commission. Persistent but 
yain efforts were made to get him elected to the episcopate. Archbishop 
Parker thought him too severe for the see of London, but afterwards recom- 
mended him for the vacancy at Norwich. Later Aylmer recommended him 
to the see of Rochester, and another effort was subsequently made by 
Whitgift to get him appointed to that dignity. Ob. 1601, aet. 73. Bee

(1) This son-in-law was Dr. Adam Squire, of whom Strype gives a very bad 
account as a spendthrift and of loose habits, asserting that it was to cover 
his own infidelity that he vamped up a discreditable story about his wife 
and a certain Knight. Aylmer saw the Knight, and on hearing his protesta- 
tion of innocence, had the interview with Squire which led to fisticufis and 
a bloody nose. Strype rather admires the doughty character of the Bishop, 
who, notwithstanding his small stature and his advanced years, was mot 
afraid to come to blows with a younger man. It is fair to add that Squire 
protested that he was wrongly accused by his father-in-law. But we may 
agree with Strype that he was ‘somewhat fantastical,’ seeing that he insisted 
upon preaching his own wedding sermon. His name being Adam, he 
took for his text the words‘ Zé is not good for Adam to be alone” See 
Strype’s Life of Aylmer, pp. 122—126, 192. : 

(2) Concerning the complaint that the Apocrypha was ordered to be 
bound up with the Bible, which gaye so much offence to the ‘Seekers after 
Reformation’ for so many generations, Whitgift admits that,‘ He gaue 
commandement in deede, and meaneth to see it obserned.’ His action he 
defends by alleging that no church from the beginning of Christianity down 
to the Reformed Churches of that time had ever donc otherwise. He says— 
falling unconsciously into writing in the first person—'T knowe there is 
great difference betweene the one and the other : yet all learned men haue 


‘from the beginning, giuen to the Apocrypha authoritie, next to the 


Canonical! Scriptures. .. . A foule shame it is, and not to be suffered that 
such speeches should be vitered against these bookes, as by some hath bene : 
enough tocauscignorant people to diseredite the whole Bible.’—Bishop Cooper's 
Admonition, p. 49. There is a passing reference to the subject in Hay any 
WoREE, p. 277. It is also the theme of the 34th point in THE MINERALLS. 

Cartwright in his controversy with Whitgift maintains the Puritan con- 
tention. T'ohim Whitgift replies that the Apocryphal books ‘ may as well be 
read in the Chursh as counted portions of the Old and New Testament : and, 
forasrauch as there is nothing in them contrary to the rest of the Scripture.’—-

But you see, my worshipful Priests of this crew, to whom 
J write, what a perilous fellow Master Marprelate is. He 
understands all your knavery, and, it may be, keeps a 
register of them. Unless you amend they shall all come 
into the light one day. And you, Brethren Bishops, take 
this warning from me. Ifyou do not leave your persecuting 
of godly Christians and good subjects, that seek to live 
uprightly in the fear of God and the obedience of her 
Majesty, all your dealing shall be made known unto the 
world. And J shall (z) be sure to make you an example to 
all posterity (2). You see I have taken some pains with 
you already; and I will owe you a better turn and pay it 
you with advantage, at least thirteen to the dozen, unless you 
observe these conditions of peace which I draw between me 
and you. .For I assure you, I make not your doings known 
for any malice that I bear un | to you, but [for] the hurt s8 
that you do unto God’s church. Leave you your wicked- 
ness, and Pll Jeave the revealing of your knaveries. 


Conditions of Peace to be inviolably kept for ever between 
the reverend and worthy Master Martin Marprelate, Gentle- 
man, on the one party, and the reverend fathers, his brethren, 
the Lord Bishops of this land. 

1. In primis, the said Lord Bishops must promise and 
observe, without fraud or collusion, and that as much as in 


Whitgift’s Defense of the answere, p.721. T. C. easily replics that a book 
answering to this qualification could be compiled after the manner of gather- 
ing elezant and moral extracts from classical authors, from the writings of 
Cato, Theognes, and Cebes. And adds further that in the Apocrypha ‘there - 
be many places partly, plainly contrary to the Holy Scripture ; partly, 
frivolous, and ynworthy to be read.’—Yhe Second replie of T. Cebit. 
p. £400. In the celebrated Conference held at Lambeth on Dec. 10th, 
1584, and the day following, at which Martin insists that Dr. Sparke gave 
the Archbishop the xon-plus, the question of the Apocrypha was discussed. 
Whitgift then asserted that ‘the books called the Apocrypha are indeed parts 
of the holy seripture.’ ‘ You cannot,’ said he to Travers, ‘shew that there is 
any error in the apocrypha.’—Brook’s Lives, Ji. 317. For his argument 
with Underdown at a celebrated Conference held at Lambeth Dec. 5th, 
1583, see “Hist. Intro. 72, note.

2. That hereafter they admit none unto the ministry but. 
such as shall be known both for their godliness and learning, 
to be fit for the Ministry; and not these neither without 
cure [a pastoral sphere], unless they be college ministers of 
either of the Universities ; andin no case they suffer any to 
be non-residents. And that they suffer Master Cartwright’s 
answer to the Rhemish Testament to be published. 

3. That neither they nor their servants, viz. their arch- 
deacons, chancellors, nor any other of the High Commission, 
which serve their vile affections, urge any to subscribe con- 
trary to the statute 138 Eliz., and that they suspend or 
silence none, but such as either for their false doctrine or 
evil life, shall show themselves to be unworthy the places 
of ministers; so that none be suspended or silenced either 
for speaking, when their text giveth them occasion, against 
the corruptions of the Church; for refusing to wear the 
surplice, cap, tippet, &c.; or, omitting the corruptions of 
the Book of Common Prayers, as churching of women, the 
cross in baptism, the ring in marriage, &c. 

4. That none be molested by them or any their aforesaid

munion; or, for resorting on the Sabbath, if they have not

5. Lastly, that never hereafter they profane excommunica- 
tion as they have done, by excommunicating alone, in their 
chambers, and that for trifles ; yea, before men’s causes be 
heard. ‘Chat they never forbid public fasts; molest either 
preacher or hearer, for being present at such assemblies. 
Briefly, that they never slander the cause of Reformation, 
or the furtherers thereof, in terming the cause by the name 
of Anabaptistery, schism, &c., and the men Puritans, and 
enemies of the State.

shall be bound to keep inviolably on your behalf. And I, 
your brother Martin, on the other side, do faithfully promise 
upon the performance of the premisses by you, never to make 
any more of your knavery known unto the world. And, 
howbeit, that I have before threatened my brother Bridges 
in the cause of his superior priest, and your antichristian 
callings, notwithstanding, I will write no more of your 
dealings, unless you violate the former conditions. 

The conditions, you see, are so reasonable [that] I might 
bind you to give over your places, which are antichristian. 
But I do not, lest men should think me to quarrel, and seek 
occasions for the nonce to fall out with my Brethren. There- 
fore, I require no more but such things as all the world will 
think you unworthy to live, if you grant them not.. And 
this I do the rather, because you should not, according to 
your old fashion, say that my Worship doth for malice lay 
open your infirmities ; nay, I have published not one of your 
secret faults. What you have not blushed to commit in the 
face of the sun, and in the justifying whereof you yet stand, 
these things only have I published. The best servants of 
God, I know, have their infirmities. But none of them 
will stand in the maintenance of their corruptions, as you 
do; and that to the dishonour of God, and the ruin of His 
Church. You must either amend, or, shortly, you will 
bring our Church to ruin. There|fore, it is time that 40 
your dealings were better looked unto. 

You will go about, I know, to prove my Book to be a libel; 
but I have prevented you of that advantage in law; both by 
bringing in nothing but matters of fact; which may easily be 
proved, if you dare deny them; and also, in setting my name 
to iny Book. 

Well, I offer you peace upon the former conditions, if you 
will keep them; but if you violate them, either in whole or 
in part—for why should you break any one of them ?—then 
your learned brother Martin doth proclaim open war against 
you, and intendeth to work your woe two manuer of ways,

For his stomach could not be at all strengthened with the 
drink he got abroad. But better were a man not to feel bis

Therefore, at length, Sir Geoffrey bethought him of a feat 
whereby he might both visit the alestond(z), and also 
keep his oath. And so he hired a man to carry him upon 
his back to the alehouse. By this means he did not go, 
but was carried thither, whereunto he made a vow never 
to go. 

IT doubt not, in my visitation, but to get a hundred of 
these stratagems; especially if I travel near where any of 
the vicars of hell are; as in Surrey, Northampton, and 
Oxford shires. And I would wish the pursuivants, and the 
Stationers, with the Wolf, their beadle, not to be so ready to

Oh, well bowled! When John of London throws his 
bowls he will run after it and cry, ‘Rub, Rub, Rub,’ (x) 
and say, ‘ The devil go with thee.’ 

But what think you shall be handled in my Lambethisms ? 
Truly this: I will there make a comparison of John Whit- 
eift’s Canterburiness with John Bridges’s Lambethisms. To 
speak in plain English, I will there set down the flowers of 
errors, Popish and others, wherewith those two worthy men 
have stuffed the books which they have written against the 
cause of Reformation, in the defence of the government of 
Bishops. J] have in this book as you shall see, gathered 


decidedly interesting, and are here quoted with Arber’s few elucida~ 
tions :— 
Item, paid the xth of June [1588] for a Dynner when bothe the 
wardens [F. Coldeck and H. Conneway], master Watkyns, and 
master Denham, and the Pursuyvant, with John Wolf, Thomas 


Strange, and Thomas Draper wente to Kingston, liijs ijd/ 
Item the same mens supper at Kingston xs vjd/ 
Item to the poore woman whose house was serched at 

Kingston ijs/ 

Item the boatehire to and from Kingston xiiijs/ 
Item for twooe lynckes the same tyme viijd/ 


Item for a warrant for Penrye and Northe goinge and 
comminge by water [i.e., to Lambeth Palace] to get 


yt signed lijs viijd/ 
Item paid to Watson the Pursuyvant the same tyme for 
goinge to Kingston XS 


With this happy extract before us we sce vividly the whole expedi- 
tion. The pleasant river journey up to Kingston ; the trouble with the 
housewife whose house they uselessly ransacked, and who had to be 
solaced with a couple of shillings ; the dinner before the search, and the 
more substantial supper after ; then the late journey home with the 
links to light their way. Martin adds the completing touch of comedy— 
‘knave Draper’ cast into limbo for being the occasion of spending so 
much money on a false scent. After such a foolish jollification some one 
had to suffer to save the face of the Company. 

John Wolf, or Woolfe, the Beadle of the Stationers’ Company, men- 
tioned above, is described by Strype as a ‘notcd London printer,’ who, 
this same year, 1588, printed an official account of the Armada, trans-~ 
lated from the Spanish. Later on he printed Bancroft’s Dangerous 
Positions (1593). Sea above, p. 53, note (1), for some references to Wolf’s 
career. 

(1) A rub is an obstacle in the track of the bowl, or an inequality 
in the ground, either impeding the progress of the bowl, or giving a bias 
to its direction. Thus in Richard I1., iii. 4. 38, we read : 

‘1 Lady. Madam, we'll play at bowls. 
‘Queen. "Twill make me think the world is full of rubs, 
And that my fortune runs against the bias.’ 
Aylmer having given too much speed to his bowl, cries after it, ‘rub, 
rub, rub’; but when it rolled heedlessly on beyond the ‘jack’ the pro-~ 
fane little bishop could only ery, ‘The devil go with thee.’

some flowers out of John of London’s book; but my 
Lambethisms shall be done otherwise, I trow. 

And now if it please you of the Convocation-house to 
hear of any of the former books (1), then break the league 
which I offer to make with you; but if you would have my 
friendship as I seeke yours, then let me see that you per- 
secute no more; and especially, that you trouble none for 
this book of mine. For this must be an especial article of 
our agreement, as you know. And Dean John, for your 
part, you must play the fool no more in the pulpit. 

We will end this matter with a pretty story of a certain 
mischance that befel a bishop’s corner cap; as followeth. 
Old Doctor Turner—I mean not Doctor Perne, the ‘ Old 
Turner ’—had a dog full of good qualities. Doctor Turner, 


haying invited a Bishop to his table, in dinner-while, called 


his dog, and told him that the Bishop did sweat. (You 
must think he laboured hard over his trencher.) The dog 
flies at the Bishop and took off his corner-cap—he thought 
belike it had been a cheesecake—and so away goes the dog 
with it to his master. Truly, my masters of the Clergy, I 
would never wear corner-cap again, seeing dogs run away 
with them. And here endeth the story. 

May it please you that are of this House, to tell me the 
cause, when you have leisure, why so many opinions 


44and | errors are risen in our Church, concerning the 


ministry and the joining with preaching and unpreaching 
ministers ? ‘J'o tell you my opinion in your ear, I think 
it to be want of preaching; and J think your Worships to 
have been the cause of all the stir. Some Puritans hold 
readers for no ministers; some hold you our worthy 
Bishops for little better than fair parchment readers; and 
say that you haye no learning. Now, whether readers be 
ministers or no, and whether our Bishops be learned or no, 
I would wish you, Brethren Bishops, and you Brethren 
Puritans, to make no great controversy; but rather labour

that all evil ministers may be turned out of the Church. 
And so, I hope there should be a speedy end of all those 
questions between you. For then, I doubt not, that ‘lord 
bishops,’ whereat the Puritans so repine, should be in a 
fair reckoning within short space; even next to the door, 
save the dog. And I see that you, Bishops, are well 
towards this promotion already. And truly, though the 
Puritans should never so much as repine at the matter, yet, 
T tell you true, Iam glad you are so esteemed among men. 
And for mine own part, I think my Masters, that many of 
you, our Lord Bishops and clergymen, are men very 
notorious for their learning and preaching. 

And hereof, under Benedicite between you and me (the 
Puritans may stand aside now) I will bring you some 
instances. Jirst, his Grace and my Lord of Winchester 
have been very notable clerks ever since Master Doctor 
Sparke set them at a non plus, some of their Honours being 
present, in the Conference between him and Master Travers 
on the Puritans’ side, and the two Archbishops and the 
Bishop of Winchester on the other side. Doctor Spark’s 
argument was drawn from the corruption of the translation 
of the 28th verse of the 105th Psalm in the Book of Common 
Prayer, and the contrariety of the translations allowed by 
the Bishops themselves. For in the Book of Common 
Prayer you shall read thus, ‘And they were not obedient 
unto his word’; which | is a plain corruption of the text. 45 
In other privileged English translations it is, ‘ And they were 
not disobedient unto his word’; which is poourding to the 
verity of the original (1).

By the way, ere I go any further, I would know with 
what conscience either my Brother Cant. or any else of our 
Bishops can urge men to allow such palpable corruptions 
by subscribing unto things mere [simply] contrary to the 
Word? Here also I would show, by the way, and I would 
have all my sons to note, that their uncle Canterbury’s 
drift, in urging subscription is not the unity of the Church, 
as he would pretend, but the maintenance of his own pride 
and corruption, which would soon come to the ground, if the 
Word had free passage. And therefore he proveth the same, 
by stopping the mouths of the sincere preachers thereof. 

For, if the unity of the Church had been his end, why 
hath not he amended this fault in all the books that have 
been printed since that time; which now is not so little as 
three years; in which time many thousand of Books of 
Common Prayer have been printed. If he had other busi- 
ness in hand than the amending of the Book of Common 
Prayer, why had he not, nay, why doth he not, leave urging 
of subscription until that be amended? Can he and his 
hirelings haye time to imprison and deprive men, because 
they will not sin by approving les upon the Holy Ghost— 
which things they cannot nor could not choose but commit, 


but if of the signs and wonders, that Moses and Aaron did before Pharaa, 
or of Moses and Aaron themselucs, then is it on the other side trne, 
that they were obedient to his commandement. This might have satisfied 
any learned and peaceable Divine, and pacified their immoderate con- 
tention against the booke of common praicr. This was then, and is now, 
the answer to that frivolous obiection, and this is the Nonplus that 
the Libeller vaunteth of. More modestie might have become D{octor] 
Sparke, and the reporter, euen conscientia sue imbecillitatis, in that 
conference.’—Bishop Cooper’s Admonition, p. 60. This quotation is chiefly 
interesting as an illustration of Whitgift’s rule never to admit himself 
to be in error, Rather than do that he delivers himself of this piece of 
sophistication. The text followed by the Book of Common Prayer is no 
doubt corrupt, The correct text was followed in the translations of 
the Scriptures allowed to be read. Avoiding altogether the points 
raised by Dr. Sparke, and now by Martin, he suggests that both read- 
ings, though contradictory, are correct. At the Conference he suggested, 
while acknowledging his ignorance of Hebrew, that there might be an 
ambiguity in the original. He was however assured by ‘ravers and 
Sparke that no such ambiguity could be alleged. (Vide Brook as 
above.) Yet all holders of bencfices were compelled to subscribe to Whit- 
gift’s Articles and to declare that the Book of Common Prayer coniained 
nothing contrary to the Scriptures,

whosoever will [subscribe] or have subscribed unto the Book 
and Articles—and can he have no time in three or four years 
to correct most gross and ungodly faults in the print, whereof 
the putting out of one syllable, even three letters, dis, 
would have amended this place? But it lieth not in his 
Grace to amend the corruptions of the Book. Belike it 
heth in him to do nothing but sin, and to compel men 
against their consciences to sin, or else to bring extreme 
misery upon them. If it lay not in him, yet he might have 
acquainted Parliament—for there was a Parliament since 
the time he knew this fault—with the | corruptions of the 
Book. 

And I will come nearer home to him than so, in the Article 
concerning the Government, whereunto men are urged to sub- 
scribe. You must, say the Articles, protest that there is no- 
thing in the ministry of the Church of England, that is not 
according to the Word ; or, to such like effect they speak. 
I say that I cannot subscribe unto this Article; because, 
contrary to the express commandment of our Saviour Christ, 
and the examples of His Apostles, there be ‘ Lords’ in the 
ministry. Or, such as would be accounted ministers, will 
also be called and accounted ‘ Lords,’ and bear civil offices. 
The words of Christ are those: ‘The kings of the Gentiles 
reign over them, and they that bear rule over them are 
called gracious lords; but you shall not be so’ (xz) (Luke 
22%) J say that out of this place it is manifest that it 
is utterly unlawful for a minister to be a ‘Lord’; that is 
for any ‘Lord Bishop’ to be in the ministry. And there- 
fore I cannot subscribe unto that Article which would have 
me justify this to be lawful. 

Now I will cease this point, because I doubt not but the 
Articles of Subscription will be shortly so made out of 
fashion, that the Bishops will be ashamed of them, them- 
selves; and if no other will take them in hand, I’ll turn 
one of mine own breed unto them, either Martin Senior, or 
some of his brethren.

To go forward. His lordship of Winchester is a great 
clerk; for he hath translated his Dictionary called Cooper’s 
Dictionary verbatim out of Robert Stephanus’s Thesaurus ; 
and ill-favoured, too, they say (1). But what do I speak of 
our Bishops’ learning? As long as Bishop Overton, Bishop 
Bickley, Bishop Middleton, the Dean of Westminster, 
Doctor Cole, Doctor Bell, with many others are living, I 
doubt me whether all the famous dunces be dead, And if 
you would have an ill-sample of an excellent pulpit-man, 
indeed, go no further than the Bishop of Gloucester now 
living; and in him you shall find a plain instance of such a 
one as I mean (2). 

On a time, he, preaching | at Worcester before he was 
bishop, upon Sir [St.] John’s Day, as he traversed his 


"matter and discoursed upon many points, he came at the 


length unto the very pith of his whole sermon, contained in 
the distinction of the name of John; which he, then showing 
all his learning at once, full learnedly handled after this 
manner. ‘John, John; the grace of God, the grace of 
God, the grace of God. Gracious John; not graceless 
John, but gracious John. John, holy John, holy John; not 
John full of holes, but holy John.’ If he showed not 
himself learned in this sermon, then hath he been a dunce 
all his life. 

In the same sermon, two several Johns, the father and 
the son, that had been both Recusants, being brought 
publicly to confess their faults, this worthy Doctor, by 
reason that the young man, having been poisoned beyond 
the seas with Popery, was more obstinate than his father, 
and, by all likelihood, he was the cause of his father’s per- 
verseness, with a vehement exclamation, able to pierce a

making a Dictionary, or rather but for mending that which Sir Thomas 
Eliot had made before.’

note (1), and Bishop John Bullingham, ante, p. 70, note (1).

The Puritans, it may be, will here object, that this worthy 
man was endued with these famous gifts, before he was a 
bishop ; whereas since that time, say they, he is not able to 
say ‘bo!’ to a goose. You weigh this man, belike, my 
masters, according to the rest of our Bishops. But, I 
assure you, itis not so with him. For, the last Lent, in a 
sermon he made in Gloucester town, he showed himself to 
be the man that he was before. For he did in open pulpit 
confirm the truth of his text to be authentical, being the 
prophecy of Isaiah, out of the Book of Common Prayer ; 
which otherwise would, it is to be feared, have proved 
apocrypha. His text was, ‘A child is born unto us,’ 
which, after, he sweetly repeated very often as before, to the 
great destruction (r) and admiration of the hearers, saying, 
‘Achildis born. Achildis born. A child is born, | unto 48 
us. This,’ saith he ‘is proved, you know, where in that 
worthy verse of the Book of Common Prayer [it says] Thy 
honourable, true, and only Son.’ Afterwards, repeating the 
same words again, ‘A child is born unto us, a child is born 
unto us,’ ‘Here,’ saith he, ‘I might take occasion to com-

very manifest, that the Prophet here speaketh, By Thy 
nativity and circumcision. What! should I prosecute the 
condemnation of this man, as though other [of] our Bishops 
and-pulpit-men have not as commendable gifts as he ?

Some kind of ministry, ordained by the Lord, was temporary, 
saith he. As, for example, the Mosaical priesthood, and the 
ministry of apostles, prophets, &c. But the ministry of pastors, 
doctors, elders, and deacons was ordained by the Lord ; therefore, 
it was temporary (2). 


Alack, alack, Dean John, what have you done now! The 
Puritans will be o’ the bones of you too bad, for this kind 
of arguing. And they will reason after this sort

Church and become orderly, when he coulde profit nothing with him, sent 
him againe to the Sessions to the Lord Maior and the Indges. After 
they had dealt with him, and could finde at his hands nothing but rail- 
ing, they sent againe to the Bishop, and he finding him in vnspeakable 
disobedience to her Maiestie and her Lawes, offered him the oath, which 
he contemptuously and spitefully refused. Which being certified accord- 
ing to order, hee was sent to the Queenes bench, and was condemned, 
and thereupon sent to prison. And this is that wonderful tragedie 
wherin this fellow so greatly triumpheth, wishing belike (as his whole 
Libel] seemeth to desire) that no malicious schismatike should be 
punished for mouing sedition in the Jande.’—Bishop Cooper’s Admonition, 
59, 60. Strype, who repeats Aylmer’s defence, adds a pitiful plea from 
Benison to the ‘Lords of the Council’ that they would move the 
Queen to order Aylmer to pay him some compensation for his bad usage ; 
charges for close imprisonment for 30 weeks in the Clink, the cost of a 
man to sue for his deliverance, the loss of his ‘household stuff,’ his 
valuable books, and the ruin of the freehold which was his only support. 
From this it would appear as if he bad only been separated from his 
wife, after being married a fortnight, for a period of between six and 
seven months. Aylmer flippantly dismisses the question of the duration 
with a ‘I cannot tell how long.’ But the man in the dark and foul 
inner dungeon of the Clink counted off thirty weeks. This however 
was only a small part of Benison’s imprisonment. Strype might have 
observed the discrepancy between his statement that Benison was sent 
to King’s Bench Prison, and the poor man’s petition that he had been 
for 80 weeks in close imprisonment in the Clink, The fact is that he was 
cast in King’s Bench Prison in 1579 and was only released in 1584. It 
would not have been uncustomary for him to have been transferred 
from one prison to another several times during those years. In a peti- 
tion which he addressed to the Queen and Council Benison accuses 
Aylmer of trying to separate his wife from him, and piteously complains 
that he is half-dead. The Lords of the Council took a righteous view of 
the case and warned Aylmer that if Benison proceeded to law he 
would obtain damages for false imprisonment ‘which would touch your 
lordship’s credit,’ and advised that the Bishop should pay a reasonable 
sum as compensation for the wrong he had done Benison. (Tunis is 
dated Noy. 14th, 1584, and is signed by Burghley and ten others of the

tunity. The Catholic narrative reports her to have said, ‘ Master Doctor, 
i will have nothing to do with you or your doctrine.’ So she died an 
‘unrepentant Papist.’ This was on Feb. 8th, the day of her execution 
at Fotheringay Castle. Meanwhile Blizabeth had gone through her de- 
testable piece of hypocrisy, weeping copiously, protesting her out- 
raged feelings, and finally persecuting Davidson, her unfortunate secre 
tary, for doing that which with her authority he had done ; that is, for 
transmitting the signed and sealed death warrant to the Council for due 
execution. When, in the beginning of August, the body of Mary was 
transferred with considerable ceremonial pomp from Fotheringay to 
Peterborough for interment, we know beforehand the type of sermon 
we are to expect, in continuation of the whitewashing process. Martin 
has given us a vital extract. The defence of Wickham by Cooper in his 
Admonition, p. 64, is characteristic and noteworthy. ‘What [Bishop 
Wickham’s] wordes were I have forgotten, and yet I heard them deliuered 
by a learned man that was present... but they were nothing sound- 
ing to that which the Libell layeth downe. And the person considered at 
whose funerall hee preached, he could not with comelinesse speake less 
in her commendation than he did.’ The apologist is not moved by 
simple charity for the dead. He is evidently of the mind that the 
Almighty must think twice before He damn a person of Mary’s quality. 
Martin’s date, Aug. 2nd, 1587, is wrong. The body was removed from 
Fotheringay on Monday, July 31st, and deposited in a vault overnight, 
The ceremonious obsequies, including Bishop. Wickham’s sermon, took 
place the next day, Tuesday, Aug. Ist. An interesting account of the 
execution and funeral, based on the State Papers, is given in Mr. Ewald’s 
volume, Studies Restudied, pp. 154—163, See also Yudor Tracts, ed. 
by A. F. Pollard, 475 ; S. P. Dom. Mary Queen of Scots, Aug. Ist, 1587. 
White (Eliz. Bishops, 285.) supplies the information that an account 
of the Bishop of Lincoln’s sermon exists in MSS., Ashmolean, 836, 
86. :

[St.] Asse [Asaph] is this priest. But you, Dean Catercap,

8. Some men that | break the law of God are traitors to 51 
her Majesty; as, for example, the Jesuits. But all our 
Bishops are ‘some men that break the law of God’— 
because they continue in unlawful callings. Ergo, by your 
reason, they are traitors to her Majesty. But I deny your 
arguments ; for there be many breaches of the law of God, 
whereof they may be guilty, and yet no traitors. 

9. Some men that will not have their lordsbips, and 
their callings, examined by the Word, are limbs of anti- 
christ. As, for example, the Pope and his cardinals. But 
our Lord Bishops are ‘some men which will not have their 
lordships and their callings tried by the Word.’ There- 
fore, they are limbs of antichrist. 

10. Some men would play the turncoats with the Bishop 
of Gloucester, Doctor Reynolds, Doctor Perne (I will let 
Doctor Goodman, Abbot of Westminster, alone now) (2). 
But all the Lord Bishops, and you, Brother Catercap, are 
‘some men.’ Hrgo, you would become Papists again. 

11. Some men dare not dispute with their adversaries, 
lest their ungodly callings should be overthrown, and they 
compelled to walk more orderly. But our Bishops are 
‘some men.’ Trgo, they dare not dispute, lest their ungodly 
calling and places should be overthrown. 

12. Some men are thieves and soul murderers before 
God; as, for example, all nonresidents. Hvery Lord 
Bishop is a nonresident. Ergo, he is a thief and a soul 
murderer before God. 

(1) This must be William Hughes, one of the most unworthy of 
Elizabeth’s bishops, ‘probably the greatest pluralist the Hnglish Pro- 
testant Church has ever known’; when consecrated he held the arch- 
deaconry and ten other benefices, all in commendam, and afterwards 
increased the number by six ; sixtcen in all and nine of them sinecures, 
He leased the episcopal manors on long terms to his wife, children, sisters, 
and cousins.—White’s Eliz. Bishops, 196 £. 

(2) See ante, p. 73, note (3) for ref. to Goodman ; and p. 56, note (1), for

changed his creed as often as the change in the sovereign’s creed made it 
politic.—See Hist. Introd, 113.

13. Some men are become apostates from their ministry, 
sinners against their own consciences, persecutors of their 
brethren, sacrilegious church robbers, withstanders of the 
known truth, for their own filthy lucre’s sake; and are 
afraid lest the Gospel and the holy discipline thereof should 
be received in every place. But our Bishops are ‘some 
men.’ Therefore, by your reason Master Doctor, they are 
become apostates from their ministry, sinners against their 
own consciences, persecutors of their brethren, sacrilegious 
church robbers, and withstanders of the known truth, &e. 

14. Some priest is a pope; as, for example, that priest 
which is Bishop of | Rome is a pope. But his Grace of 
Cant.is ‘some priest.’ Therefore, Master Bridges, by your 
manner of reasoning, he is a pope. 

You may see what harm you have done by dealing so 
loosely. I know what I shall say to these Puritan reasons. 
They must needs be good, if yours be sound. Admit, their 
syllogisms offended in form as yours doth ; yet the common 
people, and especially Dame Lawson, and the gentlewoman 
whose man demanded of her, when she sat at the Bishop of 
London’s fire, ‘Why, Mistress, will you sit at Caiaphas’s fire?’ 
—will find an unhappy truth in many of these conclusions, 
when, as yours is, most false. And many of their propositions 
are tried truths, having many eye and ear witnesses living. 

Men, when commonly they dedicate books unto any, enter 
into commendations of those unto whom they write. But 
I care not; an I owe you, my Clergy- Masters, a commendation 
and pay you, when you better deserve it. Instead thereof 
I will give you some good counsel and advice, which, if you 
follow, I assure you, it will be the better for you. 

First, I would advise you, as before I have said, to set 


at liberty all the preachers that you have restrained from 


preaching; otherwise it shall be the worse for you. My 


reason is this. The people are altogether discontented for 
want of teachers ; some of them already run into corners (1), 


(1) That is, persecution is driving the reformers to hold secret meet- 
ings. And how wise and farseeing is the observation that follows, that

and more are like, because you keep the means of know- 
ledge from them. Running into corners will breed Anabap- 
tistry; Anabaptistry will alienate the hearts of the subjects 
from their lawful governor. And you are the cause hereof. 
Ana will not her Majesty then, think you, require the hearts 
of her subjects at your hands, when she shall understand 
that they are alienated, as God forbid, they should [be], 
from her, by your means? Yes, I warrant you. 

And if they should put up a supplication unto her 
Highness that their preachers might be restored unto 
them, I doubt not but they should be heard. I can 
tell | you she tendreth (t) the estate of her people, and 53 
will not discourage their hearts, in casting off their suits, 
to maintain your pride and covetousness. You were then 
better to set the preachers at liberty, then to suffer your 
cruelty and evil-dealing to be made known unto her. For 
so they shall be sure, J doubt not, to prevail in their suit, 
and you to go by the worse. And try if her Majesty be 
not shortly moved in this suit. Toit, my Masters, roundly ! 
—you that mean to deal herein, and, on my life, you set the 
Prelates in such a quandary as they shall not know where 
to stand. 

Now, Masters Prelates, I will give you some more counsel ; 
follow it. Repent, Clergymen, and especially, Bishops. 
Preach faith, Bishops, and swear no more by it. Give 
over your lordly callings; reform your families, and your 
children: they are the pattern of looseness. Withstand 
not the known truth, no longer. You have seduced her 
Majesty and her people. Pray her Majesty to forgive you, 
and the Lord, first, to putaway your sins. Your government 
is antichristian; deceive the Lord no longer thereby. You 
will grow from evil to worse unless betimes you return. 
You are now worse than you were twenty-nine years ago. 
when the law is made the vehicle of injustice and oppression, it generates 
lawlessness. 

(1) The verb to tender used in its now obsolete sense, to care for, to 


pity. ‘To see a prince in want would move a miser’s charity. Our 
western princes tendered his case.’—Fuller (Webster’s Dict.).

Write no more against the cause of Reformation ;~ your 
ungodliness is made more manifest by your writings. And 
because you cannot answer what hath been written against 
you, yield unto the truth. 

If you should write, deal syllogistically ; for you shame 
yourselves when you use any continued speech; because 
your style is so rude and barbarous. Rail no more in the 
pulpit against good men; you do more hurt to yourselves 
and your own desperate cause, in one of your railing 
sermons than you could in speaking for Reformation. 
ror every man that hath any light of religion in him 
will examine your grounds, which, being found ridiculous, 
as they are, [he] will be decided, and your cause made 
odious. 

Abuse not the High Commission, as you do, against the 
best subjects. The Commission itself was ordained for 


54. very good purposes; but it | is most horribly abused by 


you, and turned clean contrary to the end wherefore it was 
ordained. Help the poor people to the means of their 


salvation, that perish in their ignorance. Make restitution 


unto your tenants, and such as from whom you have wrongly 
extorted anything. Usurp no longer the authority of making 
ministers and excommunication. Let poor men be no more 
molested in your ungodly courts. Study more than you do, 
and preach oftener; favour nonresidents and Papists no 
longer; labour to cleanse the ministry of the swarms of 
ignorant guides, wherewith it hath been defiled. Make 
conscience of breaking the Sabbath by bowling and tabling ; 
be ringleaders of profaneness no longer unto the people ; 
take no more bribes; leave your simony; favour learning 
more than you do, and especially godly learning. Stretch 
your credit, if you have any, to the furtherance of the 
Gospel. You have joined the profanation of the magistracy 
to the corruption of the ministry: leave this sin, Allina 
word, become good Christians; and so you shall become 
good subjects and leave your tyranny. And, I would advise 
you, let me hear no more of your evil dealing.

HISTORICAL NOTE 


1. THe Eprroms is similar in form to Tum Eristiz ; both, 
as earlier explained, forming a complete work. It is a small 
Elizabethan quarto of 46 pages (without pagination, sig. 
A.—G. 1. vers.), printed in Waldegrave’s handsome black letter 
—the ‘ Dutch letter’ of the contemporary documents. Of the 
four Marprelate Tracts printed by Waldegrave, which were 
all in this type, the present work shows most care. It has 
an ornamental line at the head of the title-page, and at the 
beginning of the text. It is furnished with an analytical 
headline to each page (in Roman type). Four sizes of the 
b. 1. are used in the title-pages of Tum Iipistin and Tx 
Iépitoms, and a still smaller size in the marginal notes. 

2. The press left East Molesey late in October, 1588—- 
when Mrs. Crane reached her house on the first of November 
it had been removed—and was taken to Fawsley House by 
Jeffs, a farmer of Upton, a small village lying a mile west 
of Northampton. Permission had been granted by Sir 
Richard Knightley to John Penry to print certain books on 
the religious condition of Wales, so Six Richard avers. Ie 
gave Penry his gimmal-ring as authority to the keeper, 
Lawrence Jackson, to receive the press and its appurte- 
nances. Tradition locates the press in the nursery of the 
house, a room in an octagonal tower in the centre of the 
frontage of the building as it now exists, and supposed to 
have been reached by a spiral staircase. ‘The room has, 
however, vanished in subsequent alterations to the structure. 
The incident of the gimmal-ring gives colour to the state- 
ment of Sir Richard Knightley that he was away from home 
when the press arrived, and knew very little of its activity. 
Tue Errromz was probably ready for circulation before 
the end of November. It is referred to in the trial of Giles 


106 HISTORICAL NOTH 


Wigginton on Dec. 6th. For full particulars of the travels 
of the secret press and the circumstances attending the 
printing of Tue Epvrromn, see the Historical Introduction, 
pp. 156 ff. 

3. ‘Tue Eprrome professes to give a critical summary of 
the First Book of Bridges’ Defence. That bulky volume 
could only be dealt with piecemeal by those who were 
driven to write and print and sell their works with the 
utmost secrecy. The question, we may repeat once more, at 
issue between those secking a further evangelical reformation 
of the Church and those who had accepted preferment under 
Elizabeth, was one of polity, of the external government of 
the Church. Martin states it specifically in the present 
Tract (p. 126). The Puritans held that the form was 
definitely given in the New Testament and could not be 
altered; the Bishops and their supporters held that it could 
be arranged to meet the needs of the time, and that Hpisco- 
pacy, as organised under Elizabeth, was such an expedient 
form. 

4. But though formally a critical review of the first of 
the sixteen books into which Dean Bridges divided his 
Defence, ‘Tus Epriroms is almost more noteworthy as giving 
the widest publicity to Bishop Aylmer’s notorious book, An 
Harborowe for Faithfull Subiectes, published by him at Stras- 
burg in 1559; and.expressly as a reply to John Knox’s 
First Blast of the Trumpet against the monstrovs regiment of 
Women, which was issued the previous year. Aylmer’s 
defence of the ‘regiment of women’ was not of the sort to 
win the favour of Elizabeth. His denunciation of the 
avarice and corruption of bishops, however, was so outspoken 
that on that account alone his preferment in Elizabeth’s 
establishment was blocked for many years. He reached at 


' last the Metropolitan see, and became one of the most money- 


loving ecclesiastics of his age. We can therefore easily 
comprehend his wrath against Marprelate for giving fresh 
and wide currency to the fierce reforming views which he 
entertained in the days of his poverty and exile.

HISTORICAL NOTE 107 
is 
Much of Tre Errroms consists of an ironical defence of 
the Episcopate and its supporters against the attacks of their 
‘Brethren’ the Puritans. Martin can occasionally give 
them also a thrust in the ribs; for some of them were over- 
hasty in their disavowal of Martin because of his wit and 
banter, and some because of his daring personal attack upon 
Archbishop Whitgift, ‘The Puritans are angtie with me’ 
he notes in the present Tract (p. 118). His rejoinder to 
them is in eftect— 
You are angry with me for jesting. But J am com- 
pelled to jest; for my opponent Dr. Bridges is an 
unconscious humourist. Moreover, Tam a plain man 
and speak the truth. Why should you object to that ? 
You object to a Pope at Rome, why then should you 
not object to a Pope at Lambeth ? 

5. As our reprint does not correspond page for page with 
the original, it was impossible to retain the analytical head- 
lines in their places. We have therefore adopted Petheram’s 
convenient device, and printed them in italics in the margin.

O READ OVER DR. JOHN BRIDGES, FOR IT IS 
A WORTHY WORK: 


Or an Epitome of the 


First Book of that right worshipful volume 
written against the Puritans in the defence of 
the noble Clergy, by as worshipful a priest, John 
Bridges, Presbyter, Priest, or Elder, Doctor of 
Divility, and Dean of Sarum. Wherein 
the arguments of the Puritans are 
wisely prevented (1), that when 
they come to answer Mr, 

Doctor they must needs 
say something that 
hath been spoken. 


Compiled for the behoof and overthrow of the 
Unpreaching Parsons, Vicars, and Curates that have learnt 
their Catechisms, and are past grace (2): By the 
Reverend and Worthy Martin Marprelate, 
Gentleman, and dedicated by a Second 
Epistle to the Terrible Priosts. 


In this Epitome, the foresaid Vicars, &c. are very insufficiently 
furnished with notable inability of most vincible 
reasons, to answer the cavil of the Puritans. 


And lest Mr. Doctor should think that no man can write 
without sense but his self, the senseless titles of the several 
pages, and the handling of the matter throughout the 
Epitome show plainly, that beetleheaded ignorance must 
not live and die with him alone. 

Printed on the other hand of some of the Priests.

MARTIN MARPRELATE, Genripman, Primate 
AND Merrroronran or aun Ture Martins IN 


ENGLAND, 
To all clergy-masters wheresoever, saith as followeth (1): 


Wuy, my clergy-masters, is it even so with your Terrible- 
ness? May not a poor gentleman signify his good will 
unto you by a Letter, but, presently [at once], you must 
put yourselves to the pains and charges, of calling four 
bishops together ; John Canterbury, John London, Thomas 
Winchester, William of Lincoln (2); and posting over city 
and country for poor Martin? Why, his meaning in writing 
unto you was not that you should take the pains to seek 
for him. Did you think that he did not know where he 
was himself? Or, did you think him to have been clean 
lost, that you sought so diligently for him? I thank you, 
Brethren, I can be well, though you do not send to know 
how Ido. My mind towards you, you shall from time to 
time understand by my 'pistles. As now; where, you 
must know, that I think not well of your dealing with my 
Worship, and those that have had (of) my books in their 
custody. IJ’ll make you rue that dealing of yours, unless 
you leave it. I may do it; for you have broken the

(1) For particuars as to Giles Wigginton’s refusal to take the oath, 
see THE EPIstLe, p. 59, note (1). Also the Introduction. 

(2) Richard Schilders, of Middleburgh in Holland printed many of 
the works of English Puritans. In a London ‘ Indenture’ for subsidies he 
is called ‘Richard Painter alias Skylder.’—Pudlications of the Huguen. 
Soc., X., ii. 171. He came over from Hainault to England in 1567, and 
was followed in 1568 by ‘Trokyn his wyfe.’ In that year he was 
admitted as a ‘brother’ of the Stationers’ Company. But in November, 
1578, the Court of the Company prohibited him from exercising the full 
liberties of a master printer and only allowed him to work. ‘in the servyce 
of the freemen of this mistery.”? He had migrated to Holland and was 
established in Middelburg in 1584.—Arber’s Transcripts, J. 366, IT. 
882; Ames’ Typ. Antig. 683. J. Dover Wilson, Richard Schilders and 
the English Puritans, a paper read before the Bibliog. Society and sum- 
marised in its News Sheet, Noy. 1910. 

(3) On the oath ex officio mero see the ‘Hist, Intro. pp. 75, 80.

1588, to be the wonderful year (1), by removing you all out

Martin hath told the truth, you cannot deny it, that some 
of you do injuriously detain true men’s goods, as John of 
London; and some have accounted the preaching of the 
word to be heresy, as John of Canterbury; &c. ‘All of you

J perceive (2). I will grow to a point with you. Have but 
a free disputation with the Puritans, for the unlawfulness of 
your place, and if you be not overthrown [ will come in, and 
do unto you what you think good: for then I will say that 
you are no popes. ‘There was the Demonstration of 
Discipline, published together with mine Mpistles: which

you defend your legs against Martin’s strokes, while the

monly and deservedly called, with respect to this nation especially.’ See 
also Hist. Intro. 144. F 

(2) See ‘danced in a net,’ Tue Epistin, p. 75, note (3). 

(3) In his preliminary epistle ‘To the Supposed Governors of the 
Church of England, &c.,’ Udall’s words are, ‘ Venture your byshopprickes 
upon a disputation, and wee will venture our lines, take the challenge 
if you dare.’ In regard to Udall and his writings generally, see the 
Hist, Intro., 212 (8). : ; 

(4) It is to be observed that both here and in the reference just made 
to the Demonstration, the author’s name is not mentioned, though no one 


could know better than Martin that it came from the pen of John 
Udall.

THE EPITOME OF THE FIRST BOOK 
OFTHIS WORTHY VOLUME 


WRITTEN BY My BRoTHER Sarum, Dean Joun 
Ste feliciter incipit (1) 


The whole volume of Mr. Dean’s, containing in it sixteen 
books, besides a large Preface, and an Epistle to the Reader: 
The Epistle and the Preface are not above eight sheets of 
paper, and very little under seven. You may see when men 
have a gift in writing, how easy it is for them to daub paper. 
The complete work (very briefly comprehended in a portable 
book, if your horse be not too weak, of an hundred, three- 
score and twelve sheets, of good demy paper(2)) is a 
confutation of The Learned Discowrse of Ecclesiastical 
Government (3). This Learned Discourse is a book 
allowed (4) by all the Puritan preachers in the land, who 
would have all the remnants and relics of Antichrist 
banished out of the Church, and not so much as a lord 
bishop (no not his Grace himself) dumb minister (no not 
dumb Jobn of London his self), nonresident, archdeacon, 
abbey-lubber, or any such loiterer, tolerated in our ministry. 
Insomuch as, if this stronghold of theirs be overthrown (5), 
ho, then, all the fat is run to the fire with the Puritans! 

(1) fhe ancient writer, after a custom already grown quaint in 
Martin’s day, wearied with his task, would ingenuously express his feel- 
ings on the last page, with such words as Winit, or Haxplicit, leliciter, 
&c. Martin says of Dean Bridges and his Defence, Thus prosperously he 
begins. 

(2) It is a substantial 4to, pp. x +1402; that is, it contains, in all, 
four sheets and a half more than Martin assigns to it. 

(3) The Learned Discourse is the running headline of A Briefe and 
Plaine Declaration inserted by the printer. It is a thin 8vo., measuring 
only a few inches. It is fully described in the Hist. Intro., 1835—139. For 
brief references to Dr. Bridges and his work, see ibid., 139—143. 

(4) Sanctioned. 

(5) t.e., The Learned Discourse.

reasons, very notably out of reason, that it hath not one 
stone in the foundation more than it had. 

Trust me truly, he hath given the cause ‘ sicken a wipe 
in his bricke’ (2) and so lambskinned (3) the same, that the 
cause will be the warmer a good while for it. The reason(s)

coming out of the Learned Discourse the Doctor ina sermon

the Puritans are like to have 2 good and a sound cause of it 
as long as they live. In this one thing I dare prefer him 
before any that ever wrote; to wit, that there be not three 
whole periods for every page in the book, that is not graced 
with a very fair and visible solecism. Oh, most excellent 
and surpassing eloquence! He speaketh everything so fitly 
to the purpose, that he never toucheth the matter in question. 
A rare gift in a learned writer. He hath used such variety 
of learning that very often he hath translated out of one 
man’s writing six or seven pages together (mote here a new- 
found manner of bookmaking). And, which is more strange, 
he bringeth those testimonies for his purpose, whose very 
words, translated and set down by him, are as flat against 
the purpose whereto he bringeth them, as fire in quality is 
contrary to water. Had not he a right use of his wits, 
think you, while they were thus bestowed ? (1).
