in the teeth therewith? He hath made their betters to

woful experience. What small credit and less gain there is 
to be had, either in writing or in disputing with these 
fellows ! 

To the matter. The state of the whole controversy 
between my brethren bishops and my brethren the Puritans, 
and so, between this worthy Doctor and these Discourses is, 
whether the external government of the Church of Christ be 
a thing so prescribed by the Lord in the New Testament, as 
it is not lawful for any man to alter the same, any more than 
it was lawful to alter the form of regiment [rule] prescribed 
under the Law in the Old Testament. And see whether 
there be any government in the Church, (as necessarily there 
must be, or else all confusion will ensue) the same must be 
by those offices and officers alone, and by no other, which 
the Lord hath set down and limited in His Word. Or, else, 
whether man may alter these offices and officers at his will 
and pleasure, and make new offices and officers as he may in 
the civil governments. The Puritans say that these offices 
and officers, which our Saviour Christ and His apostles did 
ordain, are unchangeable, and that it is not lawful for any 
prince to alter them, no not though the circumstances of 
times, places, and persons should seem in regard of con- 
venience to enforce himthereunto. The Doctor, and allthe 
lordly priests in the land, hold the contrary ; and swear it 
to be lawful for the magistrate to ordain what government 
he will in the Church; yea, that the church governors, con- 
trary to the flat commandment of our Saviour Christ, (Luke 
2275 25) may be lords; and that the church government, 
prescribed by our Saviour Christ, and enjoined by the 
apostle, was not immutable, as the regiment [rule] | under 
the Law was. Insomuch as, in the opinion of Master 
Bridges and the rest of the clergy, Paul was deceived (Eph. 
415) in saying that Pastors and Doctors were to continue in 
the Church until we all meet together, that is, unto the end 


(1) This concise statement of one of the principal issues in the con- 
troversy between the oficial hierarchy and the Puritans is considered 
in the Iniroduction. Here it is sufficient to note that the main dispute 
is ecclesiastical and not theological.

Notwithstanding, methinks your syllogism should have four 
terms. 1. The church government. 2. All things belong- 
ing to church government. 8. An uniform prescript, &ec. 
4. A government prescribed in the Word. 

And ten to one Brother, you never dreamt to have met 
with your Brother Martin, when you wrote this volume. 
Well, seeing we are now come together, let me, about this 
point of church government, fathermillerly spur a question 
unto you. Tell me then bethout dissimblation (1) what the 
Bishops and you mean, when the question is concerning 
church government, to run by and by into the controversy 
of ‘things appertaining to church government’; which, 


for the most part, are indifferent, and not set down in the 


Word, but left to the discretion of the Church ? As though 


and how. many offices and officers, the Church is to be 

governed? In what causes it is lawful for church governors 

to employ themselves? Whether it be lawful for one of 
them to meddle with the office of another? Or, for one 

to do that action, wherein the whole Church should be an 

agent? Whether they may be magistrates and church 

governors both at onetime? As though (say) there were no 

difference between these questions, which are grounded upon | 
the certain prescript rule of the Word that cannot be changed, 

and other questions, which, although they belong to the 

service of God, and the outward government of the Church, 

yet depend not upon anything prescribed and exactly set 
down in the Word ; but upon the grounds of what, in regard 

of the changeable circumstances of time and place, may be 

most comely, most decent, most orderly, and best belonging 
to edification.

convenient, that prayer should begin at 8 or 9 o’clock; 
whether the sermon should continue an hour, or an hour

the book is without pagination. Already some passing references have 
been made to the Harborowe in Martin’s first tract (ee THE EpIsTix, 
pp. 22, 77, note (1)), but, the new series of quotations given from its pages 
may be regarded as one of the outstanding features of the present Tract, 
and one of the chief services rendered by Martin in the controversy of the 
Reformers with the Bishops, The full title of Aylmer’s work is ‘An 
Harborovve For Faithfull and Trevve svbiectes agaynst the late blowne 
Blafte, concerninge the Gouernmét of VVemen, wherein be confuted 
all such reasons as a ftraunger of late made in that behalfe, with a breife 
exhortation to Obedience. Anno M.D. lix. Proverbes 82. ‘ Many: daughters 
there be that gather riches to gether: but thou goest aboue them all. 
As for fauour it is deceitfull, and bewtie is a vaine thing: but a woman 
that feareth the Lord: She is vvorthie to be prayfed. Geue her the 
fruit of ber handes, and let her ovvne vvorkes prayfe her in the gate. 
| At Strafborowe the 26. of Aprill.’ [1559]. It is printed in Roman 
type, sig. A-—-R in fours. Brit. Mus. press mark, C. 38. e. 2. Martin 
commences numbering the pages of his copy with sig. B 1, the title-page, 
Hpistle to the Reader, and a table of contents occupying the first sheet. 
The work is an answer to John Knox’s VWirst Blast of the Trumpet 
against the Monstrovs regiment of women, published at Geneva the 
previous year, 1558, The Harborowe, though subsequently repudiated 
by Alymer, is thoroughly characteristic of the man, violent and extrava- 
gant in its langnage, but with a keen sense of the real issues of the 
ecclesiastical controversy, where personal aggrandisement and advantage 
do not completely corrupt his judgment. He opens his argument with 
this fine mixture of metaphors. ‘Scing therfor that by frovvning 
fortune, and God’s vvrath, for th’ offences of th’inabitantes, Hnglande 
is of late both in honour and possessions, not a lytle maymed, Yea, takinge 
a fall through the negligence of the Nurce halfe made a creple: It is 
necessary for al good men, and the dutie of all faithfull Subicctes, to haue 
an eye to it, that it ranne not vpon the rockes, and make fhipp wrake.’ 
—Sig. B J. The notorious passage on the conduct of bishops, and some 
like extracts are given by Martin later on in the present Tract; but 
in order to give a complete account of the book, and therefore of its 
writer, one or two brief extracts may be added. Lamenting the ser- 
vility of the Parliament under Mary, he breaks forth, ‘Would God 
that that court of daies, had feared no more the fearcenes of a woman, 
than they did the displeasure of such a man [Hen. VIII.]. Then should 
‘they not haue stouped contrary to their othes and alledgiaunce to the 
crowne, against the preuilege of that house, vppon their marye bones to 
receiue the Devels blessinge brought vnto them by satans Apostle the 
Cardinal.’—Sig. H 3 and vers. No Puritan could speak more contemp- 
tuously of everything pertaining to Popery ; its doctrine is ‘ deuelishe,’ 
the host is ‘the God in the boxe,’ the eucharist a ‘blestered masse.’ 
Here and there he angles quietly for the favour of Elizabeth, though 
he can be disdainful enough of women in general ; and the worst sort 
of them, after a dozen or more strong expressions of disparagement, 
he declares to be ‘in euery wise doltified with the dregs of the Devils 
dunghil.’—Sig. G 3. He appeals strongly to the patriolism of his 
fellow-countrymen. ‘Play not the milksoppes in making curtsy who 
shall go first: but shew your felues true Mnglishe men in readines, 
courage, and boldnes: and be ashamed to be the least, feare neither 
freuch, nor Scot. For first you haue God, and al his army of angels 
on your side: you haue right and trouth, and seeke not to do them 
wronge, but to defend your own right. Think not that God will suffer

a larger commission ; where you say, that the Word of God 
is able to make the civil government perfect; yes, and that 
the perfection of the civil government must be out of the 
Word, and in the Word, inclusively (1). But for all this 
you must give me leave to doubt how this reason of yours 
i;  followeth. Christ hath prescribed the inward government;

your second reason will make the matter more clear unto 
me; which is in the same page, and thus framed: ‘ We are Page 55. 
His Church if we hold fast the confidence of our hope unto

Church set down in the Word.’ | This reason, to omit what ce 
ground it has in the Word, 1s very plausible even in nature; 
is it not think you? Aman is a man, though he go naked. 
Therefore by Master Dean’s reason, the Lord hath ordained 
no covering for his nakedness. Again a man is a man, if 
he be once born, though he never cat meat; therefore it is 
not the ordinance of God he should eat meat. Let our 
eavilling brethren go see now, what may be brought to 
reproach the credit of such inforcible proofs. Master 
Doctor doubtless will stand to his tackle whatsoever they 
bring. If they should be so ignorant as to deny the con- 
sequence of both these reasons, they must stay until Master 
Dean has read over his predicables and predicaments with 
Friar Titlemane’s rules De inveniendis mediis ; (2) viz., until 
he has got a bishopric; before he prove either of them. 
And it may be then, too, that he will prove what they deny, 
as Master Canterbury has proved, that which Master 
Cartwright confuted.

In the meantime, mark how stoutly Master Dean goes 
forward. And although (page 56) he meet by the way with 
his known sweet friend Bellarmine’s—a Popish writer’s— 
distinction of ‘agreeable, and not contrary, to the Word’ 
(the Papists (1) affirming all their traditions to be agreeable, 
and none of them contrary, to the Word), yet his answer 
(page 57) to the place of Paul (2 Tim. 87) is as good and 
as canonical as any of the former reasons, [and] concluded 
thus— 


‘The place of Seripture which doth not deny, but that the 
civil government, which must be inclusively according to the 
Word, may be elsewhere prescribed than in the Word, that place 
also doth not forbid the church government to be fetched from 
some other fountain than the prescription of the Word. But 
this place (2 Tim. 37) doth not deny but that civil government, 
being a government, nor [and not] prescribed in the Word, may 
be learned elsewhere than out of the Word, and yet be accor | ding 
to the Word. Also it doth not deny but that the church 
government may be a church government according to the 
Word, which is not therein prescribed’ (2).

‘ But Christ, knowing the bounds of His office, would not meddle 
with extreme policies, translating of realms, and depriving of true

can | be no quiet, nor (5) well ordered commonwealth.’

(1) Elizabeth came to the throne on the death of Mary, Nov. 17th, 
1558, Aylmer’s Harborowe is dated ‘Strasborowe the 26 of Aprill,’ 1559. 
Martin’s point is therefore of prime importance. Nevertheless he is 
probably mistaken in making ‘Protestant bishops’ ‘now living’ the 
objective of Aylmer’s denunciation. For although Knox’s First Blast 
was only published the previous year, and the HWarborowe must there- 
fore have been written subsequently, still the new bishops were as yet 
scarcely well in the saddle, and the reference must be chiefly, at least, to 
the Marian bishops. At the same time it must be borne in mind, apart 
from the theological change efiected under Elizabeth and the repudiation 
of the Pope’s authority, the official powers and claims of the Protestant 
bishops and of the Roman bishops were the same, Both alike combined 
the ecclesiastical and civil functions. In the above quotations there are 
a couple of insignificant variations from the original ; ‘pomp and pride’ 
are in the reverse order, and after ‘hell’ instead of ‘nys’ Martin has 
“Her.” 

(2) Martin omits ‘too far.’ 

(3) Martin omits ‘ whole.’ 

(4) Should be ‘there.’ 

(5) Martin omits ‘any.’

I assure you, Brother John, you have spoken many things 
worthy the noting, and I would our Parliament-men would 
mark this action done in king Henry the EKighth’s days, and 
follow it in bringing in reformation, and putting down lord 
bishops, with all other points of superstition. They may, 
in your judgment, not only do anything against their king’s 
or queen’s mind, that is behooveful to the honour of God 
and the good of the Commonwealth, but even withstand the 
proceedings of their sovereign. 

But methinks you have a palpable error in the 48th, 
49th, and 50th pages of your book (1), which is, that women 
are incapable of the ministry, not in regard of their sex 
but of certain wants and imperfections in their sex; viz., 
their want of learning and courage; so that if a woman 
should be brought up in learning, and trained in disputa- 
tions, and were not milder in nature than men (all of which 
wants In women, you speak, page 48) but knew their quarter- 
stroke (which knowledge you requixe in the minister, page 
49) then, by your reason, they might preach in your diocese. 
Whosoever will read your 50th and 5ist pages shall find 
this to be your judgment.

have set down out of his book, and judge whether such 
things as he wrote could proceed from a religious heart, and

he leave his tyranny.

all this while. My brother London and I were so busy,

(1) Passing reference has already been made to Bishop Overton in 
THE EPIstLe, p. 90, where Martin dubs him a dunce, and his ignor- 
ance is again referred to in Hay any Works, p. 320. But there were 
more serious and well-attested facts which made Overton a notorious 
figure, even among the worldly bishops of Elizabeth’s reien. He started 
his clerical career as a scandalous pluralist ; indeed, before he was 
actually ordained he was made (1359) a canon of Winchester. He took 


orders in 1560, and in the space of ten years managed to augment his 


ecclesiastical plunder by five rectories, two canonries, and a cathedral 
treasureship, But unprincipled pluralism is a hunger which grows by 
being fed ; so we find Overton, in 1579, riding post from Chichester to 
London. He had suddenly heard that the rich archdeaconry of Lewes 
was yacant and had come to sue for it at the hands of the Queen. He 
had however been forestalled by Drant, also a prebend cf Chichester, 
who had ridden to town that same morning, but earlier. The result was 
a violent feud between the two men. Overton obtained the bishopric 
of Lichfield through the efforts of Dr. Becon, who had considerable 
influence with the Earl of Leicester. In return he promises to advance 
the interests of Becon. Writing to Mrs. Becon, Overton says ‘if it shall 
so fall out by his [Dr. Becon’s] mediation I be hereafter p[re]ferred 
to some good Dishopricke . . . IL pray you to let me be a suetor to him 
and to you that we may be togither and live togither. . . that ave 
may have mutual joy and comfort together like dear brethren and 
sisters : and I promise unto you before the eternal God I have not nor 
shal have any thing to[o] dear for him and you wether in Spiritualities or 
Temporalities to do you good and yours’ (S. P. Dorm. Eliz. exxxvij. 31 ;, 
quoted by F. O. White). Her husband so far benefited by the Bishop’s 
elevation that he was appointed to the chancellorship. But the Bishop, 
pluralist though he was, and notwithstanding that the Queen granted him 
three half-years’ subsidies to furnish his estate, and that there were 
other moneys coming to him; having also two rich rectories—Stoke 
on Trent, end Hanbury in Staffordshire—in commendam, was always 
impecunions. He therefore gave, for a consideration, to his son-in-law, 
Zachary Babington, a graccless person by all accounts, a presentation 
to thesame Office, both Becon and he to hold conjunctivim et divisim, with 
sole occupancy to the survivor. Before long Overton, cancelling the 
previous presentations, made his son-in-law sole chancellor, with endless 
law-suits following. He endeavoured to raise money by exacting a ‘toll 
of ‘twelve pence in the pound,’ which he called a subsidium charitativum, 
and claimed by precedent. The poorer clergy, by cajolery and intimi- 
dation, paid ; not so the cathedral chapter, headed by the resolute Dean 
Boleyn, a ‘hasty man,’ one who once threatened ‘to nail’ the Dean of 
Canterbury ‘to the wall with his sword,’ and not in the least intimidated 
by Overton. (See Tun Proresratyon, p. £17). The Bishop threatened 
a writ De Scandalis Magnatum, only to find that the actions would 
not lie. He later tried to blackmail two aged canons by conventing them 
before the High Commission in the depth of winter, when a phenomenal 
fall of snow lay on the ground, unless they agreed each of them to lend 
him a hundred pounds for a year or two. In the litigation which fol- 
lowed it was alleved that he had granted to a son-in-law named Plasted 
‘several leases of most of his lands, besides offices, annuities, and they 
[the Dean and Chapter] knew not what.’ His quarrel with Becon 
became very bitter; the Bishop, prompted by his wife, calling Mrs. 
Becon by a most calumnious name, and Becon retorting by calling the 
Bishop “beastly knave,’ ‘horson knave,’ ‘perjured man,’ ‘simoniacal

158 THE MARPRELATE TRACTS 


I grant, indeed, that you Brethren, Puritans, say the 
truth as it ought to be, that bishops or ministers ought 
not to be lords in any wise, either as ministers, or as civil 
magistrates. ‘Thus, indeed, it ought to be, I and my 
Brethren, the Bishops, do grant unto you. And you know 
we would it were so. But you know, also, that our laws 
will have church governors to be lords; and what, should 
our bishops (good, noble men) refuse that which the law 
would have them to take? Get you the law to be against 
their lordly callings, and see whether they will not give 
over their lord-bishopdoms, whensover law compelleth them. 
And whensoever they give over they shall have no cause to 
thank such envious brethren as you are. Howsoever it be, 
you see the Apostle, speaking of all sorts of ministers, by 
your own confession, speaketh nothing of any lord, or 
lordly government among them all; and, therefore, 
speaketh nothing of church government. Again, all those 
functions, whereof the Apostle maketh any mention (as 
my Brother Bridges hath well noted) are ordained to the 
building of the body of Christ, in the unity of faith and 
knowledge. Now, I would any Puritan of you all durst say 
that our church governors, that is, our venerable and 
worshipful lord bishops, are ordained of God for the building 


E4of His body; which I know | you will say to be done by 


preaching. As though lord bishops, being civil governors, 
should preach! Were it meet, I pray you, to see Stephen 
Gardiner, being then of the Privy Council, in the pulpit? 
Councillors now must have something to do with pulpit 
matters—must they, IJ pray you? Wull you allow that 
civil governors should be ordinary preachers in your new 
platform of a Reformed Church? I know you will not. 
And what reason is it then, that you should require bishops 
to be ordinary. preachers, seeing every bishop is a civil 
governor? I tell you true, I am so far from thinking that 
bishops ought to be ordinary (1) preachers, sceing they are 
civil governors, that I hold it to be a sin for them to preach 
(1) That is, by order or regular appointment.

though you would have any to preach who had not an eccle-

Brethren, to answer this question of yours, you are to know

Now, Brethren, you must not think the worse of this

even since he hath joined these two offices together, he hath 
proved his own saying to be true for his part, in that his 
whole endeavour hath been, ever since he was bishop, 
that we should have no quiet, nor any well-ordered 
Church, or Commonwealth. I hope by this time you see 
it | plain that bishops sin, both because they are civil 
governors, and, being civil governors, because they are 
bishops.

noted already (@)), that we might never see that day in

His Grace of Canterbury, I tell you, hath condemned 
the preaching of the Word (as being the only ordinary 
means to Salvation) to be an heresy (2). This Seripture of 
Paul, that God hath appointed preaching pastors to continue 
in His church unto the world’s end, is a chief ground of the 
former heresy. I will allow of no such Scripture, I trow, 
as may impeach the opinion which my Lord of Canterbury 
conceived of the preaching of the Word. 

You see therefore, my Friends, that Master Dean in this 

point will have nothing to do with you, or Paul’s testi- 
mony. And you are not ignorant, I am sure, how soon 
all lords will be out of the ministry, if we had none in 
England but the pastors spoken of by Paul ; and therefore 
Master Doctor hath prayed against this order. Yea, and 
he hath brought such a reason against this, your platform 
of government, as is just secundum usum Sarum (3). For, 
indeed, it is Popish, and therefore you might smell it afar 
off. 
‘If the Lord (saith he, page 62) (4) had thought this government 
needful for His Church, then He would not have suffered His 
Church to be without the same. But He suffered His Church 
of a long time to be without this government. Ergo, He 
thought it not needful.’ 


Ah, craft, craft; craft and subtilty, that can in jest 
deceive his brethren with a Popish reason in this sort. 
But, my Masters, you must not think that our Brother 
Sarum bringeth this in good earnest, but only to try

(1) Said to be from the French name of an evil disease, though used 
at this time, in all probability, without any consciousness of its deriva- 
tion. 

(2) Petheram is entirely astray in identifying this expression as a 
Puritan name either for Gammer Gurton'’s Needle or for dramatic 
literature generally. Bridges in his Defence has a passing reference to 
the ‘Legende aure,’ that is the Legenda Aurea. This was his curious 
authority for the view, in contradiction to the opinion of Cartwright, that 
miracles are not restricted to the age of the Apostles. (See xote (5), 
p. 166.) The original title of the work referred to was Lhe Lives of 
the Saints. It consists of a medley of monkish tales about the saints of 
the Roman Calendar, which, despite their pious intention, read to-day 
like chapters from the adventures of the redoubtable Baron Munchausen. 
Compiled by Jacob de Voragine (who died Archbishop of Genoa), it had 
an extraordinary popularity in the Middle Ages, translations of it into 
the chief European languages quickly appearing. It was turned into 
Iinglish by Caxton, and had its title altered into Legenda Aurea, so, 
it is said, by his successor, Wynken de Worde. A black letter edition 
of 1527, which was consulted, does not contain the popular story about 
the saint preaching to the pigs, but the printer adds a hint on his own 
recount. The pictured initial letter at the opening of the chapter 
represents Anthony conventionally attired in ample garments, a halo 
around his head, an open book in one hand, in the background a church, 
and in the foreground a pig! There is a direct reference to the 
‘legende aure’ in Tur Prorestatyon, p. 413. John Fox, explaining 
a monkish reference to ‘the church story ’ as an authority, has this foot- 
note: ‘By this 'church story he meaneth belike Legenda, Aurea, otherwise 
called The Legend of Lies.’—Acts & Mon., 1V., 629. 

(3) For the rumour that Bridges was the author of Gammer Gurton’s 
Needie—the needle which was found at Jast in Hodge’s breeches—see 
Tue EPIstie, p. 33, and the note there discussing the authorship. There 
is an allusion to the matter earlier in Tue Epiromr, p. 140. 

(4) Printed without author’s name. Dexter (Bibliography) conjec-

INTRODUCTORY NOTE 


Tur Miyerauis, the brief contemporary title by which 
this Tract was known, is a broadside and exists in the 
unique copy at the Archbishop’s Library at Lambeth. 
The special efforts made to extirpate all the Marprelate 
writings, added to the common risks of destruction operating 
for three centuries, sufficiently explain their rarity. Buta 
broadside had far less chances of surviving than an ordinary 
pemphlet. We can therefore scarcely hope to hear of the 
discovery of a second copy. 

The Marprelate press was removed from Fawsley House 
early in 1589. It first lay at an empty farmhouse at Norton 
by Daventry, and later was removed to the White Friars, 
the house of John Hales, at Coventry. Hales was a con- 
nection of Sir Richard Knightley’s, who had married his 
aunt. It was that circumstance which imduced him to 
harbour the secret press, so he told the judges at his trial. 
Robert Waldegrave continued his services as the printer, 
taking with him the black letter type which he used 
exclusively for the Marprelate Tracts printed by him. 
Penry’s own tracts printed by Waldegrave at Coventry are 
in Roman type. 

Tue Minreranus appeared about the 20th of every, 
1589. During the first fortnight of the year the official 
reply of the Bishops to the first Marprelate Tract, Tue 
Evisriy, containing also a single reference to the second 
Tract, Tue Eprromm, was published, under the title of 


_ An Admonition to the People of England, bearing the initials 


JT’. C., to which some reference is made in the Introductory 
Note to the next T'ract, at the close of the epistle ‘ To the 
Reader.’ The initials are omitted from Arber’s reprint.

tye INTRODUCTORY NOTE 


‘he principal work of the Marprelate press at Coventry 
was to print a reply to the Bishops’ Admonition. Mean- 
while, to keep the public interest well in hand, while the 
larger Tract was being set up, the ‘Minmrann anp Mrra- 
PHISICALL ScHooiPornts’ was hastily written and printed. 
lt was ‘a pretty thing to be set out before the other 
Bookes,’ Penry declared, according to the evidence of 
Henry Sharpe, the Northampton bookbinder., 

Sharpe had been shown by Penry the ‘copy’ of the 
broadside before it was printed. When he saw the printed 
copy he thought there were references to Dr. Some which 
he did not remember to have heard when the manuscript 
was read to him. And, as Penry was at the time engaged 
in a controversy with Some, Sharpe concluded that Penry 
wrote THe Minerauis. The reference is to §§ 16, 25, 
which state as the ground of their proposed ‘school points’ 
Some’s view of baptism which he urged in his controversy 
vith Penry. But Sharpe’s observations are too vague and 
uncertain to be of value as evidence of authorship. 

In regard to authorship one point is not to be overlooked. 
School-point 85 would suggest that the writer defended the 
Queen in bestowing bishops’ livings upon laymen. But the 
real Martin was undoubtedly against all alienation of church 
property to laymen—see the references given in a note 
to § 85; also the definite and grave views upon the question 
expressed in Tur Proresratyon (p. 407). But itis just 
possible that the Bishop of Winchester is called upon to 
defend against all comers the view, that the Queen cannot 
lawfully ‘bestow the bishops’ livings upon laymen,’ not 
because Martin disagreed with the Bishop, but because he 
thought it allowable tactics, in such an unequal contest, to 
create mischief between the Queen and the Bishops. 

The text in the original broadside is arranged in two 
paragraphs, which extend across its width; the thirty- 
seven School-points being placed between them in a double 
colurnn, The printed surface-measures 12} X 93 inchés.

INTRODUCTORY NOTE eae 
75 

took the bulk ‘towards London,’ leaving fifty copies for 
Sharpe’s benefit at Northampton. There are several 
very early lists which name six out of the seven 
Marprelate Tracts, the omission being Tua Mineraxus. 
But there are many contemporary references to the broad- 
side, and one early list gives the names of the first six 
Tracts, omitting Tne Proresraryon, also stating where 
‘they were printed. 
The School-point was the theme which the University 
scholar exhibited and was prepared to defend, according to 
the methods of formal logic, against all comers. Martin 
selects a number of extracts from the speeches of the 
bishops and their supporters and constitutes them school- 
points. Many of these points were serious matters to the 
minds of the Evangelical reformers ; some represent clerical 
scandals; some reveal Martin’s own ingenuity chiefly; and 
others give publicity to grotesque views uttered by the 
Church defenders. 

The story of the production of Tum Mineraus is given 
more fully in the Hist. Intro., pp. 180 f. 

The press mark of the unique copy of the Tract at 
Lambeth is 80. 6. 24 (7). It is folded into a small volume 
with other Tracts, and is slightly cropped by the binder.

(THE MINERALLS] 


Certain Mineral and Metaphysical Schoolpoints (x) to be 
defended by the Reverend Bishops and the rest of my Clergy- 
masters of the Convocation House, against both the Univer- 
sities and all the Reformed Churches in Christendom. 
Wherein is laid open the very quintessence of all cater- 
corner (2) divinity. And withal, to the preventing of the 
cavils of these wrangling Puritans, the persons by whom, 
and the places where, these miseries are so worthily main- 
tained are, for the most part, plainly set down to the view 
of all men, and that to th’ eternal praise of the most reverend 
Fathers. 

1. That the Puritans may as well deny the Son of God 
to be Homoouseos, that is, con-substantial with God the 
Father, as they may deny the superiority [preéminence] of 
archbishops and bishops to be Jawful.(3) ‘Phe defendant in 
this point is Father John of Fulham, in his preface before 
Barnardeus de Loques’ book of The Church, published in 
English (4). 


(1) ‘Mineral’ as used here seems to be one of Martin’s oddities of 
speech. In the Index to Hazlitt’s Collections, the Tract is entered 
under the short title ‘ Moral and Metaphysical Conclusions.” But Martin 
probably used the word with the meaning material and as complementary, 
to the word metaphysical, 

(2) An allusion to the square cap worn by the prelates. 

(3) In the great controversy concerning the person of Christ, Arius held 
that fis nature, though not the same, yet was /ike—homoiousia, éuo.vela 
—that of God the Father ; while his orthodox opponent Athanasius held 
that the nature was the same—homoousia, déuoovofa —or consubstantial, 
as is expressed above. 

(4) The work of de Loque was originally written in French under, 
the title Les Principaux abus de la Messe, &c., 2 vols., 8vo, La Rochelle, 
1579, It appeared in an English dress a couple of years later as A 
Treatie of the Churche, containing @ true discourse to knowe the true 
church by, and to discerne it from the Romish Church and. all other false 
assemblies, or counterfeit congregations. Written by M. Bertrande 
de Logue of Dolphinee and dedicated unto my Lord the Vicount of 
Lurenne, And faithfully translated out of the French into English, by 
7. Wf{ilcox]. It is an 8vo, 422 p.; the ‘Treatie’ itself occupies 
384 pp. [Lamb. Pal, Lib. xxviij. 9, 14; B. M. 3936, aa. 40.] In the 
British Museum copy an old hand, though not contemporary, perhaps, 
has added to the ‘Admonition to the Reader,’ which occupies 8 pp., a 
MS. note to the effect that it was ‘stated in Martin M his Protestaton 
that this was penned by the B: of London.’ The reference should have 
been to Tur MINERALLS. Zhe Dialogue wherein is plainly laid open,

4. That our Saviour Christ in his sermons usually sware 
by His faith; for He said ‘Amen, Amen,’ which isas much 
to say as ‘By my Faith.’ The defendant in this point is 
Father Thomas of Winchester (3), alias profane T. C. [The 
Admonition] page 62. 


&e., Sig. B 2, also ascribes this ‘Admonition’ to Bishop Aylmer. If 
required some hardihood on Aylmer’s part to introduce to English’ 
readers this work, the translation of which is assigned by the British 
Museum authorities to the Puritan minister Thomas Wilcox. Indeed, 
Aylmer himself, in this introductory chapter, refers to his hesitation in 
publishing de Logue’s work, because of the wrong use that might be 
made of it, ‘especially the ninth chapter’; the title of which runs, 
‘Touching the degrees of Ministers in the Church,’ &c. B. de Loque does 
not condemn the titles allowed in the Reformed Churches, but desires 
‘to elevate [expose] and impugn the tyranie and ambition of the 
popish prelacy . .. who leaving their function of preaching and teach- 
jing have ysurped I knowe not what authoritie and power of commanding 
what they list in the church of God,’-—the very allegation of the Puritans 
against the English prelacy. The particular accusation contained in the 
above ‘school-point’ refers to the close of Aylmer’s preface: ‘Now 
whereas many make much adoe about the titles of Bishops Metro- 
politans and Archbishops and the Scripture is still alledged as an aduer- 
sarie in this auarell : and containing exprefsly no such name. Thus may. 
they make our Saviour Christ inferiour to his father concerning his 
diuinitie because the title [the Greek word is misprinted] is no where 
literally expressed, although the same by sundrie places may be well and 
justly gathered.’ The ZMalogue above referred to repeats this point 
against Aylmer ; adding the words ‘ fiat contrary to the saying of our 
Sauior Christ, Luke 22 [vv. 66-71].’—Sig. B 2 rect. and vers. 

(1) Marmaduke Middleton became Bishop of Waterford in 1579, and 
of St. David’s in 1582. It may be assumed that if this serious charge 
could be disproved or denied, the disproof or denial would have appeared 
in the Admonition. About three years later than the date of Martin’s 
writing Middleton was formally degraded from his episcopal office. 
See THe Epist.E, pp. 90, 95, and note ; Hay any Work, p. 215. The 
original has L. G., clearly a misprint for L[ord] Bfishop]. 

(2) See Tre Evistis, p. 56, note (4) ; Hay any Worker, p. 271. 

(3) The defendant in this case ought to be Bishop Aylmer; for 
Cooper in his Admonition only inserts the defence supplied by Aylmer.

MINERAL AND METAPHYSICAL SCHOOLPOINTS 187 


5. That Moses in giving a bill of divorcement, Deut. 24, 
brake the moral law of God. The defendant in this point 
is Thomas of Winchester, ahas profane T. C., page 111 (x). 

6. That Papistry is better than the sincere profession of 
the Gospel which falsely men call Puritanism. The 
defendant in this point is Father Edmond [Freke] of 
Worcester (2). 

7. That the public fasts and the prayers of the Puritans 
were the cause of the invasion of the Spaniards, and of all 
other troubles and turmoils within theland. The defendant 
in this point is Father William [Overton] of Lichfield and 
Coventry, alias Parson of Solihull (3). 

8. That the long prayers of the Puritans before and after 
their sermons are nothing else but ‘ beeble-babble, beeble- 
babble. The defendant in this point is Father John 
[Aylmer] of Fulham in Master Cawdry’s examination (4). 


That defence is that ‘By my faith’ is much the same as ‘ Amen,’ and 
since Christ used the expression ‘Amen’ then Martin’s deduction is, 
that Aylmer would charge Christ with swearing. See THe EpImst1e, 
p. 22, note (2). 

(1) Cooper is contending that Jaws may sometimes be righteously 
broken, and instances the case of David and his men eating the shew 
bread and the Maccabees fighting upon the Sabbath. He then gives the 
case above: ‘Yea, in a morall commandement of God touching mariage, 
we see God to vse a maner of dispensation, in respect of the frailtie of 
mans nature.’ 

(2) We have not traced the reference, but it will be remembered that 
Freke before being translated to Worcester had been for uine years 
Bishop of Norwich, the centre of the Separatist movement—the most 
vigorous and uncorproimising section of Puritanism. 

(3) For some particulars about Overton, see Tm Hrirome, p. 166, 
note(I). He was quite equal to making such an assertion in order to 
raise the cry ‘Puritani ad leones,’ #1, has ‘Solyhall.’ 

(4) Usually ‘bibble-babble,’ = idle chatter. ‘ Malyolio, Malvolio, thy 
wits the heavens restore | endeayour thyself to sleep and leave thy vain 
bibble-babble.’—'welfth Night, iv. 2. Aylmer’s style will be at once 
recognised. Robert Cawdry was rector of Luffenham in Rutlandshire, 
which living he received from Burghley. Afler ministering for twenty 
years and gaining a good reputation both for his abilities and for his 
practical piety, he was charged with refusing to make the sign of the 
cross in baptism, and some such ceremonial defects. On refusing to take | 
the oath ex officio he was utterly deprived of all ministerial exercise. At 
his examination (December, 1586), before Bishop Aylmer, Dr. Stanhope 
and Dr, Walker, the Bishop delivered himself of the following dignified 
sentiments. ‘Are not we the queen’s servants? And is not the sur- 
plice the livery which she hath appointed to be worn? And do you 
think she will be content if we refuse to wear it? Besides, the long 
prayer which you use before your scrmons is nothing but bibble babble,

188 THE MARPRELATE TRACTS 


9. That there is no other way of trial before the 
High Commission but by appeaching [impeaching] and 
accusing a man’s self, and that no State can stand without 
such answering and swearing. The defendants in this 
point are Thomas Cooper, John Cant. [Whitgift] and some 
others at the examination of Master Wigginton (1) at 
Lambeth, in December last, 1588. 

10. That it is as lawful for our Lord Bishops to make bad 
ministers as it was for the Disciples of our Saviour to pluck 
the ears of corn on the Sabbath to slake their hunger. The 
defendant in this point is Father Thomas [Cooper] of 
Winchester, alias profane 'I’. C. (2). 

11. That reading is preaching. ‘The defendant in this 
point is Father John a Bridges, page[s] 564, 565 (3). 

12. That the Magistrate may JawfwWly maim and deform 
the body of Christ, to wit, the Church. The defendants in 
this point are all the twenty-four orders of bishops, and 
especially Father Canterbury. 

18. That more good may be wrought by our ordinary 


bibble babble.’—Brook’s Lives, i. 433. See further reference to Aylmer’s 
views in School-point, No. 22, p. 190. 

(1) Giles Wigginton, vicar of Sedbergh, in the North Riding, is 
frequently referred to in the Tracts, indeed Whitgift told him that 
publica fama strongly alleged him to be their author. For some reference 
to his deprivation and long series of persecutions, see THE EPISTLE, 
p. 59, and note (1). Wigginton has left a vivid and interesting account 
of his arrest and his trial at Lambeth on Dec. 6th, 1588, before the Arch- 
bishop, Bishop Cooper, Dean Goodman, Dr. Aubrey, Dr. Richard Cosin, 
all of the High Commission, from which we have quoted at length in 
the Hist. Intro., pp. 83 ff (§ 5 Wigginton’s Opposition and its 
Penalty.) ; 

(2) Cooper first states the reformers’ objection to an incompetent 
ministry, St. Paul having laid it down as one of the necessary qualifica- 
tions of a minister that he should be ‘ Aptus ad docendum, that is, able 
to teach.’ Tis reply is that no man can perfectly satisfy all the qualifica- 
tions, and if all save those that are perfect are excluded the churches iwill 
lose the greatest part of their ministry. Then ‘God sometime beareth 
with breach of his commandement.’ ‘Christ himselfe may seeme to give 
the reason for their defence when he saith, The Sabboth was ordeined 
for man and not man for the Sabboth.’ In the margin there is a refer- 
ence to Mark 2—the case of the Disciples plucking the cars of corn on 
the Sabbath day.—Cooper’s Admonition, 109—111. 

(3) Dean Bridges in these pages asserts the sufficiency of the Sacra- 
ments when administered without a sermon, but with the liturgical 
forms, which include scriptural extracts, appointed ; ‘the best preacher 
in the world cannot say more.’

service than by preaching. The defendant in this point is 
Father John a Bridges [Defence] p. 652 (1). 

14, That the cross in baptism and organs in cathedral 
churches are as necessary as a preaching ministry. The 
defendant in this point is Father Goodman [Dean] of 
Westminster (2). 

15. That our Lord Bishops in England are the bishops 
of the devil. The defendant in this point (I thank him) is 
Father John o’ Sarum, [Defence] pag[es] 889, 840 (3).

defendant in this point is Father Robert Some, page 158 of

(1) The contention in the Defence is that the service achieves all 
that the ‘Brethren’ claim for preaching ; possibly ‘all this and more 
too.’ Rather than be condemned ‘it may better bee called a fruite~ 
full kynde of preaching.’ 

(2) This no doubt alludes to the discussion upon the Six Articles 
presented by the reformers to the Lower House of Convocation in 1562. 
The 3rd Article proposed to allow the sign of the Cross in baptism to be 
omitted, aud the 6th, ‘that the use of organs be removed.’ Goodman 
resisted the proposed articles, but there appears to be no record re- 
maining of the discussion which took place.—Strype’s Annals, I., i., 
502, 503. See reference to Goodman in Tus Episrir, p. 73, note (3). 

(3) It is Martin’s contention that the office of bishop as held in the 
Church of England is a human invention—a corruption of the Gospel 
model. In Book iv. of the Defence Bridges, answering Beza con- 
cerning the man-made bishop, boldly asserts there can be but two kinds 
of bishop . the bishop of God divinely ordained, and the man-made, who 
is none other or better than ‘a Bishop of the deuill.’ So Martin draws 
the above conclusion, The point is again referred to in HAy ANY WORKE, 
pp. 254—256, and is discussed in the Hist. Intro., pp. 258, 259. 

(4) Dr. Some strongly contends that heretical baptism is valid ; those 
baptised under such auspices are not to be rebaptised, quoting Augus- 
tine and all learned men—Cyprian excepted. But he recognises one 
difficulty which his position creates. Heretics have lawful baptism, 
nevertheless he says ‘If any shall aske whether it be lawfull to offer 
our infants to baptisme out of the Church becanse all learned men 
(except the Donatists, &c. in Augustines time and M. Penry and his 
worthie disciples in our time) haue and doe affirme, that true baptisme 
hath bene and may be out of the Church : My answere is negatiue,’ &c.— 
A Godly Treatise, 158, 159. 

(5) Cosins does not appear to have published anything before this 
date ; but he had taken part as a doctor of law in many ecclesiastical 
cases.

32. That the doctrine of our Saviour Christ concerning 
the equality of ministers (Luke 22°°), and the doctrine of

and all the Terrible Priests (r).

in the government of His own house as Moses was; for

all the twenty-four orders of Bishops, and all the clergy- 
master's. 

84. That the Creed of the Apostles and of Athanasius, 
the Nicene, &c., contain many palpable lies in them; for the 
Apocrypha (which hath many outrageous lies in it, ag in 
2 Esdr. 14%, Judith 11° #8, Tob. 5’) is in authority next to

asties is raised in order to induce the authorities to take away their ‘lands

to take heede, that they bee not intrapped with this sophistrie of

(1) In reply to the Puritan statement that a simple democratic order 
of church government, with many presidents [bishops], governors, and 
chief ministers in every congregation, was practised by the Apostles 
and in the primitive Church, Cooper first ingenuously wrote, ‘I wili not 
deny it.’ But afier the book was printed the Episcopal Committea 
thought it was too generous an admission to make, even in the interests 
of historic truth ; so they pasted over it a cancel-slip containing the 
words ‘That is not yet proved,’ as appears in all the copies of this 
original edition, Then Cooper proceeds, ‘But let them struggle while 
they (that) lust, they shall neuer find’ a commandement in the Scriptures 
charging that it should for cuer be so. It were too great a bridle of 
christiau liberty in things external, to cast vpon the church of Christ.’ 
Such a system he thinks might be the best in times of persecution under 
tyrants, but uuder the rule of Christian princes, with the consent of 
the magistrate, the Church has liberty to alter such things to the needs 
of the time.

85. That it is not lawful for her Majesty to bestow the 
bishops’ livings upon laymen. The defendant in this 
point is Father Thomas of Winchester, profane T. C. 
[Admonition] page 252 (x). : 

36. That it may be accounted for one of our Bishops’ 
great faults, that they have not hitherto, by excommuni- 
cation constrained our Prince [ie. the Queen] and 
Magistrates to do that which, by persuasion, they would 
not do. The defendant in this point is Father Thomas of 
Winchester, profane T. C. [Admonition] page 187 (2). 

37. That the State of England cannot possibly stand 
without Lord Bishops. And so, that the Crown of England 


placed in authority ‘next to the Canonicall Scriptures..—See THn 
EPISTLE, p. 78, note (2). 

(1) This occurs in the penultimate sentence in the Admonition. Cooper 
defends the lordly possessions of the Bishops by a Parthian shot, as 
Axvber remarks. He likens the murmuring of the ‘Seckers after Re- 
formation’ against the ‘liberal benefit’ which the Queen had bestowed, 
not upon bishops, for their mame cannot be mentioned in such a con- 
nection, but, as this sage old student more knowingly puts it, ‘towards 
the maintenance of the Ministery and Preachers of his vvorde,’. to 
Judas murmuring against the generosity of Mary of Bethany. Then he 
concludes, ‘I conlde with better reason and authoritie proone the Con- 
trary Proposition to that which they take vpon them to maintaine: that 
is, Zhat it is not lawfull to bestow such liuings upon Lay men, as are 
appointed by godly lawes for Ministers and Preachers of the worde of 
God. But the shortnesse of the time will not now serue to follow that 
course,’ The sentence which he prints in italics is one of several hints 
to the Queen on the question of church property, contained in the 
Admonition. The truth is that Elizabeth was as unscrupulous as the 
church dignitaries were in seizing such property. But this 35th point 
has additional interest as an item of evidence upon the authorship of the 
Tracts. The real Martin was not in favour of alienating church pro- 
perty. See Hay any WoRKE, p. 268 ; JusT CrNSURD, p. 368, note (4) (note 
on Bishop Underhill) ; and especially Tun PRrorestaryon, p. 407 ; also 
Hist. Intro., 100 ff. ‘ 

(2) At the page indicated Cooper tells us that the Pope used his 
power of excommunication ‘to bring the neckes of Ismperors and Princes, 
vnder his girdle, and to make the whole world subiect to him.’ But tne 
Bishops ‘by their preaching ’ ‘haue bin principall instruments to oner- 
throw the same in the Church of Rome’ [as it existed in England under 
Mary]. None can therefore accuse the Bishops of abusing the power of 
excommunicatiou after the Romish example, by endeavouring ‘to excom- 
municate the Prince and gouernours, of purpose to make them subiect 
to their authoritie in the Church. And happily that may bee a fault, 
yea and a great fault that is found with them in these days, that they 
doe not so, and constraine the Prince and Rulers to doe that, which 
by perswasion they will not doe.’ The Bishop’s irony is a clumsy 
weapon. Jie here claims credit to the Bishops for not constraining (i.e. 
compelling) Blizabeth to do that which she would not do by mere per- 
suasion. :We wonder if the Queen ever noticed this playful stroke.

cannot stand without the Crown of Canterbury. The 
defendant in this point is Father Thomas of Winchester,

(1) Cooper says ‘The lawes of Unglande to this day, haue stoode 
by the authoritie of the three Estates: vvhich to alter now, by leauing 
out the one, may happily seeme a matter of more weight then all men 
doe judge it. ...41 thinke there is no vvise man but seeth what 
daunger may followe in these perillous times, not onely by fulfilling tha 
thing, but also by offering to doe it.’ Like all men who stand to profit 
by laws as they are, the Bishop was strongly adverse to legislative change, 
and, like all ecclesiastics, he sheltered his own interest behind the larger 
constitutional question, You cannot touch the condition of the bishop 
withont wounding the State. So he proceeds: ‘It hath beene alwayes 
dangerous, to picke quarrels against lawes setled. And I pray God, that 
the very rumour hereof, spread by these mens bookes, haue not already 
bred more inconuenience then without hurt will be supprefsed : I may 
not put all that I thinke, in writing.’ The Bishop's uneasiness at the 
mention of reform may be dismissed + the claim of the Episcopate to be 
considered at this time one of the three estates of the realm is a weightier 
matter. The very able and learned writer of ‘A Petition directed 
to her most excellent Maiestie’ [1589] discusses the question with much 
legal knowledge and acumen, Matt. Sutcliffe had at an earlier date 
made the like “claim, and the argument of the Petition is addressed first 

of all to him, and to his observations in an English treatise against the 
Jesuit Parsons. The effort of the bishops, let ‘it be clearly understood, 
is to identify defamation of themselves with defamation of her Majesty, 
inasmuch as they are members of ‘hir Maiesties body politike and 


- uphelde by hir lawes.’ Granted, says our author, that such writers as 


Martin Marprelate do defame the bishops, then do they not defame her 
Magesty, according to ‘the statute of Newes’ (quoted by him as 23 liz. 
ca. 2, Newes 6). There are, he says, two general Bodies Politic in this 
land (@) her Majesty, (0) the Body Politic of the Realme, containing 
Three Estates—the Queen’s Majesty, the Lords, and the Commons, giving 
as marginal references 11 Hen. VI1. 27 ; 7 Hen. VII. 24, 15 [Hen. Vil] 
36 and 37; Hen. VIII. Dier. 60. Since the time of Henry IT. the 
Bishops have attended the King’s Court along with the Barons, retiring, 
however, from any case involving loss of life or limb ; but they wera 
present by grace and favour and not de jure, being called, if they were 
godly, for consultation on»Church affairs. Now, however, he says, 
referring directly to the words of Bishop Cooper quoted above, they 
boldly insinuate that the Statutes have no force without them. But in 
proof that they are wrong, he points out that many laws have been 
made without them, when they were absent, and when they utterly 
refused to assent to their being passed. ‘The writer’s réferences on this 
point are interesting : ‘ Jewell, Def. Apo. pag. 644 ; Nowell, Dor{ man): 
Disp(roof| p. 13; ‘Fox Afcts] and M[onumeuts] p. 421; Bilson [later 
Bishop of W. inchester ] Book in 4° [a reply to Aue Apology for the 
fing. Colleges at Rome and Rheims, entitled Vhe true Difference bet. 
Christian Subjection and Antichristian Rebellion—lb85] p. 536; Lam- 
bert, Peramb{ ulation | of Kent, p. 221.’ He then concludes his argument 
by observing that seeing Bishops are not one of the three Estates of the 
Realm, or of the Body Politic of the Realm otherwise than common 
subjects be, it canuot be said that they are members of her Majesty’s 
Body Politic. Therefore the defaming of them no more touches the

Good Reader, if thou know of any that dare argue or 
dispute against any of the former points, that is, if thou 
Know of any that dare defend Christ Jesus and His 
prerogative, the truth of His word, the credit of St. Paul, 
the verity of the Apostles’ Creed, her Majesty and her 
prerogative, and stand to the received truth in the Reformed 
Churches, and gainsay Popish errors; briefly, if thou know 
of any that dare defend the State of England, not to be so 
disordered, as before is set down (Article 29), and dare 
withstand the public general dishonour and slander of the 
whole English nation (Article 80), let him set up his name 
and we will send a pursuivant for him. Whosoever he be, 
the matters shall be according unto order quietly tried out 
between him and the bare walls in the Gatehouse or some 
other prison.

INTRODUCTORY NOTE 


In our introductory remarks to Tur Mrverauus reference 

was made to the removal of the Marprelate Press from 

Fawsley and its neighbourhood to Coventry, where that 

ad interim broadside and also the present Tract were printed 

by Waldegrave, set up in his handsome black letter type. 

The original is a small quarto of 58 pp. (sig. A—-Bi vers.= 

10 pp. + 1-47 + blank). The last two pages are signatured 

Hi, end in all the copies we have been able to examine, 

they occur as a single leaf attached by paste to the 
remainder of the work. This additional labour has to be 
taken into account in estimating the time occupied in the 
production of Hay any Works, which also for other reasons, 
as we gather, was longer than was expected. The illness. of 
his assistant while at J’awsley may have disorganised 
Waldegrave’s arrangements. Steven, Sir Richard Knight- 
ley’s servant, was despatched to Coventry for copies too 
soon by a week, and that notwithstanding the haste of 
John Hales to get the press away from his premises. 
Waldegrave stated, according to Henry Sharpe’s evidence 
(Harl. MSS. [Baker’s Transcripts] 7042.23), ‘that one of 
Master Hales men kept him so closely at worke, that for 
that tyme, he had lyved as in a Prison, and could not have 
oftentymes warme meate. The Tract occupied three 
weeks in printing and was put into circulation about 
March 22nd, 1589. 

Hay any Worke owes its title to the appearance during 
the first days of January, 1588-9, of the official reply to the 
first attack of Marprelate. This was entitled An Admonition 
to the People of England, and was signed T. C., naturally 
suggesting the earlier Admonitions bearing the same 


oo 
initials, but written by the celebrated Puritan leader 


200 INTRODUCTORY NOTE 


Thomas Cartwright. The author ofthe present Admonition, 
however, was Thomas Cooper, Bishop of Winchester. Like 
all the official defences published by the hierarchy during 
the previous twenty years, it was a collaboration, the 
reputed author acting as editor to the contributions of 
the various episcopal disputants and revisers. Whitgift’s 
replies to Cartwright in the controversy which followed the 
publication of the Admonition to Parliament were greatly 
delayed by sending the manuscript backward and forward 
to Archbishop Parker and the committee of bishops 
appointed to co-operate in the work of revision. In the 
present case the Archbishop was associated with the Bishops 
of London, Rochester and Lincoln in supervising Bishop 
Cooper’s reply to Marprelate’s Hpistin, each bishop con- 
tributing a personal reply to the charges laid against him. 
This will explain why, published in January, 1589, the 
episcopal Admonition contains only the barest reference to 
the second ‘Martin’ which was in the hands of the 
bishops early in December. 

Martin lost no time in taking up the episcopal challenge, 
adopting as his title a familiar London street cry, ‘Ha’ ye 
any work for the Cooper?’ The time of the year is 
indicated in his opening lines where he refuses to tell the 
bishops where he is because, he says, ‘I love not the air of 
the Clink or Gatehouse [two London prisons] in this cold 
time of Winter.’ 

Beyond the several replies of the Bishops concerned to 
the personal charges of Marprelate, the Admonition contains 
a general defence of the Kpiscopate in regard to their 
covetousness, the tyranny of their ecclesiastical courts, and 
their worldly ambitions. The Scriptural authority and the 
expediency of the State in supplying bishops with liberal 
incomes are set forth at large. But Martin tells the truth 
when he says to them-—‘ You bestow not full fifty pages in 
the answer of anything that ever was published in print; 
the rest are bestowed to maintain the belly, and to confute 
——what think you ?——even the slanderous piventions of your

INTRODUCTORY NOTE 201 


ee 
own brains, for the most part.’ The serious part of 
Hay any Works is devoted to setting forth the scriptural 


2 


authority claimed by the Puritans for the rule of the _ 


Church by Pastors, Doctors, Elders and Deacons; which 
offices they contend are divinely ordained, and are 
integral elements of the body-—i.c., the Church, and cannot 
be changed by mere human choice. 

A fresh crop of charges is preferred against the Church 
dignitaries and the clergy; the defence of the old charges 
offered in the Admonition is also severely examined. The 
reader will not fail to note the deepening opposition of the 
‘precise brethren, who look askance at their champion. 
Oppressed though they be, the boisterous jocularity of 
Martin and his personal ridicule of the bishops offends their 
solemn sense of propriety. The self-defence of Marprelate 
in this respect is a noteworthy feature of Hay any Worke. 
It completely reveals his personal attitude. There are 
matters on which he will not jest; but his course in his 
Tracts has been regular and lawful. Only by jesting could 
he draw the attention of the multitude to the actions of the 
Bishops. Therefore he used the weapon of fun and ridicule 
—though, he protests, he ‘ never profaned the Word in any 
jest.’ ‘The Lord being the author both of mirth and 
gravity, is it not lawful for the truth to use either of these 
ways, when the circumstances do make it lawful ?’ 

The Archbishop, as the fountain-head of the forces of 
persecution, is not long absent from Martin’s pages, but the 
edge of his invective, as in Tne Eprromn, is turned against 
the meaner frailties and vices of Dr. John Aylmer, the 
Bishop of London. The Tract had been prepared hastily, 
but Martin, addressing the bishops, says it ‘may serve for 
an answer unto the latter part of your book until Morz 
Worx ror tnx Cooper be published.’ 

The history of the production of the Tract will be found 
in the Historical Introduction; see pp. 180 f., ‘(18) The 
Coventry Pamplhiets,’

HAY ANY WORKE FOR COOPER (1). 


Or a brief ’Pistle directed by way of an 
H{ublication (2) to the Reverend Bishops, coun- 
selling them, if they will needs be barreled up for fear of 

smelling in the nostrils of Her Majesty and the State, 
that they would use the advice of Reverend Martin, 
for the providing of their Cooper. Because the 
Reverend T. C.—by which mystical letters is 
understood, either the bouncing Parson of 
Eastmeon or Tom Cokes his chaplain— 
hath showed himself in his late ‘ Admoni- 
tion to the People of England’ (2) to be 
an unskilful and beceitful (3) tub- 
trimmer. 


Wherein, worthy Martin quits himself like a man, 
I warrant you, in defence of his self and his learned 
’Pistles, and makes the Cooper’s hoops to fly off, 
and the Bishop’s tubs to leak out of all ery (4). 


Penned and Compiled by MARTIN the Metropolitan. 


Printed in Europe, not far from some of the Bouncing Priests.

(1) In the Introductory Notes to the present Tract the selection of 
the London streect-ery, which may be found in Tempesta’s curious 
volume on the Cries of London, is explained. Bishop Thomas Cooper of 
Vinchester is further identified as the ‘Parson of Hastmeane,’ that is, 
of Eastmeon, near Petersfield, in Hants, no doubt one of his commendams. 
The alternative reference to ‘Tom Cokes, his chaplain,’ written below, 
p. 216, ‘Thomas Cook,’ is Martin’s satirical suggestion as to the ability 
displayed in the writing of the episcopal Admonition. The other T.C., 
Tom Cokes, might well have written it. 

(2) The words ‘bath showed himself in his late Admonition to the 
People of England are omitted from the original title-page and are 
given in the ‘ Faults Escaped’ at the close of the Tract. 

(3) It is part of. Martin’s literary apparatus to assume from time to 
time the punning blunders of an illiterate rustic, 

(4) Ont of all measure.

THE EPISTLE TO THE TERRIBLE PRIESTS 


A Man of Worship to the Men of Worship; that is, 
Martin Marprelate, Gentleman, Primate, and Metropolitan 
of all the Martins wheresoever, to the John of all the Sir 
Johns (1), and to the rest of the terrible Priests, saith, 
Have among you, once again, my Clergy Masters! For— 


O Brethren, there is such a deal of love grown of late, I 
perceive, between you and me that, although I would be 
negligent in sending my ’pistles unto you, yet I see you 
cannot forget me. J thought you to be very kind, when you 
sent your pursuivants about the country to seek for me. 
But now that you yourselves have taken the pains to write, 
this is out of all cry. Why, it passeth to think what loving 
and careful brethren I have; who, although I cannot be 
gotten to tell them where I am, because I love not the air of 
the Clink or Gatehouse (2) in this cold time of winter, and by 


(1) Sir was a common title for a clergyman ; the Shakespearean in- 
stances of Sir Hugh Evans in The Merry Wives of Windsor and Sir 
Topas in The Twelfth Night (where the name is borrowed from Chaucer’s 
Sir Thopas) are familiar to everybody. It arose from the order of 
admitting to a degree at the Universities. The candidate was addressed 
in a formula beginning ‘ Domine (and the candidate’s name) ego admitto 
te,’ &c. Then ‘his name appeared in the University and College 
books with the prefix for that [i.e., the Bachelor’s] degree (in Latin. 
Dominus contracted Ds; in Enelish Sir, contracted fr.) See Register 
of the Univ. of Oxford, edited by Andrew Clark, M.A., Vol. I1., 
Part I., p. 50. The lists at Cambridge are still published with the 
contraction Ds. Clerzymen were supposed, at least in the pre-Eliza- 
bethan days, to possess the Bachelor’s degree, and so were addressed by 
the title Sir, and as the equivalent of Dominus the title was also used 
where Saint is conventionally employed. The title ‘Sir John’ for 
clergymen generally, and especially for the inferior sort, was used 
more or less humorously. ‘Thus in the following from William Tyndale, 
the martyr: ‘The popes Kingdome is of the worlde. Jor there one 
sort one [one discriminates or distinguishes one as] youre grace / youre 
holynesse / youre fatherho[o]d: Another / master doctor / father / 
bacchelare / master person / master vicar / and at the last cometh in 
simple syr Jhon.’—The Practyse of Prelates (1530), Sig. B. 

Martin himself enters into a half-serious defence of bis practice of 
Writing ‘Sir’ for ‘Saint’ later in this tract. See below, p. 224. 

(2) For the Clink and Gatehouse, see Hist. Intro., pp. 131 f. The 
reference to the winter agrees with the chronology of the Tracts. 
Bishop Cooper’s Admonition was published in the first days of January, 
1689, and the present Tract in March.

214 THE MARPRELATE TRACTS 


reason of my business in ’pistle-making, will notwithstanding, 
make it known unto the world that they have a month’s 
mind (1) towards me. Now, truly, Brethren, I find you 
kind. Why, ye do not know what a pleasure you have done 
me. My Worship’s books were unknown to many before 
you allowed T. C, to admonish the people of England to 
take heed that, if they loved you, they would make much 
of their prelates, and the chief of the clergy. Now, many 
seek after my books, more than ever they did. Again, 
some knew not that our Brother, John of Fulham, was so 
good unto the porter of his gate, as to make the poor, blind, 
honest soul to be a dumb minister (2). Many did not 
know, either, that ‘Amen’ is as much as ‘By my faith!’; 
and, so, that our Saviour Christ ever sware by His faith. (3) 
Or, that bowling and eating on (4) the Sabbath are of the 
same nature; that bishops may as lawfully make blind 
guides as David might eat of the shewbread; or, that 
Father Thomas tub-trimmer of Winchester, good old 
student, is a Master of Arts of forty-five years’ standing. (5) 
Many, I say, | were ignorant of these things, and [of] many 
other pretty toys, until you wrote this pretty book. Besides, 
whatsoever you overpass in my writings, and did not gainsay, 
that I hope will be judged to be true. And so, John a’ 


(1) Month’s mind =a yearning remembrance. See Hist. Intro., 
95.9: 

(2) See further reference, p. 278. 

(3) Seep. 279. 

(4) Al, ‘of.’ 

(5) Martin has classed Bishop Cooper with the less learned bishops, 
Tue EpIstte, p. 87 (Gvhere the celebrated controversy with Dr. Sparke 
is mentioned), and p. 90 (where he accuses him of ‘conveying’ the 
learning of his Vhesaurus from R. Stephanus’ work); and Cooper 
replies that he ‘hath not ysed (God bee thanked) to vaunt himselfe of 
great learning. Neyther doth he disdaine to be accounted vnlearned of 
these men, which many years since contemned Bishoppe Jewell .as a 
man of no deepe learning, and euen of late daies could saye that Hrasmus 
was no Diuine. His praier is, that the small measure of knowledge, which 
it pleased God to gine him in the continuance of fiftie yeeres studie, may 
be imployed to the glorie of God, and the benetite of his Countroy. It 
is knowen fiue and forty yeres since that he was Master of Arts, and 
Student of Diuinitie, and disputed in that facultie: since which time 
hee was neuer drawen from that exercise of good learning.’—Admonition, 
72 verso (the separate pagination is omitted by a printer’s error). 
See in the present Tract, p. 281, and the Hist. Intro., 127, 165.

Bridges’ treason (1), out of the 448th page of his book, you 
grant to be true. Yourselves you deny not to be petty popes. 
The Bishop of Sir David’s, in Wales, you deny not to have 
two wives ; with a hundred other things which you do not 
gainsay (2). So that the reader may judge that I am true 
of my word, and use not.to lie like bishops. And this hath 
greatly commended my Worship’s good dealing. But, in 
your confutation of my book, you have showed Reverend 
Martin to be truepenny (3) indeed; for you have confirmed 
rather than confuted him. So that, Brethren, the pleasure 
which you have done unto me is out of all scotch and noteh (4). 
And why should I not again be as ready to pleasure 
you? Nay, then I should be ag ungrateful towards my 
good brethren, as John of Canterbury is to Thomas Cart- 
wright. The which John, although he hath been greatly 
favoured by the said Thomas, in that Thomas hath now, 
these many years, let him alone and said nothing unto hin, 
for not answering his books (5), yet is not ashamed to make a 
secret comparison between himself and Thomas Cartwright. 
As who [should] say, John of Lambeth were as learned as 
Thomas Cartwright. What say you, old Dean John a’ 
Bridges? Have you not showed yourself thankful unto her 
Majesty in overthrowing her supremacy in the 448th page 
of your book? J will lay on[e] load on your skin-coat for 
this gear, anon. 

And I will have my pennyworths of all you brethren, ere 
T have done with you, for this pains which your J’. C. hath 
taken with me. ‘This is the Puritans’ craft in procuring me 
to be confuted, I know(6). I'll be even withthem, too. A

crafty, whoresons brethren-bishops, did you think because 
the Puritans’ T. C. did set John of Cant. at a non- 
plus, | and gave him the overthrow, that therefore your 
T. C., alias Thomas Cooper, Bishop of Winchester, or 
Thomas Cook (x), his chaplain, could set ine at a non-plus ? 
Simple fellows! methinks he should not. 

J guess your T. C. to be Thomas Cooper, but I do not 
peremptorily affirm it, because the modest old student of 
fifty-two years’ standing setteth Winchester after Lincoln 
and Rochester, in the Contents of his book; which blas- 
phemy would not have been tolerated by them that saw and 
allowed the book, unless Mistress Cooper’s husband had 
been the author of it (2). 

Secondly, because this T. C., the author of this book, is 
a bishop, and therefore Thomas Cooper, he is a bishop, 
because he reckoneth himself charged, among others, 
with those crimes, whereof none are accused but bishops 
alone (page 101, line 26) (3). Ha! old Martin; yet I 
see thou hast it in thee, thou wilt enter into the bowels 
of the cause in hand, I perceive. Nay, if you willcommand 
me, I will give you more reasons yet. The style and the 
phrase is very like her husband’s, that was sometimes wont 
to write unto Dr. Day of Wells. You see, I can do it, 
indeed. Again, none would be so grosshead as to gather, 
because my Reverence telleth Dean John that he shall have 
twenty fists about his ears more than his own, (whereby I 


bene in more than twentie prisons / And for once imprisonment by 
the byshops, I haue bene more then thrise imprisoned by the preachers or 
their procuringe /’—‘ A New Years Guift, edited for the Congregational 
Historical Society by Champlin Burrage, M.A. See below, p. 238, and 
especially p. 245, where Martin has the significant sentence, ‘It is their 
[the Puritans’] weakness [that] L am threatened to be hanged by you 
| Bishops ].’ 

(1) His name is given on the title-page as ‘Tom Cokes.’ He is 
probably to be identified with the Thomas Cook in the list of deacong 
ordained by the Bishop of London, April 25, 1560.—Strype’s Grindal, 59. 

(2) The scande!l which led to Martin describing the Lishop of Win- 
chester as Mistress Cooper’s husband has been sufficiently alluded to 
in the Introduction. He was no doubt much to be pitied. Her associa- 
tion with Dr. Day is again referred to a few sentences further on. 

(3) The charge is that the bishops uphold an unlearned ministry with 
yarious serious results issuing therefrom; the apologist, identifying him- 
self with the accused bishops, trusts that God will ‘regard the innocencie 
of our hearts.’

(1) See THE EPiIstLe, p. 18, note (4), and present Tract, p. 246. Staf- 
ford-law’ is a law identified popularly with other towns besides Stafford. 
It is the law of force majeure ;. you first hang your man and subsequently 
try him. 

(2) Martin was unfortunate that while correcting the episcopal Greek 
his printer made him spell] the word wrongly. In the original it is 
printed ewlogeni. The transposition of the two last letters is corrected in 
the list of errata. 

(3) Martin throughout the earlier Tracts tries to enlarge the use 
of written characters, to make them signify chuckling laughter and 
other signs of emotion. 

(4) From an interesting note in Murray’s Dictionary we extract the 
following : ‘Grue is commonly taken to be O. I. gru = meal, grain (see 
Gruel). ‘Not a grue” has a curious likeness to the Greek ot8é yp, which 
appears in the Latin comedies as ne gry quidem; the difliculty is to 
know how it could have been adopted into M. English. Not a grue, no 
grue = not an atom, not a whit.’—It looks here as though Martin were 
punning, using the not infrequent expression ‘no grue’ to signify also 
“no Greek.’

had as hef play twenty nobles in a night at primero on the

Why, a round threepence serveth the turn to make good

in ’pistle-making as you have at primero, and far more

Earl the patronage of his archdeaconry for one turn. He appeared to 
enjoy the work of suppressing Romanists, and readily carried ont the 
instructions of the Council to flog a young girl who professed to be 
inspired. He was unbending in his severity towards evangelical non- 
conformity. An anecodote quoted by White from Harington’s Briefe 
View throws a sidelight on his character. He appealed to his patron 
for permission to marry, not caring to lose any chance of promotion and 
mindful of the Queen’s dislike of married clergy. Harington, however, 
gives Overton’s views of marriage as expressed in one of his scrmons. 
“The choice of @ wife was full of hazard, not unlike as if one, in a barrell 
full of serpents, should grope for one fish: if he scape harm of tha 
snakes and light on a fish, he may be thought fortunate, yet let him not 
boast, for perhaps it may be but an Nele.’—Aliz. Bishops, 265. Overton 
was a man of an overbearing and violent temper, and had on occasion 
to be corrected by the Privy Council.

The Puritans, indeed, hold it unlawful for a minister to 
have such temporal revenues as whereby then ministers 
might be well maintained; unless the said revenues come to 
him by inheritance. 

They hold it also unlawful for any State to bestow the 
livings of many ministers upon one alone; especially when 
there is such want of ministers’ livings.

They hold it unlawful for any minister to be lord over . 
his brethren; and they hold it unlawful for any State to 
tolerate such under their government. Because it is 
unlawful for States to tolerate men in those places, where- 
into the Word hath forbidden them to enter. 

They affirm that our Saviour Christ hath forbidden all 
ministers to be lords (1) (luke 22%). And the Apostle 
Peter showeth them to be none of God’s ministers which 
are lords over God’s heritage, as you Bishops are and would 
be accounted. These things, T. C., you should have con- 
futed, and not troubled yourself to execute the fruits of your 
own brains, as an enemy to the State. And in these points 
I do challenge you, T. C., and you, Dean John [Bridges], 
and you, John Whitgift, and you, Dr. Cosins (2), and you 
Dr. Capease (Copcote (2) I think | your name be), and as A 4 vers. 
many else as have, or dare, write in defence of the established 
church government. If you cannot confute my former 
assertions, you do but in vain think to maintain yourselves 
by slanders, in fathering upon the Puritans the offsprings 
of your own blockheads. And, assure yourselves, I will so. 
besoop (3) you, if you cannot defend yourselves in these 
points, as all the world shall cry shame upon you. You 
think prettily to escape the point of your antichristian 
callings, by giving out that Puritans hold it unlawful 
for her Majesty to leave any lands for the use of the 

minister’s maintenance. I cannot but commend you; for, 
I promise you, you can shift off an heinous accusation very

robber by the highway side, and desireth the judge that the 
law may proceed against him. ‘O no, my lord,’ saith the 
thief, ‘in any case let me not be dealt with. For these, 
mine accusers, have given out that you are a drunkard,’ (or, 
‘they have committed treason against the State’); ‘therefore, 
I pray you, believe my slander against them, that they may 
be executed. So, when I come to my trial, I shall be sure 
to have no accusers.’ 

A very pretty way to escape, if a man could tell how to 
bring the matter about. Now, Brethren Bishops, your 
manner of dealing is even the very same. The Puritans 
say truly that all lord bishops are petty antichrists; and, 
therefore, that thé magistrates ought to thrust you out of 
the Commonwealth. ‘Now, of all loves,’ say the bishops, 
“let not our places be called in question (z); but rather 
credit our slanders against the Puritans, whereby, if men 
would believe us when we lie, we would bear the world in 
hand (2) that these our accusers are malcontents and sottish 
men, holding it unlawful for the magistrate to allot any 
lands for the minister’s portion, and unlawful for the 
minister to provide for his family. And therefore, you must 
not give ear to the ac | cusations of any such men against 
us. And so, we shall be sure to be acquitted.’ But, Brethren, 
do you think to be thus cleared? Why, the Puritans hold 
no such points as you lay to their charge. Though [if] 
they did, as they do not, yet that were no sufficient reason 
why you, being petty popes, should be maintained in a 
Christian commonwealth. Answer the reasons that I 
brought against you; otherwise, ‘come off, you Bishops, 
leave your thousands, and content yourselves with your 
hundreds’ saith John of London (3). So that you do 
plainly see that your Cooper, IT. C., is but a deceitful

(4) St. Mary Overie, a famous Southwark church at this time, and 
frequently mentioned in the literature of the period. The name is a con~ 
traction of St. Mary ‘over the way’ or ‘over the water,’ that is on the 
south side of the Thames. The name has been lost through the merging of 
the adjoining small parishes into a new ecclesiastical area. First the 
parochial districts of St. Mary Magdalen and St. Margaret-on-the-hill 
were united. The fine old priory church of St. Mary Overie then became 
the church of the new parish, under the name of St. Saviours. It is the 
cathedral church of tho now see of Southwark.—See Maitland’s Hisé. 
of London, Stowe’s Survey of London, and Newton's London in the Olden

(15 Bankside, Southwark, between London Bridge and Blackfriars 
Bridge, had’a very evil reputation. Gabriel Harvey, in his Four Letters 
(1592) mentions, in his indictment of Greene, ‘his infamous resorting 
to Bankside . . . and other filthy haunts.’—Archaica, by Sir E. Brydges, 
vol. ij., p. 7. In the time of the Tudors it consisted of a single row 
of houses built on a bank or levee. At one end of the Bankside stood the 
Clink Prison, Winchester House (the Bishop’s town house), and St. Mary 
Overie’s. At the other end was the Falcon Tavern, and behind it were 
the Paris Gardens. A little to the west of the Clink and behind the 
houses stood the GJobe Theatre, and close beside it the Bull Ring.— 
Besant’s London, 356. In the old maps the riverside running west- 
wards from Southwark Bridge is named ‘Stew Bank,’ after the candid 
fashion of the time. The careful reader will not need to be told that the 
Globe Theatre mentioned above was not erected at the date of the 
present Tract. The Globe was the ‘new theatre’ put up in 1596. Bank~ 
side was in the parish of St. Mary Overie ; concerning it and its evil 
haunts, see further, THHSES MARTINIAWZ, p. 310, note (2).
