(1) Glibbery, of Halstead, in Nssex, must have been an eccentric person 
even amongst the Elizabethan clergy. The reference to the games, 
however, brings vividly before us an outstanding -feature in Hnuglish 
life during the Middle Ages; surviving, but with diminishing respect, 
through the Tudor period and onwards, and faintly trace able in many. 
country customs even to-day. To some extent the May-day revels, 
the Robin Hood show, and other public entertainments, such as the 
visit of some nobleman’s wrsenarius or bearward, were recognised as 
a public charge. In the reigns of Hen. VIII. and Edw. VI. grants are 
noted in the town records of Shrewsbury for the show of Lord Abbot 
of Markham—sometimes Marall, Mardol, or Mayvoll (May #'ool)—the 
Lord of Misrule ; and it is noted that the buffoon was generally a clerical 
character. In the records of the same ancient town we learn that in 
MWary’s days grants were made for the representation of Robin Hood. 

‘Sol pro tunicis et aliis vestimentis ac pictura earunden pro Robyn 
Hiood. Et in vino dat’ eisdem int’ lusoribs, (Paid for jackets and 


: other vestments and the painting of the same for Robin Hood 


[59s. 2d.]. And in wine given to the same interluders [I4s. ].’ 
See Owen and Blakeway’s /Hist. of Shrewsbury, i., 333. 


“The connection between the Robin Hood play and the Morris—that is, 


Moresco or Moorish—Dance is obscure. A further note on the Robin 
Hood play will be found in Tur Just CrNsuRE AND ReEPRoor, p. 369, note 
(2) where one ‘ Anderson parson of Stepney’ is accused of taking the 
Potter’s part in the Play. The Vice takes us back to the old English 
Moralities, plays embodying some moral lesson, the ethical value of 
which may be gauged from the fact that usually the Vice was the 
buffoon of the interlude, representing either some specific vice, as envy, 
covetousness, &c., or vice in general. ‘Now issued in from the reareward 
madam Vice or old Iniquitie, with a lath dagger painted according to 
old Vice in a comedy.’—Owle’s Almanacke (1618), quoted by Nares. 
In further illustration of Martin’s charge against Glibbery, Maskell 
quotes from a copy in his possession of ‘ ‘Articles to be enquired of by 
the Church-wardens and Sworn-men within the Dieocesse of Lincoln, &c. 
1585,’—four years earlier than the date of Martin’s writing. The 
27th’ article sct down in this document by Bishop Wickham is ‘ Whether 
your Minister and Church-wardens haue ‘suffred any Lords of misrule or 
sommer Lords, or Ladies or any disguised person [dressed, that is, in 
character] in Christmas, or at maigames, or morris dancers or at any 
other time, to come vnreuerently into the Charel 1yard, and .there to 
daunce ot play any vnsemely part with scoffs, iests, wanton gestures, or 
Tibald talk, namely in the time of common praier: and what they be 
that commit such disorder or accompany or maintaine.’——Martin Marpre- 
late, p. 96. The latter part of the article indicates why the games fell 
into disrepute.

make all the hoops of your bishopricks fly asunder. There-

Our church government is an unlawful church government, 
and not allowed in the sight of God. 

Because, that church government is an unlawful church 
government, the oflices and officers whereof the civil magis- 
strate may lawfully abolish out of the church. (Mark my 
craft in reasoning, Brother T.C.) I say the offices and 
officers, for, I grant that the magistrate may thrust the 
officers of a lawful church government out of the church if 
they be Diotrepheses, Mar-Elms (1), Whitgifts, Simon 
Maguses (2), Coopers, Pernes (3), Reynoldses (4), or any such 
hike Judases (though the most of these must be packing 
offices and all) but their offices must stand, that the same 
may be supplied by honester men. But the offices of arch- 
bishops and bishops, and, therefore, the oflicers much more, 
may be lawfully abolished out of the church by her Majesty 
and our State. And truly this were brave weather to turn 
them out (5); itis pity tokeepthem in any longer. And that 
would do me good at the heart, to see John of London (and 
the rest of his brethren) so discharged of his business, as he 
might freely run in his cassock and hose after his bowl, or 
flourish with his two hand sword. O, ’tis a sweet trunch- 
fiddle (6). 

But the offices of archbishops and bishops may be law- 
fully abolished out of the church by her Majesty and the 
State; as I hope one day they shall be. Therefore—mark, 
now, T’. C., and carry me this conclusion to John o’ Lambeth 
for his breakfast—our church government by archbishops 
and bishops is an unlawful church government. You see,

Brother Cooper, that I am very courteous in my minor; for 
I desire therein no more offices to be thrust out of the 
church at one time but archbishops and bishops. As for 
deans, archdeacons and chancellors, I hope they will be so 
kind unto my Lord’s Grace as not to stay, if his Worship 
and the rest of the noble clergy-lords were turned out to 
grass. J will presently prove both major and minor of this 
syllogism. And, hold my cloak, there, somebody, that I 
may go roundly to work. For I’se so bumfeg (x) the 
Cooper, as he had been better to have hooped half the 
tubs in Winchester, then write against my Worship’s 
’pistles. 

No civil magistrate may lawfully either maim or deforme 
the body of Christ, which is the Church; but whosoever 
doth abolish any lawful church officer out of the Church 
government, he doth either maim or deform the Church. 
Therefore, T. C., no civil magistrate, no prince, no state, 
may, without sin, abolish any lawful officer, together with 
his office, out of the government of the Church; and per 
consequens (2), the offices of archbishops and lord bishops, 
which her Majesty may without sin lawfully abolish out of 
the church, are no lawful church officers; and therefore, 
also, the church government practised by John Whitgnft, 
John Mar-elm, Richard Peterborough (3), William of 
Lincoln (4), Edmond of Worcester (5), yea, and by that 
old stealcounter (6) mass-priest, John o’ Gloucester (7), with 
the rest of his brethren, is to be presently thrust out of the

explanation.

(3) Richard Howland.

Fourthly, that every Christian magistrate (1) is bound to 
receive this government by pastors, doctors, elders and 
deacons into the Church within his dominions, whatsoever 
inconvenience may be likely to follow the receiving of it. 
Becanse no likelihood of inconvenience ought to induce the 
magistrate willingly to permit the Church under his govern- 
ment to be maimed or deformed. 

Bifthly, that the government of the Church by lord 
archbishops and bishops is a government of deformed and 
unshapen members, serving no good use in the Church of 
God. Because it is not the government by pastors, doctors, 
elders and deacons; which, as 1 have showed, are now the 
only true members, that is, the only true officers of the 
visible body. 

Sixthly, and lastly, that they who defend this false and 
bastardly government of archbishops and bishops, and | with- 
stand this true and natural government of the Church by 
pastors, doctors, elders, and deacons are likely, in a while, 
to become Mar-prince, Mar-state, Mar-law, Mar-magistrate, 
Mar-commonwealth. As for Mar-church and Mar-religion, 
[these] they have long since proved themselves to be. 

These six points do necessarily follow of that which before 
I have set down, namely, that it is not lawful for any to 
abolish or alter the true and lawful government of the Church, 
because itis not lawful for them to maime or deforme the 
body of the Church. 

And I challenge you, T.C., and you, Dean Jobn, and you, 
John Whitgift, and you, Dy Cosins, and you, Dr. Copcot, and 
all the rest that will, or dare, defend our established church 
government, to be tried with me in a judgment of life and 
death, at any bar in England, in this point. Namely, 


- That you must needs be, not only trattors to God and His Word, 
but also enemies unto her Majesty and the land, i defending the 
established church government to be lawful.

But our archbishops and bishops, which hold it lawful for 
her Majesty and the State to retain this established form of 
governinent, and to keep out the government by pastors, 
doctors, elders and deacons, which was appointed by Christ, 
whom you, profane T.C., call ‘ you know not whom,’ hold it 
lawful for her Majesty and the State to bid God to 
battle against them. Because they bid the Lord to 


14 battle against them which main and deform | the body of 


Christ; viz., the Church. And they, as was declared 
maim and deform the body of the Church, which keep out 
the lawful office[r|s, appointed by the Lord to be members 
thereof, and, in their stead, place other wooden members of 
the invention of man. Therefore you, T.C., and you Dean 
John, and you John Whitgift, and you, the rest of the 
beastly defenders of the corrupt church government, are 
not only traitors to God and His Word, but enemies to her 
Majesty and the State. Like you any of these nuts, John 
Canterbury ? 

I am not disposed to jest in this serious matter. I am 
called Martin Marprelate. There be many that greatly 
dislike my doings (x1). Imay have my wants (2) I know;

forIamaman. But my course I know to be ordinary (1) 
and lawful. I saw the cause of Christ’s government, and of 
the Bishops’ antichristian dealing to be hidden. The most 
part of men could not be gotten to read anything written in 
the defence of the one, and against the other. I bethought 
me, therefore, of a way whereby men might be drawn to do 
both; perceiving the humours of men in these times 
(especially of those that are in any place) to be given to 
mirth. I took that course. I might lawfully do it. Aye, 
for jesting is lawful by circumstances, even in the greatest 
matters. ‘The circumstances of time, place, and persons 
urged me thereunto. I never profaned the Word in any 
jest. Other mirth I used as a covert (2), wherein I would 
bring the truth into ight. The Lord being the author both 
of mirth and gravity, is it not lawful in itself, for the truth 
to use either of these ways, when the circumstances do make 
it lawful ? 

My purpose was, and is, to do good. I know IJ have done 
no harm, howscever some may judge Martin to mar all (3). 
They are very weak ones that so think. In that which I 

have written, I know undoubtedly that I have done the Lord, 
and the State of this Kingdom, great service. Because I have 
in some sort discovered (4) the greatest enemies | thereof. 15 
And, by so much the most pestilent enemies, because they 
wound God’s religion, and corrupt the State with atheism 
and looseness, and so call for God’s vengeance upon us all, 
even under the colour of religion. I affirm them to be the 
greatest enemies that now our State hath; for if it were not 
for them, the truth should have more free passage herein,

than now it hath. All states thereby would be amended. 
And so, we should not be subject unto God’s displeasure, as 
now we are by reason of them. 

Now let me deal with these that are in authority. 

I do make it known unto them, that our Bishops are the 
greatest enemies which we have. For they do not only go 
about, but they have long since fully persuaded our State 
that they may lawfully procure (x) the Lord to take the 


‘sword in hand against the State (2). If this be true, have 


I not said truly that they are the greatest enemies which 
our State hath? The Papists work no such effect, for they 
are not trusted. ‘The atheists have not infected our whole 
State; these have. The attempts of our foreign enemies 
may be pernicious, but they are men as we are. But that 
God, with whom (3) our bishops have [made], and do make 
our Prince, and ow governors to wage war, who is able to 
stand against Him ? 

Well, to the point; many have put her Majesty, the 
Parliament, and Council, in mind, that the church officers 
now among us are not such as the Lord alloweth of; because 
they are not of his own ordaining. ‘They have showed that 
this fault is to be amended, or the Lord’s hand to be looked 
for. The bishops on the other side, have cried out upon 
them that-have thus dutifully moved the State. They with 
a loud voice gave out that the magistrate may lawfully 
maintain that church government which best fitteth our 
Estate as living in the time of peace. What do they else 
herein, but say that the magistrate in the time of peace, 
may maim and deform the body of Christ’s Church? That

either this government to be unlawful, or that the magistrate 
may presume to place those members in God’s church, 
which the Lord never mentioned in His Word. And, I 
beseech you, mark how the case standeth between these 
wretches and those whom they call Puritans. 

1. The Puritans (falsely so called) show it to be unlawful 
for the magistrate to go about to make any members for 


_the body of Christ. 


2. They hold all officers of the church to be members of 
the body (Rom.,12°; 1 Cor, 125), . 

3. And therefore they hold the altering, or the abolishing, 
of the offices of church government to be the altering and 
abolishing of the members of the Church. 

4, For the altering and abolishing of which members 
they hold to be unlawful, because it must needs be a maim 
unto the body. 

5. They hold Christ Jesus to have set down as exact, | 
and as unchangeable, a church government as ever Moses 
did (Heb. 8°). 

These, and such like, are the points they hold, Let their 
cause be tried, and if they hold any other points, in effect, 
but these, let them be hanged every man of them. Now, I 
demaud, whether they that hold the contrary im these points,

the body (for if they be not members what should they do 
in the body?) they hold it lawful for the magistrate to 
attempt the making of new members for that body. 

3. ‘The alteration or abolishing of these members by the 
magistrates, they hold to be lawful; and, therefore, the 
maiming or deforming [to be lawful].

you Mar-State, Mar-Law, Mar-Prince, Mar-Magistrate, Mar- 
Commonwealth, Mar-Church, and Mar-Religion! Are you

speech. What! May the magistrate cut off the true and 
natural members of the body of Christ? O, impudency, not 
to be tolerated! But our magistrate, that is, her Majesty,

you of{f], that is, displace you and your offices out of our

and many | other causes which you, Bishops Mar-State, do 25

(1) In the following quotation the word ‘ciuill’ in the first sentence 
is probably an error and should be ‘canon’; even then the argument is 
sufficiently far-fetched. ‘The vse and studie of the Ciuill (7) law will 
be utterly overthrowen: For the Ciuilians in this Realme liue not 
by the use of the Ciuill law, but by the offices of the Canon law, and such 
things as are within the compasse thereof. And if you take those 
offices and functions away, and those matters wherewith they deale in 
the Canon Lawe-: you must needes take away the hope of rewarde, and by 
that meanes, their whole Studie. And matters of Tithes, Testaments 
and Matrimonie, judgments also of Adulterie, Slaunder, Je. are in these 
judgements meere temporall, and therefore to bee dealt in by the tem~ 
porall Magistrate onely: Which as yet haue eyther none at all, or 
very fewe lawes touching those things.’—-Admonition, 77 recto and verso 
{no pag.). The meaning of these confused sentences is that most 
human interests at this time were determined by Canon Law: the 
changes demanded by the reformers would abolish the lucrative offices 
held by those who were learned canonists ; thenceforth no one would 
count, it worth while to study Canon Law: besides, how difficult it 
would be to transfer these causes to the civil jurisdiction, when the 
corpus of civil law contained so few enactments bearing upon such 
matters. The extreme simplicity and puerility of the argument seems 
characteristic of the episcopal mind.

must understand, doth account no Brownist to be a

(1) It is clear that when churches are voluntary associations pf 
Christians, ‘gathered’ voluntarily out of the general population, ac~- 
cording to the Congregational theory taught by Browne, the minister 
cannot with justice be supported by a pnblic tax such as the tithe. 
And in this connection it is well to remember that all churches to-day, 
including the State establishment, are voluntary associations. Martin 
in the above sentence draws a distinction between the Brownist and 
the Puritan ; some of the latler clung to the Hrastian idca of outwardly 
controlling the Church through the rule of the civil magistrate. These 
of course had no objection to having their religion supported by 
taxing other people. Martin does not always identify himself with 
the Puritan standpoint, and it is not easy to say how far he does so here, 
or in the next paragraph. One is always conscious of a certain measure 
of detachment of view in Martin. In this quality of mind be is much 
like the able writer of A Petition directed to H. M.

(1) This interesting generalisation of the true form of church govern- 
ment as understood by the ‘seekers after reformation’ is discussed 
in our Introduction. Here it is only necessary to guard the reader 
against. giving the word ‘ aristocratic” its ordinary modern connotation. 
Martin is not thinking so much of official grades within the church, as 
though the eldership were a kind of prelacy. Me is rather thinking of 
the elders as few in number. For his church is also democratical, and it 
is the Christian demos that elects the eldership. No doubt the democracy 


of the church would elect the best—the aristoi—to the honourable office 
of the eldership.

(1) See the same usage above, p. 234, note (1). 

(2) His knowledge of LElizabeth’s character gave the edge to 
Martin’s logic. Bridges was ont of touch with the realities of the case 
when he allowed only two categories of bishops in England, bishops 
of God and bishops of the devil, aud would not allow that the man-made 
bishop was other or better than a bishop of the devil. ‘he system estab- 
lished on the death of Mary was frankly Hrastian, and so Elizabeth 
kept it in practice. here was not a bishop of them all but owed his 
position to her will, and some even to her caprice. She was quite 
capable on her own initiative of unfrocking any of them. If the epis- 
copal junta approved of Bridges’ view of the episcopal appointment 
and authorisation they must deny being man-made, and face Elizabeth, 
who, not in esse but in posse, was the ‘supreme Governor’ of the 
church ; that is, lay themselves open to a charge of treason. See THE

against Whitgift, 7.e., tbat he held his ecclesiastical courts by virtue of 
Popish canons and not in the name and by the authority of her Majesty.

language of Hodge, the conventional rustic in Gammer Gurton’s Needle, 
ActI., Scene II. Petheram in a note on this usage quotes Steevens’ remark ~ 
in his edition of Shakespeare’s Lear, ‘When our ancient writers have 
eccasion to introduce a rustick, they commonly allot him the Somersetr 
shire dialect. Mercury, in the second Book of Ovid’s Metamorphoses, 


assumes the appearance of a clown, and our translator Golding has made 
him speak with the provinciality of Shakespeare’s Edgar.’

Reverend Martin. 


I hope, Tl’. C., that thou dost not mean to serve the Church 
with worse than we have. What, worse than John of 
Canterbury ? Worse than Tom Tubtrimmer of Winchester ? 
Worse than the vicars of hell, Sir Geoffrey Jones, the parson 
of Mickleham (1), &c.? I pray thee, rather than we should 
have a change from evil to worse, let us have the evil still. 
But I care not, if I abide the venture ofthe change.. There- 
fore get John with his Canterburiness removed, &c. (whom 
thon acknowledgest to be evil), and I do not doubt if worse 
come in their stead, but the devil will soon fetch them 
away, and so we shall be quickly rid both of evil and worse. 
But, good T. C., is it possible to find worse than we have ? 
I do not marvel, though thou callest me libeller, when thou 
darest abuse the prophets far worse than in calling them 
libellers ; for J tell thee true, thou couldest not have, any way, 
so stained their good names, as thou hast done in comparing 
them to ourbishops. Call me libelicr as often as thou wilt ; 
I do not greatly care. But, and thou lovest me, never liken 
me to our ‘ bishops of the devil.’ Tor I cannot abide to 
be compared unto those. For by thine own comparison, in 
the 9th page, they are just Balaams, up and down (2). 


Reverend T. C., pages 8, 9, 10. 


Though our bishops be as evil as Judas, the false apostles 
and Balaam, yet, because they have sometimes brought 
unto us God’s message, we must think no otherwise of 


Euangelists, and therefore may thinke our selues thrise happy, if wee 
haue tollerable Ministers, though they bee farre from the rule that 
Christian perfection requireth.’—P. 5. ; 

(3) &t. Micklain. See THE Epistle, pp. 83, and 92, § 2.

of Gods trueth, and the light of his holie word, as in decde you haue : the 
cogitation of this benefite shoulde moue your mindes more fauourably to 
thinke of them, and more charitably to iudge of their doinges. . . . For 
men will thinke this: If these people did fauour the Gospell they would 
rather seeke meanes to hide the blemishes and imperfections of their 
Prelates and Preachers, then thus odiously to amplifie and paint foorth 
their discredite to their vtter shame and reproche in the worlde.’-— 
Cooper’s Admonition, 9.

Reverend Martin. 


First, T. C., Thave truly gathered thine argument, though 
thou namest neither Judas nor the false apostles. Prove it 
otherwise! Then hast thou, reverend Martin, proved thy- 
selfa liar. Now secondly, then, seeing it is so, I pray thee, 
good, honest ‘I’. C., desire our Judases (who was also one of 
the first apostles) not to sell their Master for money. 
Desire our false apostles (who preach no false doctrine for 
the most part) not to insult our poor Paul; and desire our 
good Balaams not to follow the wages of unrighteousness. 
The counselis good. For Judas, though one of the first 
publishers of the Gospel (so were not our bishops in our 
time) yet hung himself. The false apostles had their reward, 
I doubt not. And Balaam, assoon as ever the Israelites 
took him, was justly executed for his wickedness. The 
forced blessing, wherewith he blessed them, saved him not.

Yea, I beseech you that are in authority, in any case not 
to believe any truth against our bishops; for these Puritans,.

no worse than Balaam was, there is no reason why they 
should be dishked. You know this is a troublesome world ; 
men cannot come into any mere | living without friends. 
And it is no reason why a man should trouble his friend 
and give him nothing; a hundred pounds and a gelding is 
yet better than nothing (1). To bowl but seven days in 
the week is a very tolerable recreation (2). You must know 
that John of London hath sometimes preached (as this 
profane T. C. hath given out to his no small commendations) 
thrice in a year at Paul’s Cross (3). It is reason that 


and sundry others of the like sort, whose wickednesse and corrupting of

equivalent for rascal; of Anabaptism as a religious socialism and as a 
general revolutionary propaganda, except among a few Continental refu- 
gees possibly, there is little or no trace at this time, and at no time was 
it an Emelish movement. The doctrines of Henry Niklaes, who pro- 
pounded the mystic conception of the Family of Love, never affected 
English Puritanism ; and it is doubtful if they were on the Continent or 
in ‘England ever associated with any immoral theory of life. Martin’s 
satire, which must not be overlooked, lies in his brief but accurate 
summary of Cooper’s method. ‘The accusation is that the bishops are 
covetous, &c. Cooper’s refutation is that it cannot be proved that they 
are horrible idolaters

(1) Ten per cent. interest on the moneys he lent. 

(2) This is an accurate smumary of Cooper’s argument on the pages 
referred to. 

(3) Bishop Westfaling is recognised by Martin as something of an 
exception amongst Elizabeth’s bishops ; his superiority to ecclesiastical 
corruption was so unusual. This brief elliptic introduction of his name 
I therefore take to mean that this one sober and incorruptible prelate 
cannot save the clergy from a general condemnation. See Tun WeistLy, 
p- 25, note). 

(4) Pulcher’s is the common London abbreviation for St. Sepulchre’s. 
Parson William Gravat or Gravet, here described as one of Aylmer’s 
‘boosing companions’ (the expression sounds curiously modern), was in- 
stituted to St. Sepulchre’s in 1566 and held a prebend and a couple of 
livines in commendam, We is referred to in TH» Just CENSURE, p. 369, as 
‘drunken Gravat.’ In June, 1588, he was appointed one of the censors 
of the press by Whitgift. He was a Peterhouse man, and published 
sermons and a short catechism. Ile was apparently one of a number 
of divines selected in 1582 by the Privy Council to hold conferences with 
the Jesuits and seminary priests. The Council supplied a series of rules 
to guide the conference.—Strype’s Whitg., I., 193.

Greeks should give up their troublesome orators. Demosthenes replied 
with the fable of the wolf in like case suggesting to the sheep to give 
up their noisy dogs. ‘fiuen so the subtile serpent Sathan . 
endeuoureth cunningly to perswade the shepheardes, that is, the chiefe 
Gouernours of this realme, to put away their barkine dogges, that is to 
put down the state of Bishops, and other chiefe of the Cleargie, to take 
away their lands and linings, and set them to their pensions, the sooner 
by that meanes to work his purpose.’--P. 28. 

(c) ‘The craftie enemie of the Church of. God .. . if he shall by any 
cunning bee able to pull away the reward of learning, hee right well 
seeth that hee shall haue farre fewer dogges to barke at him, and almost 
none that shall haue teeth to bite those hell houndes, that hee will sende 
to deuoure and destroy the flocke of Christ. . . . If the state of the 
Cleargie shall be made contemptible, and the best reward of learning 
a@ meane pension: he foresecth that neither yong flourishing wittes will 
easily incline themselues to godly learning, neither wil their parents 
and friendes suffer them to make that the ende of their tranaile,’— 
Pp. 23,20. 

‘Sathan’ and the ‘hell houndes’ are then divided into three classes :. 
(1) ‘such as be Papistes in heart and yet can clap their handes, &c.’ ; 
(2) ‘worldly and godlesse Epicures which can pretend religion,’ but 
whose real desire is that ‘they may bee partakers of that spoyle’ 
which in the proposed alterations may be hoped for; (3) ‘the thirde 
sort, in some respect the best, but of all other most dangerous ’—they, 
keep the others in countenance and invest their own proceedings with 
the character of zeal and godliness. These last are those that ‘in doctrine 
agree with the present state,’ that is, the Puritans.—Pp. 29, 3).

I would not have any true minister in the land want a 
sufficient living. But, good souls, I commend you yet, 
that are not so bashful but you will show your griefs. 
Is it the treading under foot of the glory of God that you 
fear, good men? No, no, say they, we could reasonably 
well bear that loss; but we die if we diminish the allowance 
of our kitchen. Let us be assured of that and our lordly 
callings, and we do not greatly care how other matters go. 
I will, when Morz Worx is published, help these young 
students unto a means to live; though they have none of 
your bishopdoms, if they will be ruled. by me.

of them calleth himself’. . . Martin,’ &c.

Bishopdom was reasonably caperclawed (1)? I have only 
published a ’Pistrm and a ’Prromm; wherein, also, I grant 
that I did reasonably ’pistle them. Therefore, T. C., you 
begin with a lie, in that you say that I have published 
either three or four books (2).

(1) See below, p. 282. Dr. Prime is again given the alias Wynken 
de Word (the old printer, apprentice and successor to Caxton) in THE 
Just CENSURE AND REPROOT, p. 863. It is there suggested that Dr. Prime 
was the author of a grammar ; a Latin grammar it would necessarily be. 
Wynken de Word was famous as a printer and publisher of school 
books and grammars; the Vulgaria and numerous Latin primers of 
Robert Whittington and the popular disciplinary manual for youths, 
Stans puer ad mensam, by John Sulpitius (see Almond for a Parrat 
(Peth.) 29), bear his imprint. This may have occasioned Dr. Prime’s 
nickname. Prime was a Fellow of New Coll., Oxon., and is credited by 
Wood (Athene Owon.) with being notorious for his puritanical pro- 
clivities. But seeing he had Bishop Cooper for his patron, and had only 
the previous November been special preacher at St. Mary’s, Oxford,

right in discounting his sympathies with ecclesiastical reform. His 
name occurs among a number of Oxford notabilitics who commended 
Case’s Moral Questions, and, more significantly, coupled with the names 
of Reynolds and Bilson as having been led astray by the Reims N. T. 
and its annotations. See Strype’s Annals, T11., i. 519, ii. 157.

?eview, from the MS. notebook of Dr. Plume, he appears as an 
ex-champion wrestler, and, when Primate of all England, still proud 
of his university fame as an athlete. At colleze he was given to 
‘rakchelling,’ by which ominous word we should understand nothing 
worse than a devotion to wrestling, cock-fighting, and the general 


rowdiness of the less intellectual undergraduate. Francis Pew, who had’ © 


often reproved him at Jesus College for such conduct, being asked by 
Bancroft when arebbishop, ‘ Did’st ever think to see me in this honour ?’ 
answered, with permission, ‘I believed I should sooner bave seen you 
hanged.’ Dr. Lanrence Chaderton, the Puritan (see THe HEpirome, 
p. 167, note (4)), is said to have shared in his earlier days at Cambridge 
Bancroft’s renown as a wrestler. Perhaps the remembrance of their 
bouts and rivalries led the Archbishop to leave Chaderton in the peace-

caine up to Lambeth he was singled out of the waiting crowd to the

pasted the word caw upon the word dare. And so, where

(1) Jolle = to beat.—Halliwell. 

(2) Martin and his contemporaries use the word discipline as a 
current and recognised name for the form of church government which 
the Puritans weré seeking to establish. John Udall entitled his exposi- 
tion of their views, 4 Demonstration of Discipline. 

(3) The words covered over are, ‘I will not deny if.’ 

(4) Deceive the world.

G6) BEA; 

(7) Here signifying authority. The pall (or pallium) was a garment 
worn by the Pope and then sent by him as a mark of special favour to 
such high ecclesiastics as patriarchs, metropolitans, primates, and more 
yarely to bishops. The Roman archbishop could not exercise his func- 
tions until he had received his pall, which he could not take with him 
from one see to another, nor could it be used by his successor ; and so the 
bestowal of this inexpensive garment—a slight scarf of white wool 
bordered with purple crosses, Jater, in Blizabeth’s time, of white silk— 
became a great source of papal revenue, and indeed of extortion.

Lo, T’. C. you see that I have a good gift in imitation ; 
and, methinks, I have brought your words into a 
marvellous good sense, whereas, before, in the cause 
of Waldegrave, they were ill-favouredly wrested. And 
as for his wife and children, they have just cause to 
eurse John of London, and John of Canterbury for their 
tyrannising over him, by imprisoning and spoiling his goods, 
and vexing his poor wife and children, with continual rifling 
his house with their pursuivants—who in November last 
violently rushed into his house, breaking through the main 
wall thereof after midnight, taking away his goods; for some 
of the pursuivants sold his books up and down the streets 
to watchmen and others (1). Ah, you antichristian Prelates, 
when will you make an end of defending your tyranny by 
the blood and rapine of her Majesty’s subjects? You have 
been the consumers of the fruits of Waldegrave’s labours. 
For have you not sent him so often to prison, that it seemed 
you made a common occupation thereof? Jor as soon as 
any book is printed in the defence of Christ’s holy Discipline, 
or for the detecting of your antichristian dealings, but your 
ravening pursuivants fly city and country to seek for 
Waldegrave; as though he were bound by statute unto you, 
either to make known who printed seditious books against my 
Lord’s face, or go to prison limself—and threatened with 
the rack! And are you not ashamed to say that he ever 
violated his faith? You know, well enough, that he is 
neither archbishop nor lord bishop. 

The case thus stood. After he had remained a long time 
in prison—not that time when Hartwell, his Grace’s secre- 
tary, wished that his Grace might never eat bit of bread after 


42he | released him—nor at that time when you, profane 


I’. C., told bim that all Puritans had traitorous hearts—nor 


danger, to their undoing. His wife and children have cause to curse 
all wicked and ungodly Wibellers.’—Bishbop Cooper’s Admonition, p. 41. 

(1) Only Waldegrave’s wife and children would be found at home at 
this time ; the information that he had returned from Molesey (vhere 
he had just printed the Marprelate UrrstLe) reached the authorities, 
as so often in this story, too late to be of service. Waldegraye was at 
the time at Fawsley setting up the ‘second Martin.’ See THe Just 
CrnsuRke AND Ruproor, p. 352, note (2).

go to the same. The same will Dr. Cosins witness—that

old Porter of Paddington, whom John of London bedeaconed

Bury [St. Edmund’s]. And by that time my Visitors will 
be come out of Cornwall, Devon and Hampshire. 

And now, fare thee well, good Profane T. C. I | cannot 48 
now meddle with the long period which thou hast in the 88rd 
[and] 34th pag[es] of thy book. It is but thirty-eight lines. 
Thou art longer-winded than Dean John, I see; though he 
hath longer periods than that which I set down. 

Whereas thou dost complain that the livings of our 
bishops are so small that some of their children are like to 
go a-begeging, there is a present remedy for that. Jor to 
what end else is John of Cant. unmarried, but to provide 
for the bishops’ children who shall be poorly left? Though, 
indeed, T never said in my life that there was ever any great 
familiarity (though I know there was some acquaintance) 

between Mistress Toye and John Whitgift. And I'll befy 
‘em, I’ll befy ’em, that will say so of me. And wherefore is 
Richard [Howland] of Peterborough unmarried, but to 
provide for other men’s children? O, now I remember me 
—he has also a charge to provide for; his hostess and 
cousin of Sibson. The petticoat he bestowed upon her, 
within this six months, was not the best in England. The 
token was not unmeet for her state. TFarewell, farewell, 
farewell, old Martin! And keep thee out of their hands 
for allthat. For thou art a shrewd fellow; thou wilt one 


day overthrow them. Amen. And then thou swearest by 


thy faith, quoth John of London.

INTRODUCTORY NOTE 


Wiru the publication of the Coventry Tracts Robert 
Waldegrave ceased to occupy the anxious and dangerous 
post of printer to Martin Marprelate. His place was 
occupied by John Hodgkins, ambiguously described as a 
‘saltpeterman,’ but a competent printer, and a very 
staunch and determined fellow. The secret press, much 
to his relief, was removed from the house of John Hales 
to the Priory at Wolston, a village lying six miles away 
to the south-east. This was the residence of Roger 
Wigston. He and his wife were zealous reformers, Mrs. 
Wigston being one of the most fearless and outspoken of 
all those who gave shelter and help to the secret press. 
At the Priory Hodgkins with two assistants printed the 
present tract, Trmses Manzinianm, commonly known as 
Marizixn Junior, and the Just Censure AND RuEproorn, 
commonly known as MArrin SENIOR. 

The assumption of the Tract is that it is published by 
a person calling himself Martin Junior. He found the 
‘copy, together with certain other papers, beside a bush, 
dropped on the ground by a passer-by. It had been 
lying there all night in the rain. In publishing it he 
scrupulously leaves the textas it is, but adds an explanatory 
word and an epilogue. That this is not Marprelate’s 
usual banter about the authorship and the printing of his 
books seems certain, both from the imperfect form in 
which the Tract has been printed, and from the evidence 
given later undor torture by John Hodgkins. ‘The printing 
at Wolston was superintended by John Penry, who was joined 
for a few days by Job Throkmorton, of Haseley Manor.

in roman type. It was issued from the press on July 22nd, 
1589. Thestory ofits production, taken chiefly from the in- 
teresting evidence of Hodgkins’ assistants, Valentine Simms 
and Arthur Thomlyn, preserved for us in the Manchester 
Papers, will be found in the Historical Introduction, pp. 186, 
187, 295—803. We have there discussed the significance 
of the imperfect form in which the Tract was issued in 
connection with our inquiries into the identity of Martin 
Marprelate. The point at issue is mentioned below. 

The substance of the present Tract consists of 110 theses, 
points taken from the writings of the bishops mainly, and 
offered as theses for disputation, after the manner of the 
‘schools’ at the universities. Subjects stated categorically 
were classed as theses, stated interrogatively as questiones. 
It is worthy at least of passing note that when he retired to 
Scotland Penry published a translation of a collection of 
Propostiions and Principles which had been ‘ propounded 
and disputed in the University of Geneva,’ the title of the 
original, published in 1586, being Theses Theologice in 
Schola Genevenst. It was intended that Marprelate’s Theses 
should be accompanied by references or proofs, but the 
exigencies of the writer, the extreme secrecy required, 
absence from the books of reference, the haste with which 
the ‘Tract was written, compelled their omission. Both 
the Wolston ‘Martins’ were ad wterim publications. 
Marprelate was bestowing his time and his strength upon 
the composition of the long-promised Morm Work FoR THE 
Cooper. Under more favourable circumstances he would 
not only have completed the unfinished sentences, but 
would also have winnowed out a number of superfluous 
theses. Martin Junior says, ‘I myself do perceive some 
tautologies in the Conclusions, as being the first draft.’ 
See below, p. 325. 

We note in the following pages the increasing efforts of 
the hierarchy to discover Marprelate and his press, also 
the continuing dislike on the part of the precise brethren 
of the form of the attack made upon the bishops. On the

INTRODUCTORY NOTE 289 ~ 


other hand, Martin finds increasing support for the gravamen 
of his charge in the writings of the martyrs, chief among 
them being the illustrious William Tyndale. Among the 
pioneers of the English Reformation Tyndale had the most 
Pauline grasp of the principles of Christianity, and it is he 
who must be regarded.as the father of English Evangelical 
theology. Martin makes a strong appeal to his writings. 
The bearing of the incomplete sentences in Turses 
Marrintanz upon the problem of the authorship of the 
Marprelate Tracts is briefly this. The persons most 
closely related to the unknown writer, and chiefly respon- 
sible for the publeation of his pamphlets, were, so far as 
we know, John Penry and Job Throkmorton. We have 
shown that Penry could not have been the writer, but 
it was through his hands that the |Marprelate manu- 
scripts passed from the author to the printer. On the 
other hand, the evidence identifying Throkmorton with 
Martin Marprelate, if not complete, is very weighty, 
and not easily set aside even by his disavowa]. There 
is, Moreover, no violent improbability in the assumption 
that Penry is Martin Junior, the alleged editor of Tuusus, 
and that the account given in these pages, partly confirmed 
as it is by the testimony of Hodgkins, how the ‘ copy’ 
reached the hands of the latter, is not Martinist banter, but 
actual history. But on this assumption we are met with the 
crucial question, Why were not the broken sentences com- 
pleted when Penry and Throkmorton came to Wolston Priory 
to oversee the printing? At the present stage of the inquiry 
this is the loophole through which we may escape from all 
our conjectures, and imagine some great and still unknown 
English reformer as the writer of the Marprelate ‘Tracts.

THESES MARTINIANA: 
That is, 

CERTAIN DEMONSTRATIVE 
Conclusions, set down and collected (as it should seem) by 
that famous and renowned Clerk, the reverend Martin 
Marprelate the Great: serving as a manifest and 
sufficient confutation of all that ever the College 
of Cater-caps, with their whole band of 
Clergy-priests, have, or can bring for 
the defence of their ambitious 
and antichristian Prelacies. 


PUBLISHED AND SET FORTH 


as an after-birth of the noble Gentleman Himself by a pretty 
stripling of his, Mantin Junior, and dedicated by him to 
his good neame and mincka(1) Master John Kankerbury: 
How the young man came by them, the Reader 
shall understand suficiently in the Epilogue. 
In the meantime, whosoever can bring me 
acquainted with my father, I'll be 
bound he shall not lose his labour. 


Printed by the assignes of Martin Junior, without any 
privilege of the Cater-caps. 


(1) Neame (or neme) and nuncka were employed familiatly as 
synonyms for uncle. 2

[MARTIN JUNIORS PROLOGUE] 


Martin Junior, son unto the renowned and worthy 
Martin Marprelate the Great, to the Reader 


Thou shalt receive (good Reader) before I set down unto 
thee anything of mine own, certain of those things of my 
Father’s doings, which I found among his unperfect papers. 
J have not changed anything in them, detracted anything 
from them, nor added unto them aught of mine own; 
but, as I found them, so I have delivered them unto thee. 
Mine own measure thou shalt understand at the latter 
end, In my Epilogue to my nuncle Canterbury. This small 
thing that followeth before his Theses, is also his own. 
I have set down the speech as J found it, though unperfect. 
One thing I am sorry for; that the speech pretendeth the 
old man to be something discouraged in his courses.

THESES MARTINIAN 45 


I. Toe Prurace 


I see my doings and my course misliked of many, both 
the good and the bad; though, also, I have favourers of 
both sorts. The Bishops and their train, though they 
stumble at the cause, yet especially mislike my manner of 
writing. Those whom foolishly men call Puritans, like (of) 
the matter I have handled, but the form they cannot 
brook. So that, herein, I have them both for my adver- 
saries. But now, what if I should take the course (1) 

in certain Theses or Conclusions, without inveighing 
against either person or cause? Might I not then hope 
my doings would be altogether approved of the one, and 
not so greatly scorned at by the other? Surely, otherwise, 
they should do me great injury, and show that they are 
those who delight neither in heat nor cold; and so make 
me as weary in seeking how to fit them, as the Bishops 
are in labouring how to find me. The Bishops, I fear, 
are past my cure, and it may be I was unwise in taking 
that charge upon me. If that which I have already done 
can do them any good, or anywise further the cause which 
I love, I shall be glad. If not, what hope is there of 
amending them this way? ‘The best is, I know how to 
mend myself. For good leave have I to give over my 
desperate cure; and, with this farewell unto them, I wish 
them a better surgeon. Yet, ere I leave them, I do here 
offer unto the view of the world, some part of their mon- 
strous corruptions ; in defence whereof, for their lives dare 
not they in any learned meeting or assembly dispute with 

(1) The difficulties attending the production of this Tract, as stated in 
the Introductory Note, must explain this break in the text. A correc- 
tion was probably meditated ; but, as it would appear, the corrected 
copy was delayed, and in the stress of the circumstances it had to go forth 


as above. ‘There is no scrious break in the sense. See reference on tha 
previous page to the imperfection of the text.

me, or attempt to overthrow mine assertions by modest 
writings, handled anything scholar | -like, that is, by good Aii. 
-and sound syllogisms, which have both their major and

enter into either of these courses; for as yet they have 
been far from both. Fire and faggot, bands and blows, 
railing and reviling, are, and have been hitherto, their 
'common weapons. As for slandering and lying, it is the 
greatest piece of their holy profession. And these, with 
their bare assertions, and their wretched cleaving to popish 
absurdities, are, in a manner, the only proofs and tried 
-, maxims they offer unto the Church in this age. And so, if

Winchester hath long ago sufliciently and dexterously (2) per- 
formed it. ‘I am not of opinion’ saith he, ‘that wna semper 
debet esse economia Keclesie—that the government of the 
Church. should always, and in all places, be one and the 
same,’-—especially by a company of Widers. Lo, Sir! what 
say you to this? Here is enough, I trow, for any man’s 
satisfaction, that Bishop Cooper is ‘not of opinion.’ Yea, 
but our Saviour Christ, His Apostles, and holy Martyrs 
are of opinion that the government of the Church, should 
_ always and in all places be one, especially, by a company 
' of Elders. As for my Lord of Winchester’s opinion, we 
have little or nothing to do with that; nor no great 
matter which side it lean to; whether with or against the 
truth. For if his bishopric and unruly jurisdiction were 
no more noisome and hurtful to the Church of God than 
his learning and opinion is hurtful to the cause of Disci- 
pline, he might sit long enough undistempered in his chair 
for us: the good old man might cough his fill, and be quiet, 
having his faith | ful promise and book-oath (as we have A ii, vers. 
also John a Bridges’ and Bancroft’s) that by arguments he 
will never hurt us. For they must think that it 1s not such

1. That all the officers of a true and lawful church govern-

(1) Another instance of the unfinished state of the present Tract. The 
numbers are no doubt references to the pages of Bridges’ Defence, from 
which Martin purposed making illustrative extracts. Page 812 is occu- 
pied with ‘The Pastor’s office in buriall,’ but while making large 
admissions in regard to the duties of burial and marriage, Dr. Bridges 
finds proof in the Burial Office of the care of the Church for the ministry. 
of the Word. He says, ‘I graunt them also upon necessitie or occasion, 
both that other may Ourie the dead and that the dead also may be burted 
amongst us otherwise [than is prescribed], and that properly of itself, 
it is no part at all of his proper office, no more than is the solemnizing 
of mariage. Wowbeit, it is such an action, as may be well adioyned to his 
office, without any blemish thereunto. Yea, if the publike ministration of 
the word be a proper part of his office, which our Brethren do not 
denice ; if there be any publike use and ministerie of the word at the time 
of the buriall of the dead: then how hath not the pastor his part 
therein ?’. 

Page 1401 is the last page in the Defence. It is of a benedictory 
character, urging to obedience to the laws ecclesiastical and civil, sub- 
mission to her Majesty, and giving praise to the Divine Persons and 
beseeching the Brethren to join in the ‘good clerkes part’ by saying 
‘Amen.’ With such gentle words did Bridges dismiss the men whom 
he persecuted with rigour. He was an example of a man whose bite is 
worse than his bark. On the significance of these unfinished seutences 
and incomplete references in relation to the authorship of the THxs&: 
see above, ‘Introductory Note,’ p. 289, and the references there given 
to the discussion of the matter in the Hist. Intro. 

(2) &, ‘fathers should’ by misprint.

2. That none but Christ alone is to ordain the members 


of His body, to wit, of the Church. Be | cause, A iii, 


3. That the Lord, in His Word, hath left the Church 
perfect in all her members, which He should not have done, 
if He had not ordained all the officers, namely, the mem- 
bers thereof; and so He should have the building of His 
Church unperfect; and so it must continue; for who will 
presume to finish that which He hath left undone in the 
building of His Church ? 

4, That to ordain a perfect and an unchangeable govern- 
merit of the Church is a part of Christ’s prerogative royal, 
and therefore cannot, without the great derogation of the 
Son of God, be claimed by any Church or man. 

5. That if Christ did not ordain a Church government 
which at the pleasure of man can not be changed, then He 
is inferior unto Moses; for the government placed by him 
might no man (to) alter, and thereto might no man add 
anything. Heb. 8%. 

G. That the Lord, in the New Testament, did appoint as 
perfect and unchangeable a form of Church government in 
the offices and officers thereof, as Moses did in the old. 

7. That the Lord never placed any offices in the New 
Testament but the offices of the Apostles, Prophets, 
Evangelists, Pastors, Doctors, Elders and Deacons. 

8. That unto the end of the world there were no other 
offices to be placed in the Church, but only these 
[Hphes. 47”). 

9. That none of these were, and so no offices of a lawful 
Church-government are to be removed out of the Church 
by any but by the Lord Christ | Himself, who placed them ; 
because they are the members of His body, in the placing 
or displacing whercof man hath no skill, nor yet commission 
to deal.

(1) Tygurium, i.e. Zurich. The spelling is peculiar ; the more usual 
form is Tigurum. Cotton (7ypog. Gaz.) gives Tigurinus Pagus, Turigum, 
and Turicum, as variable forms. The city of Zurich is selected as the 
home of Zwingli and the centre and chief stronghold of the reform 
movement in the Swiss cantons. 

(2) Zisea (John Trocznowski), the general who led the Bohemian 


reformers, was, during the latter part of his career, totally blind. Me

43. That the hierarchy of bishops, in their superiority 
over their brethren, and their civil offices hath been gain- 
said and withstood by the visible church of God succes- 
sively, and without intermission, for these almost 500 years 
last past.

bishops, and bringing in the equality of Ministers, is no new 
cause, but that which hath been many years ago held and. 
maintained, even in the fire, by the holy martyrs of Christ 


Jesus. 
45. That this wicked government of bishops was an 


especial point, gainsaid by the servants of God in the time 
of King Henry the eighth and Q. Mary; and in the with-

Jesus (I). 

John 185°.—‘Tesus answered, My kingdome is not of this world: if 
my kyngdome were of this worlde, then would my seruants suerly 
fyght, that I shulde not be deliuered to the Iewes: but now is my 
kyngdome not from hence.’ 

The above are to be compared with the following :+— 

Matt. 102.—‘It is inough for the disciple to be as his master is, and 
that the seruant be as his Lord is. If they haue called the Lord 
of the house Beelzebub, how muche more them of his household ?’ 

Luke 16!°.—‘ No seruant can serve two masters, for ether he sbal 
hate the one, and loue the other: or els he shal leane to the one, 
and despise the other. Ye can not serue God and riches.’ 

Remembering that both parties to the discussion professed alike abso- 
lute belief in the authority of Scripture, with this catena of texts before 
us we can easily see the strength of the onslaught against ‘ superiority ’ 
or prelacy, and especially against its worldly pomp and circumstance, 
made by the reformers, from Tyndale—from whom they derived most 
of their arguments—to Martin Marprelate. Reference has frequently 
been made to Aylmer’s Harborowe. In that remarkable book he uses 
most of these points against the bishops. He quotes, for instance, 
Luke 1214, ‘Who made me a Indge betwecne you?’ He then proceeds, 
‘As though hee would saye, It belongeth not to my office to determine 
matters of pollicie and inheritance, that belongeth to the civill Magis- 
trate, &c.’ Then he quotes John 18%: ‘My kingdome is not of this 
world.’ . . . ‘If Imperial] iurisdiction belonged to him, why refused 
he his calling ? Ifit did not, where had Paul or any other[s] any autha- 
ritic to meddle with that which he refused? Secing hee sayeth, As my 
Father sent me, so sende [ you.’ Later in the same paragraph Aylmer 
quotes Luke 22%: ‘Princes of the Nations do beare rule like Lords, 
it shall not be so with you,’ and also 2 Tim. 24: ‘None going to warre 
intangleth him selfe with the alfaires of this life: it is enongh for them 
to waite upon one office, to attende as sole priestes, not as errant [wan- 
dering] Baylliffes.’ These were bis sentiments before the dignity and 
emoluments of a lord bishop corrupted his judgment.

46. That none ever defended this hierarchy of bishops to 
be lawful but Papists, or such as were infected with Popish 
errors. 


might have been expected, than those of the reformers who so firmly 
and definitely held Evangelical principles that they went to the stake in 
defence of them. The volume edited by John Foxe, quoted several 
times in the course of the Tracts (briefly described in a note to Thesis 67, 
see below, p. 315, and a great favourite with the reforming party), 
containing the works of the martyrs Tyndale, Frith and Barnes, shows 
that those distinguished men were the true forefathers of the ‘seekers 
after reformation’ in the reign of Hlizabeth, and of the Nvangelical 
Nonconformists of later days. A few extracts from Fox’s volume will 
iustrate their views on the Roman and Anglican conception of epis- 
copacy :— 
(a) On bishops as avorldly lords and civil magistrates. 

‘Let [kynges] rule their Realmes them sclues, wyth the helpe of laye 
men that are sage, &c. Is it not a shame aboue all shames and a 
monstrous thing, that no man should be founde able to gouerne 
a wordly kyngdome saue byshops and prelates... 2?’ The fami- 
liar texts John 18%, Iuke 1295, 962 Matt. 624, are then quoted.— 
Tyndale, Obedience of a Christian Man (Works, 124 a,b). 

‘Is it not a marvelous court that they haue? wherein was neuer 
man accused of heresie, were he learned or not learned, but they 
have found him gilty ? Is it not a maruelous court that nener 
hath innocentes? .. . And if any man speak of Gods law and 
right conscience agaynst thys damnable tyranny, little will they 
stick to make him an heretick. And if that wiil not helpe (to 
colour and maintaine their oppression) then adde they treason 
against your grace, though hee bee neuer so true a subiect.’— 
Robert Barnes, Supplication to Hen. VIII. (Works, 183, a,b). 

‘After that [the office of bishop] was made so honorable and profit~ 
able, they that were worst both in learnyng and lyuyng most 
laboured for it. For they that were vertuous wold not entangle 
them selues with the vayne pride of this world, and weare three 
crownes of gold, where Christ dyd weare one of thorne.’—John 
Frith, Answere to More (Ibid. 116 a). 

(b) On the identity of bishop and elder. 

* Wherefore the Apastlas . . . ordeined. . . two officers : One called 
after the Greeke worde Byshop, in English an ouersear: which 
same was [also] called priest after the Greeke, Elder in English, 
because of his age, discretion and sadnesse [gravity ].’—Tyndale, 
Practise of Prelates (Works, 3456). See also Obedience of a 
Ch. man (Ibid. 183), also, and especially, Ax Answere to More’s 
Dialogue (Lbid. 251b). 

(c) On the functions of bishops. 

‘Bishops and priestes that preach not, or that preach ought saue 
Gods word, are none of Christes, nor of hys annoyntyng: but ser- 
uantes of the beast.’—T'yndale, he Obedience (Works, 135b). 

‘Seyng also that the office of an Apostle is to preach only, how tan 
the Pope challenge with right any authority where he preacheth 
not ?’—Tyndale, Jiid., p. 126:a. 

The following satire is equally to the point :— 

‘The holy workes of Byshops’ (marg. note).—-‘ And therefore you 
haue applyed your selues to other greater matters, as to christen- 
ing of belles, to halowing of Churches, to blessing of candles, to 
conaccrating of holy oyle, to halowing of chalesics [chalices]

54. That this their doctrme is maintained by statute,

(1) So stated on the title-page of Foxe’s Acts and Mon. 

(2) That is ‘the Conclusions which follow and which are thereby &c.’ 
The position is that Woxe’s ed. of the Works of Tyndale, Barnes, and 
Fryth and his Acts and Mon. were published cum privilegio. Having 
thus the approval of the episcopal censorship, the views they contain, 
which are embodied in the theses that immediately follow, may be 
accounted to be ‘according to the doctrine of the Church of England.’ 
Matthew Sutclitfe, an ecclesiastical lawyer much engaged in controversy,

98. ‘That our magistrates, in maintaining both the doctrine 
of our Church and also the hierarchy of our bishops, main- 
tain two contrary factions under their government, which 
their Wisdoms know to be dangerous. 

99. That this faction is likely to continue until either of 
the parties give over. 

100. That those who defend the doctrine of our Church 
in oppuguing our bishops, neither can nor will give over (2) 
the cause, inasmuch as itis confirmed by the Word professed 
in our Church, allowed by our statutes, and maintained by 
her Majesty’s privilege. 

101. ‘That the bishops will not give over, in any fiuood 
to die for it (2), as long as the State will maintain them. 

102. That the continuance of these contrary factions is 
likely in a while to become very dangerous unto our State, 
as their Wisdoms, who are magistrates, well know and 
perceive. 

103. That their Wisdoms then are bound, even for the 
quieting of our outward State, to put down either the 
doctrine of our Church, or the corruption, viz. our bishops, 
and their proceedings. 

104. That they cannot, without the endangering of them- 
selves, under the wrath of God and the odious and most 
monstrous sin of inevitable apostasy from the truth, put 
down and abolish the doctrine of our Church. 

105. That they cannot any longer maintain the corrup- 
tions of our Church, namely, archbishops and bishops, 
without the shameful contra | diction of our doctrine, and the 

discontentedness of their subjects. 


(1) Cease. The expression ‘give over’ in this sense is now only 
heard as a local dialect form. 

(2) They will not forsake their livings, ‘ giving over’ their present 
policy, and imperilling their lives thereby.

(1) That is, a solution or explanation. 

(2) The reference in this and the two following theses to Bancroft’s 
‘treason’ needs a word of explanation. Martin has, in the manner of 
formal logic, set forth his familiar syllogism (THE HPpisrLe, p. 23) :— 

No petty popes ought to be maintained or tolerated in a Christian 
commonwealth. 

But our Archbishops and Bishops are such petty popes. 

Therefore, they oucht not to be tolerated, &c. 

To this Bancroft replies by stating that upon Martin’s principles you 
could frame the following argument :— 

No petty pope ought to be tolerated, &c. 

But ‘hir Majestic is a Pettie Pope.’ 

‘Therefore hir Majestic is not to be tolerated, &c.’ 

Moreover, Bancroft says that the minor, or second member in the syllo- 
gism, may be proved thus :— 

“Whosoever doe take upon them or usurpe the same authority in 
causes ecclesiastical within their dominions, which the Pope had, 
are Pettie Popes. 

‘lier Majestie doth so. 

‘Therefore hir M. is a Petty Pope and not to be tolerated, &c.’

Martin Junior’s Epilogue 
To the worshipful his very good 
neame (1), Master John 
Canterbury 


After my hearty commendations unto your Worship (good 
nuncle Canterbury), trusting that you, with the rest of the 
Cater-caps, are. as near yow’ overthrow as I, your poor 
nephew, am from wishing the prosperity of your anti- 
christian callings. The cause of my writing unto you at 
this instant is to let you wnderstand, first, that I was 
somewhat merry at the making hereof (2); being indeed 
sorry, together with others of my brethren, that we cannot 
hear from our good father Master Martin Marprelate, that 
good and discoursing brother of yours; but especially 
grieved that we sce not the utter subversion of that 
unhappy and pestilent government of lord bishops, at 
the helm whereof ye sit, like a Pilate, or a Caiaphas 
rather. Moreover, J do you to wit, that you shall receive 
by this bearer certain: imperfect (3) writings of my 

father’s, praying your Prelacy, if you can send me, 

or any of my brethren, any word of him, 
that you would return us an 
answer with 
speed. |

nothing can be heard, inasmuch as he keepeth himself 
secret from all his sons. Some think that he is even now 
employed in your business (4); and I think so too. My

reason is, quoth Robert Some, because it was for your 
sakes and good that he first fell a-studying the Art of 
*Pistle-making. Others give out that in the service of his 
country, and her Majesty’s, he died, or was in great danger 
at the Groine (1). And those others (quoth mine nunca 
Bridges) have seen motives inducing them to be of this 
mind. Some there are also, who feare that you have him in 
your hands. Howsoever it be, somewhat is not well, that 
he is silent all this while. We his sons must needs be dis- 
quieted, seeing we can neither know where our father is, 
nor yet hear from him. If we could but hear by some 
’Pistle, though it were but of twenty sheets of paper, that 
he is well, we would not then be so inquisitive of him (2). 
But now that he hath been so long time tongue-tied, these 
four or five months (3), we must needs inquire of the matter. 
Speake then, good nuncles, have you closely murdered the 
gentleman in some of your prisons? Have you strangled 
him? Have you given him an Italian fig? (4) Or, what 
have you done unto him? Have you choked him with a fat 
prebend or two? What? JI trow, my father will swallow 
down no such pills. And he do, I can tell he will soon 
purge away all the conscience be hath, and prove a mad 
hind ere he die. But tell me, I pray you, what you mean 
to do unto hin, if you have him in hold? Do you mean 
to have the keeping of him, lest he should not be otherwise 

(1) The attack upon Corunna (the Groine) in 1587 by Drake was part 
of the process of ‘singeing of the Spanish king’s beard.’ After the 
destruction of the Armada, in the spring of 1589, Drake and Norris 
again attacked the Atlantic ports of the Peninsula, plundering Corunna 
before returning. The allusion must be to the later expedition. See 
the fuller note in THe Just CENSURE AND REPROOFE, p. 351. 

(2) Twenty sheets, folded in quarto, would give 160 pages, a fairly 
substantial *’Pistle.’ 

(3) Tue MINERALLS were issued from Hales’s house at Coventry cire. 
Feb. 20th, and Hay any Worse circ. March 20th from the same place, 
which agrees with the date indicated above, that is, four months (or 
five) from the writing of Tus Erirome. 

(4) Alluding to the method, of which the Italians were the most 
consummate practitioners, of insinuating. deadly poisons into figs. “It is 
sometimes called a French fig. ‘Whether it was by an Italian posset, or 
by French figs, or by the potage of their potinger [apothecary |—he 


was a French man-—there departed from this life the Marl of Cassils.’— 
Knox’s Reform. in Scotland, Guthrie’s ed., p. 126.

sure he hath 500 sons in the land, of good credit and 
ability, with whom he might have other gates’ welcome (2), 
than with any Cater-cap of them all. And I pray you, 
nuncles, never trouble yourselves with the keeping of him. 
J trust he shall do well, though he never come near any of 
youall. And TJ think in reason it were more meet his sons, 
than his brethren, should be charged with him, if it so came 
to pass that he were forced to lean unto others. This I 
know full well, that my father would be sorry from his 
heart to put you to any such cost as you intend to be at 
with him. A meaner house, and of less strength than the 
Tower, the Fleet, Newgate, or the Gate-honse is, would 
serve him well enough. He is not of that ambitious vein, 
that many of his brethren the bishops are, in secking for 
more costly houses than ever his father built for him: And 
therefore, good sweet neames, now, if you have him, let him 
be despatched out of your hands, with honesty and credit. 
My father is of a kingly nature, I perceive by him; he 
would do good unto you, but he would not be recompensed 
for it again. He will none of your courtesies unless it be 
for your own sakes, that you will give over your bishop- 
doms; that is the greatest benefit he accounts of from you. 
Other recompense he sceks none. 

If you demand of me, where J found this, the truth is, it 
was taken up (together with certain other papers) besides a 
bush, where it had dropped from somebody passing by that 
way (3). I hope my father’s worship will not be offended 
with me for publishing of it, being not so perfect as 
question | less he would have had it. He and you cannot 
but commend my good dealing, in setting it out; for I chose 
rather to leave the sentences imperfect (4) than to add any-

thing more than I found legible. The arithmetical numbers 
in the end of his preamble shew that, when he had written

I myself do perceive some tautologies in the conclusions, as 
being the first draft; but I would not presuine to mend 
them ; that I refer to himself, if he be yet living. If dead, 
yet posterity (2) may have his after-birth to be altogether

sorry of. For who can be able to prove the points which 
he Lath set down here, concerning the doctrine of our 
Church, maintained by statute and her Majesty’s privilege, 
so soundly, and so worthily, as he himself would perform 
it? A thirty or forty of the first Conclusions are already 
shewed in ‘Hay any work for the Cooper,’ and therefore 
they need no further proof than the reading over that 
worthy Treatise, whence they seem to have been collected. 
The rest I hope shall be shewed in ‘More work for the 
Cooper’ (3).

doctrine of our Church, then certainly you deserve to be 
chronicled for ever. Then John Canterbury, come down

now that dares persuade Martin to give over his course, 
unless the same also will shew himself an enemy to the 
doctrine of the Church of England? For Martin in his 
writings, is not so much an enemy unto the bishops as a 
defender of the doctrine of our Church. And therefore you 
Puritans, that mislike of him, take heed that you be not 
found amongst posterity (1) to be the betrayers of this 
doctrine (for your ease and quietness’ sake), which you are 
bound to deliver unto your children, without corruption 
or mangling, though it cost you your lives a thousand 
times. Tor to tell you the truth, if you do but read over 
the writings of Mr. Tyndale, Mr. Fryth, Mr. Barnes, Mr. 
Hooper, Mr. Knox, Mr. Lambert (2), &¢., which were the 
first planters of the Gospel amongst us, you shall find 
yourselves in faithfulness, courage and zeal, yea, even the 
best of you, far behind them; which I speak not but to 
your great shame, with a desire of your amendment. And 
therefore I tell you true, I think it a great blessing of God 
that hath raised up this Martin, whom you can hardly 
brook, to hold tackling (3) with the bishops, that you may 
have some time of breathing, or rather a time to gather 

(3) Gl, posterities. } : 

(2) John Lambert, a native of Norwich, and a Fellow of Queen’s 
College, Cambridge, who suffered at Smithfield in November, 1538, his 
real name being Nicholson, which he changed to Lambert when, to escape 
persecution, he crossed over to Antwerp. He was brought back to 
England by Sir Thomas More, who as a perseeutor of the reformers 
lacked nothing of the characteristic vindictive cruelty of the Romish 
Church. Lambert after some time was released, but several years after 
was inveigled into a disenssion on transubstantiation with Taylor, at 
that time incumbent of St. Peter’s, Cornhill, afterwards Bishop of 
Lincoln. For this he was tried before ten bishops and the King. The 
verdict was a foregone conclusion, and a few days afterwards he was 
burnt at Smithfield. John Bale, afterwards Bishop of Ossory, published 
an address written by Lambert to the King at the time of his con- 
demnation. On the last page Bale notes, ‘Though Johan Lambert wrote 
sumwhat more, still the corrupt copy which reached his hands contained 
no more. Jle adds, ‘In the yeare of our Lorde a. M. D. xxxviij was thys 
setuant of God brent in Smythfelde at London, by the only vvolence of 
the spirytuall mynysters of Antichrist, in october.’ The title of the Tract 
is ‘A treatyse made by Johan Lambert unto hynge Henry the vtij con- 
cernynge hys opynyon on the sacramet of the aultre as they call it, or 
supper of the lorde as the scripture nameth it. Anno do. 1538.’ Small 
8vo of 82 leaves in Gothic letter. Brit. Mus. C. 25. a. 10. Tho 
catalozue adds ‘[Marburg 1545}.’ 

(3) Same as our colloquial ‘to tackle’ a person.

Christ, His Apostles, His holy martyrs, which were the 
planters of our Church, as the wretches are like unto them- 
selves. A man would have thought, if they had not been 
desperate in their wickedness, that by the warning which 
Martin gave them, they would have been restrained from 
their villainy in some sort. But, as though their very 
reason had been clean gone, the more they [are] threatened 
to have their proceedings displayed, the more wicked do 
they manifest themselves. As if they would declare unto 
the world that they will not be made known unto posterity, 
but upon the condition that they may be [known to be] the 
most wicked that ever were mm the church of God. They 
will be so many Judases, so many Diotrepheses, so many 
Simon Maguses, as now they are wicked bishops of 
England; or else they think not themselves well dealt 
with. Wherefore, reverend Father (x), if you be as yet 
on your seat, and have escaped out of the danger of 
gunshot, begin again to play the man.. ear none of these 
beasts, these pursuivants, these Mar-Martins (2), these 
stage-players (3), these prelates, these popes, these devils, 
and all they can do. Quit you but as like a man as you 
have done in ‘ Hay any Worke,’ and I doubt not but you 
will make these roguish pyiests le in the kennel. The 
report abroad goeth, that you are drawn dry, and can say 
no more. ‘They are fools that sothink, I say. | Let these 
Conclusions be judge, whereby, I tell you true, I hope you 
shall be able to empty every bishopric in England, if weight 
of truth can do it. There be that affirm the rimers and 
stage-players to have clean put you out of countenance, 
that you dare not again show your face. Alas! poor 
hagelers, their fathers are too young to outface the least 
of your sons. And J do think that, lay aside their 
tyranny, all the bishops of England are too weak to deal 
with a scarecrow that hath but the name of reverend

The stage-players, poor, silly (1), hunger-starved wretches, 
they have not so much as an honest calling to live in the 
commonwealth. And they, poor varlets, are so base-minded, 
as at the pleasure of the veriest rogue in England, for one 
poor penny, they will be glad on open stage to play the 
ignominious fools for an hour or two together. And there- 
fore, poor rogues, they are not so much to be blamed, if, 
being stage-players, that is, plaine rogues (save only for their 
liveries) they, in the action of dealing against Master Martin, 
have gotten them many thousand eye-witnesses of their 
witless and pitiful conceits. And indeed they are marvel- 
lous fit upholders of Lambeth Palace, and the crown of 
Canterbury. And, therefore, men should not think of all 
other things, that they should anyways make Master Martin, 
or his sons, to alter their course. And hereof, good Master 
Canterbury, assure yourself. 

Well, to grow to a point with you, if you have any of your 
side, either in the Universities, or in your cathedral churches, 
or anywhere within the compass of all the bishopdoms you 
have, that dare write or dispute against any of these points 
set down by my father, here I do, by these my writings, cast 
you down the glove in my father’s name, and the names of 
the rest | of his sons. Jf my father be gone, and none 
else of my brethren will uphold the controversy against you, 
I myself will do it. And take my challenge if you dare. 
By writing you may do it, and be sure to be answered. By 
disputations, if you will appoint the place, with promise 
that you will not deal vz et armis, you shall be taken also by 
me, if I think I may trust you. Otherwise the Puritans 
will, I doubt not, maintain the challenge against you. 

But here, by the way, John Canterbury, take an odd 
advice of your poor nephew, and that is this. First, in 
regard of yourself, play not the tyrant as you do, in God’s 
Church. If you go on forward in this course, the end will 
be a woful reckoning. Thou hast been raised up out of

the dust, and even from the very dunghill, to be President 
of her Majesty’s Council, being of thyself a man altogether 
unmeet for any such pre-eminence, as neither endued with 
any excellent natural wit, nor yet with any great portion of

thine own bosom? Yea, verily. For the Lord in one day 
is able to bring more shame upon thee, and that in this life, 
than He hath heaped blessings upon thee now for the space 
of thirty years and upward. But when J do consider thy 
pre-eminence and promotion I do sensibly acknowledge it to 
be joined with arare curse of God, even such a curse as very 
few (1 will not say none) in God’s Church do sustain. And 
that is thy wicked and antichristian prelacy. The con- 
sideration of which popedom of thine maketh me think that 
thy other place in the civil magistracy, being in itselfa godly 
and a lawful calling, is so become infectious, that it will be 
thy bane, both in this life, and in the life to come. And 
I am almost fully persuaded that that archbishopric of thine, 
together with thy practices therein, show verily that the 
Lord hath no part nor portion in that miserable and 
desperate caitiff, wicked John Whitgift, the Pope of Lam- 
beth. Leave therefore both thy popcdom and thy ungodly 
proceedings, or look for a fearful end.

more of these haggling and profane pamphlets to be pub- 
lished against Martin, and in defence of thy hierarchy. 
Otherwise thou shalt but commend thy folly and ignorance

Frégeville was heartily enough in fayonr of the theology of the Re- 
formation, just as Whitgift was, and openly claimed to be. But what 
was so admirable in the English plan and is so warmly commended to 
Henry III. is its care for the clergy. The Pope had been cashiered and 
discarded, the ‘blasphemous superstition’ called the Mass had been 
suppressed, the images with the moving eyes had been broken up and 
the mechanism exposed, and the article on ‘Justification by Faith only,’ 
had been placed in the creed of the Church; and with all these vast 
and significant changes the bishops kept up the old pre-Reformation pomp 
and dignity and the chief part of the old episcopal authority. When 
Herman Wolkersheimer called to see his old friend of the days of exile, 
John Jewel, Bishop of Salisbury, he is amazed by the magnificence df the 
Bishop’s state. ‘The butler forthwith makes his appearance, bearing a 
Jarge golden goblet’ of wine; and at dinner or supper he cannot 
describe ‘the abundance or magnificence of the silver plate.’—Zurich 
Letters, 2nd Ser., p. 87. When Whitgift rode forth, his small army of 
gentlemen-at-arms and retainers made his movement a sort of royal 
progress. And never a cardinal or metropolitan of the dld order possessed 
a more autocratical and irresponsible power than the Archbishop when 
he sat in his high commission. Well might Ivégeville say, ‘France is 
bound to Queene Flizabeth for shewing the way how to come to Reforma- 
tion without endomaging the clergic.-—ftef. Polit., p. 65. He also 
undertakes to defend the English plan as a natural development from 
‘the equalitic that rested among the Bishops in the primitive Church.’ 
As that Church increased, Deacons, and later ‘other Bishops and Priests, 
were created.’ ‘But the Apostles remained as soueraine Bishops... . 
Hereof do I inferre that in the state of a mighty and peaceable Church, 
as is the Church of Ungland, or as the Church of Wrance or such like 
might be, if God should call them to reformation, the state of the Clergis 
ought to be preserued: for equalitic would be hurtful to the state and 
in time breed confusion.’—Jbid., p. 69. There is an allusion to Frége- 
ville in Tie Jusr Censure, p. 370, and in Tur PRrovrsraryon, p. 416.

INTRODUCTORY NOTE 


Tur Jusr Censure anp Reproors, as stated in the Note 
introducing Tnrsus Marrinzanm, was published on July 29, 
1859, while the secret press was at the house of Roger 
Wigston. To publish the second of these Tracts a week 
after the first, if we take into consideration the difficulties 
under which our printers laboured, their small hand-press, 
and their limited stock of type, indicates that John Hodgkins 
felt the need of haste. He was indeed daily anticipating a 
visit from the Archbishop’s pursuivants. Having completed 
his share of the work, Hodgkins at once packed up press and 
type, and the same day set out with his two assistants for 
Warrington. They eventually established their press at 
Manchester, and no sooner began their work than they weve 


‘seized by the authorities. See the Historical Introduction, 
‘pp: 186; 187, 297 ff. 


Tun Just Censune is very similar in form to THusEs 
Marrinianm, and printed from the same type—a Roman 
letter, two sizes being used on the title-page. Sharpe warned 
Peury that the authorities would know of his connection with 
these Tracts since they were printed from the same type as his 
Swpplication—published when the press was at John Hales’ 
house at Coventry (Sharpe’s evidence, Harl. MSS. (Baker’s 
Trans.) 7042. 23); Arber’s Sketch, 102). Penry made ‘a care- 


_less answere and so they past yt over.’ The type in question 


was part of that which was purchased from Waldegrave 
when he relinquished the post of printer to Marprelate. 
The present Tract is a small 8vo., sig. A-D in fours. 

The assumption of the Tract is that a third writer has 
come upon the scene, calling himself Martin Senior; whose 
task it is to censure and reprove Martin Junior for his
