rashness in printing their father’s papers in their unperlect 
condition, as well as for exasperating thereby Archbishop 
Whitgift and the High Commission. The ‘copy’ appears 
to have reached Wolston on the day that Job Throkmorton 
appeared at the Priory. 

The outstanding feature of Je Just Crnsurn is the 
speech which the writer puts into the mouth of Archbishop 
Whitgift, addressing his pursuivants on the immediate 
necessity, owing to the renewed activity of the Marprelate 
press, of taking up once more the search for Marprelate and 
his printers; men and press must be secured at all costs. 
Jt shows us, more vividly than any other document we 
possess, the situation created by the Marprelate writings : 
the popular excitement; the small result of the activities 
of the pursuivants; their vain and expensive expeditions; 
their arrival on the scene ever the day after Martin’s printers 
had decamped, no one could tell whither; the reproach of the 
subtle and plausible and altogether unscrupulous Monday; 
the gatherings at the Puritan centres in London; the 
absorbing conversations at Paul’s Cross before the preacher 
appeared, and at the churches of certain preachers favourable 
to reform; the hidden mystery under the Puritans’ great 
cloaks; the gossip at the booksellers’ in the Churchyard 
and at Blackfriars; the espionage of the taverns, for when 
the wine is in the wit is out; the examination of the carriers’ 
consignments for printed matter coming into the city and 
paper and ink despatched into the country; the need of 
watching even Lord Mayor Martin’s house, not to mention 
the houses of notorious nonconforming preachers; even the 
Court must be taken in hand, for the unclean thing circulates 
in the immediate vicinity of the throne, maugre the Queen’s 
injunctions; and the search must extend its sweep far to 
the west, through the midlands, and even to the north parts. 
And above all this is the grim vexation of the Archbishop, 
having more power in his hands than ever was granted to 
any of his predecessors since Wlizabeth came to the throne, 
yet none so helpless against the enemies of the established

order as was he against this elusive foe, this too serious 
jester. 

The more serious elements in the Tract are contained in 
the points which, in Martin Junioy’s place, Martin Senior 
would have propounded against the Bishops (pp. 364 et seq.) ; 
the suggestions for a united supplication to the Queen 
(pp. 871 et seq.) ; and the brief discursion on the Queen’s 
English (pp. 872-874). The two former are summarised in the 
Table of Contents. The latter is a vivacious account of how 
the bishops, with Evangelical convictions, read their private 
views into the ordination phrase, ‘ Receive the Holy Ghost,’ 
and the vicarious answers of sponsors at baptism; also how 
they paraphrased the supplications of the Puritans into 
revolutionary threats against the throne. 


Go 


The last pages, containing the prudent advice that it is 
better that Martin’s sons should not know their father, are 
of great interest and significance.

(1) The Archbishop has been constituted nuncka, or uncle, to the scions 
of Martin Marprelate. See title-page to THESHS MARTIN TAN. 

(2) Corunna. An expedition commanded by Drake and Norris left 
England on April 18 this year, and six days later burnt the shipping in the 
harbour of Cor uuna, and burnt and plundered the lower parts of the 
town. ‘The upper section successfully resisted the attack. The third 
weck in May, having re-embarked at Corunna, the force landed at 
Perniche and marched upon Lisbon. But Drake failing to codperate 
with the land forces, the assault upon the city ended in disaster. A large 
number of our soldiers died either of their wounds or of disease. The 
news of this, on the whole, disastrous expedition had not long reached 
England when the present Tract was being written. Drake anchored 
in P} ymouth towards the end of June. The entire force which set out 
with Drake and Norris was over 15,000 men. The remnant which found 
its way back to England numbered, it is said, no more than 6,000. Vo 
be hurt ‘at the Groine or at the suburbs of Lisbon’ must have been 
the fate of a great many Jinglishmen at this time. Sec the earlier 
reference in THusrs, p. 323. 

(3) Sce the account of finding the ‘copy’ of the first part of Tuusrs 
MARTINIAN® under a bush—THEsus, p. 324; also their ‘rain- and 
weather-beaten condition’ after lying out in the open all night.—Jbid.,

(1) Anthony Monday (or Munday) is a somewhat notorious person of 
this period. He was the son of Christopher Monday, a London draper, 
and, as he calls himself a draper, must have inherited the freedom of the 
Drapers’ Company. But he was regularly apprenticed in October, 
1576, to John Aldee, stationer, ‘for 8 yeres begynnynge at Bartholo- 
mewtyde last past.” He was destined to play many parts in his time. 
In 1678 he went to Rome, and claims to have been received into the 
funglish } Seminary y the Roman Catholic authorities, of course upon 
his profession of their faith. The object of his vow, however, was to 
gain their secrets, and presently we find him recularly, installed as a epy 
and, inter alia, a writer of tracts. His Brief Discourse of the taking of 
Edmund Campion—published on July 24, 1581 (Campion was arrested 
on duly 17)—and his Discoverie of Mdmund Campion, published on 
Jan. 225" 1582.9 Campion. haying. been executed on Dec. 1} pre- 
vious, were attacked from two sides. Jirst by one George Elliot, who 
arrested Campion, and next by a Catholic priest who defended his 
memory. The priest has many things to say derogatory of Monday, and 
among them he includes the fact that he had been, and perhaps resumed 
later, the calling of a siage-player. However, true to his Judas charactes, 
he is also credited by Mr. J. Dover Wilson with being the author of 
The Second and Third Blast (1580), a work written against the stage. 
At the time before us he was one of Whitgiflt’s most active pursuivants. 
We have already told how he traded on Wigginton’s unsuspicious natura 
and then betrayed ape before the Commission (see List. Intro., 164).

(4) William Clarke, a fellow of Peterhouse. He preached at St. 
Mary’s a sermon in which he derived the episcopal system from Satan. 
Whitgift and Perne, and one or two others, tried his case, and because 
he refused to make a public retractation, expelled him from the fellow- 
ship and the university in 1572. Ue appealed, through Burghley, to be 
restored, reeretting the vehemency of his language, and admitting there 
might be a ‘superiority among ministers ’ in matters of administration 3! 
but with the usual unfavourable result. We gained’ some reputation by 
his controversy (1580) with Campion, the Jesuit. Parsons accuses him 
of worrying Campion at his prison conference, he being ‘faint from 
torture and confinement’; also of ‘following Campion to his martyr- 
dom with harsh and pitiless reviling.’ He was ‘constant preacher’ to 
the Society of Lincoln’s Inn from 1581 till 15938, when,. despite his 
avoidance of positive opposition to the bishops, he was suspended by 
Whitgift because he did not preach in favour of them.—See D. WN. B., 
and es ere! 3r00k’s Lives, II:, 113.

strong Puritan of the Cartwright type, and an active member of *

at the time of Martin’s writing at [St. Ann’s] Blackfriars, where there 
was a famous afternoon lecture, much frequented by Puritans (see 
Throkmorton’s Defence, A ij. vers.), to which church he was in 1598

not signing Whitgift’s Articles. Brook identifies him with the Deerton

(1) A London minister of this name took part in the Conferences 
held with Barrowe and Greenwood. Certain ministers were appointed 
by the bishops because of their supposed sympathy with Church reform 
and because their sympathy did not prevent them from conformity to 
the law, to confer with the ‘two prisoners in the Fleete.’ One of 
them was ‘Master Cooper,’ whose Nonconformity had previously been 
of a more resolute type, secing that he had obtained a licence to preach 
in his parish ‘by Powles’ through the help of- Mrs. Lawson, the 
redoubtable shrew of Paul’s Churchyard. Martin speaks of Paul's 
Chain as one of the preaching places where the Puritans resorted, 
and it would seem safe to associate Cooper with Paul’s Chain. The 
Chain was a barricr on the south side of the cathedral, and designed ta 
preserve the quietness and privacy of the close during times of ser- 
vice. The parish is conjectured to be ‘St. Gregory’s by St. Paul’s.’ 


- fhe church in this parish was appropriated to the petty canons of 


St. Panl’s for their better support, Curiously enough, on April 29, 1590 
—the Conference at the Ilect was held on April 83—Martin Cooper and 
Robert Cooper were appointed fourth and fifth minor canons respec- 
tively, and it is natural to surmise that one of these was Master Cooper, 
the minister of the ‘parish by Powlcs,’ and none other than the 
Puritan whose deliverances at Paul’s Chain needed to be watched ; bub 
who, having later submitted to Whitgift, was already walking in the 
primrose way of preferment.

Flizabeth’s latest favourite. It was he who, when Elizabeth spoke’

become of me?’ He was generally opposed to the influence of the

(2) Sir Richard Martin was elected Lord Mayor on May 3, 1589, on

(4) John More (or Moore), a fellow of Christ’s College, Cambridge, 
minister of St. Andrew’s Church, Norwich. He died in Norwich in 
the year 1592. We was a popular preacher, and early came into colli- 
sion with the authorities by his refusal to wear the surplice, though 
his grounds appear to have been chiefly that the old Romish garment 
gave offence to others. He created some interest by replying to a sermon 
preached at the cathedral by Dr. Andrew Perne, Martin’s ‘old Turner.’ 
Later, in 1576, More was suspended from his ministerial office, along 
with nineteen or twenty other ministers of the city of Norwich, because 
the prelates were urging precise ceremonial conformity with great 
rigour. In the year 158£ More was one of a body of sixty ministers 
who were unable to subscribe to Whitgift’s Three Articles—and this 
when the need of ministers was so great that large numbers of un- 
educated persons had to be ordained, “whose only qualificatic jon was that 
they could Bo the service.

The most interesting item in the Orders to a modern student of the 
period is that in which the Puritans repel the accusation of schism ; 
first, because they attend their respective churches and unite in the 
ministry of the Word and Sacraments, and, also, because they assume no 
authority to compel, others to acknowledge their decrees. "The sub- 
seribers for the county of Suffolk are Knewstub[s] and Allen. It is not 
clear that Allen had a benefice in the county. Je may have been the 
same as the London minister who refused the vestments in 1564 and went 
to reside in the country to one his living by husbandry.—Sirypo’s 
Grindal, 145, 146. Martin spells the name ‘ Aline.’

last note ; a fellow of St. John’s, Cambridge, and a learned writer, says 
Fuller. Ue was obnoxious to the hierarchy because of his decided 
Nonconforinist sympathies. On leaving Cambridge he became the minis- 
ter of Cockfield in West Suifolk. He and sixty other miuisters in the 
county found themselves unable to subscribe to Whitgift’s notorious Three 
Articles. ‘Their dificulties were the usual ones with conscientious mon 
of eyaugelical convictions—the use of the cross in baptism; interro- 
gatorics proposed to infants; the declaration in the burial service 
that the deceased person, irrespective of his character, was committed to 
the earth, in sure and certain hope of eternal life ; the reading of apocry~ 
phal books in public worship. Asked by Lord Burghley if he and his 
neighbour John Oxenbridge would use the Book of Common Prayer and 
promise not to preach against it, they at once replied that this had 
been their practice ; for, for peace’ sake, they ae forborne to speak 
against those who were able to use the book more strictly than they 
were able to do. Knewstubs had the distinction of haying his house 
narrowly watched and afterwards thoroughly searched by the bishops’ 
officers. He took part in the Hampton Court Conference, and, making 
some inconyenient inquiries at one of the discussions on the limitations 
of the rulers of the Church to impose ritual upon officiating ministers, he 
was interrupted by the King. The British Solomon said ‘it smelt rankly 
of Anabaptism.’ Knewstubs wrote a book against the views of Henry 
Nicklaes, the founder of the Family of Love. He died at Cockfleld at 
an advanced age. See Brook’s Lives, IJ., 308; Strype’s Jndez:. 

(2) Robert Wright had been both private and university tutor to 
the Earl of Iissex. After many years’ residence at Cambridge he became 
private chaplain to Lord Rich, a great favourer of the ref forming 
party. Aylmer peremptorily refused to give him a licence, so that his 
yainistrations were confined to his patron’s private chapel. On Lord 
Rich’s death an indisecreet remark about making the Queen an idol soon 
brought Wright into Aylmer’s clutches. He was first imprisoned at 
Rochford in Wssex. There his tractable and courteous behaviour won 
him the favour of his keeper, who, ‘with the private allowauce of 
the Secretary of State,’ permilted him en parole to visit his wife, who 
was approaching her confinement and in great distress. He was, however, 
observed by a civilian, who reported the fact to the Bishop. It was 
only by instantly hastening back to prison, and by making the most 
humble and tearful entreaty to Aylmer, that Wright sueceeded in divert~ 
ing the Bishop’s vengeance from the keeper. He was now removed 
to the Gatehouse, and was eee there apparently several years. 
Examined before the Bishop, Wright contended that a private chap slain 
needed no licence, but. that the Bishop was mistaken in cal ling him 
simply a layman, since he had preached for seven years at the University 
with a licence, and had also been regularly ordained by the laying on

more just reprehension of the Puritans than that wherewith 
thou blamest them. For thou findest fault with the preachers 
only, and that justly, J confess, because they are no more 
forward in casting off these our popes. But I say that with 
more equity thou mightest have blamed both the gentlemen 
and the people together with the ministers, than the 
ministers alone. For the ministers though they be faulty,

and people are as deep in fault as they are. And I would 
wish them, both the one and the other, to take this, or some 
such course as I here set down, which also for a great part 
of it, though not all, I saw in a Puritan’s hand, and so came 
by a copy of it; thinking if I could have heard of my father,

land, both lords, knights, gentlemen, ministers and people, 
to become joint suitors in one supplication unto her Majesty 
and the lords of her honorable Privy Council in these 
petitions : | 


First, that there may be a redress of the great ignorance 
wherewith our whole land is overgrown, by placing able and 
faithful teachers over every congregation, as near as may be. | 

Secondly, that all unlawful and sinful callings may be removed 
out of our ministry and Church. 

Lhardiy, that the Church within her Majesty’s dominions may 
be governed by these offices and officers only, w hich the Lord 
Christ Jesus hath set down in His Word. 

fourthly, that for the quiet and orderly taking up of these 
controversies Which are risen in our Church, concerning the 
government and ceremonies thereof, between our prelates and 
those learned men which are contrary-minded unto’ them, there 
might be had a quiet meeting of both the parties, and the 
controversies determined on their side, who shall be found to deal 
for (and not against) the truth. 


Or, if this fourth petition cannot take place, I would have 
this in the stead thereof, viz. :— 


That it may please her Majesty, and the Lords of her Majesty’s 
honorable Privy Council, to see that the true subjects of the 
Jrown, may not be troubled as now they are, for defending such 
points as, being according unto the Word of God, are also 
according to the privileged doctrine of the Church of England, 
which is maintained by the statutes of this land. And that, in 
case the prelates do molest any man, as now they do, for main- 
taining the doctrine of our Church, or. otherwise contrary unto 
the Jaw of our land, it may be lawful for him or them thus 
injured (1) to have his remedy at the King’s Bench against the 
prelates.

deny but these petitions, in thy judgment, would be an easy 
suit. I trow so, too; and J think that now thou findest 
greater fault, or at| the least as great, with the Puritan

THE MARPRELATE TRACTS 


Whence hath Mar-Martin all his wit 
But from that eee of Sarum ? 

The rest comes all from great Sir John 
Who ings us all this larum. 


What can the cockatrice hatch up, 
But serpent, like himself ? 

What sees the Ape within the glass, 
But a deforméd Elf ? 


Then must Mar-Martin have some smell 
Of forge or else of fire; 

A sot in wit, a beast in mind, 
For so was dam and sire. 


Or else thou mightest have requited him in this Epitaph; 
thus— 


Lf that Mar-Martin die the death that to the dog is due, 
Upon his tomb engrave this verse, and you shall find it true. 


Mle lies endichéd here that from the ladder top 
Did once bedless the people thus, but first he kisst the rope. 


Come near, quoth he, take heed by me, 
IT love to he by riming ; 

*Tis just you see, and doth agree 
That now 1] die by climbing. 


What wretch but I, that vowed to lie, 
All falsehood still defending? 

Who may say, Fie? No beast but I, 
Lo, here you see my ending. | 


I lived a wretch, J die a wretch, 
My days and death agree ; \ 
Whose life is -blameful, his death is shameful, 
Be warned, ye rogues, by me. 


The justest I hated, the godliest I rated, 
And thus I railed my fill; 

The good J detested, the best things I wrested 
To serve miue own beastly will. 


Religion I loathed, myself J betrothed 
To all the lewd snares of sin, 

‘Tis shame to say more, take heed of a whore, 
Her (@) marks stick yet in my skin. 


(1) The above epitaph and the confession at the gallows were answered 
in Martins Months Mind, the latter part of which (at sie. E) is occu- 
pied with ‘A true report of the death and buriall of Martin Mar-prelate.’ 
But the allusions to the gallows began with Mar-Martin, who in the last 
six lines of his doggerel gives an account of Martin’s end. ‘ Here hangs 
knave Martine a traitorous Libeler he was,’ &c.

Ask you the cause? I spurned at God’s laws 
And henee comes all my wrack ; 

Where should he dwell, that fears not hell, 
But with the furies black ? 


A beast that brayes, a tongue that raves, 
Will God revenge in ire; 

Then vengeance must—for God is just-— 
Fall to Mar-Martin’s hire. 


Take example My tongue in ribaldry 
then, my clerey My heart in villainy 
Chaplains, by iy life in treachery 

this lamentable Hath wrought my fall 
fall of your Mar- I strove for the prelacy 
Martin. And so shook off honesty 


O, vile indignity ! 
Yet would this were all. 


Lo, youth; though I were loth to ’file my fingers with 
such a brothel beast as this Mar-Martin is, yet, because 
thou didst let him go by thee, methought, half unbranded, 
I was the willinger, as thou seest, to give him a wipe or two; 
which I believe he will never claw off with honesty while he 

| lives. And I would wish him, with the rest of the 
rimers, if they be wise, to take heed of my next ’Pistle. 
Indeed, I deny not, but thou hast said prettily to him; 
neither would I have thee discouraged in thy good and 
honourable course against these prelates. Nevertheless, I 
muse thou didst let him go clear away with his popery of 
Sir Nicholas Priests (1). Also, where hke a good Cathohe 
he counsels us (we thank him) to say a round Pater noster 
for Queen Elizabeth, I muse (2) thou saidst nothing to that, 


(1) Saint Nicholas, who extended his patronage in all directions in 
the most obliging manner, from schoolboys and poor virgins to sailors 
and ‘clerks,’ that is, scholars, was also, in the popular humour of the day, 
the patron-saint of thieves. Not, we are gravely informed, thal he 
approved of their predatory calling ; but owing to the accident that he 
ouce prevailed upon some of the fraternity to restore their plunder to its 
owner ; to which may be added the fact that a familiar name for the 
devil was a shortened form of the saint’s name—‘Old Nick.’ See Aing 
Henry IV., Virst Part, 1J., i. Martin had some justification for his 
special use of the epithet, as the instances of church plundering by 
bishops and clergy already given in these notes sufficiently show. Tor 
the legends and customs connected with St. Nicholas’s Day, sce Brand’s 
Popular Antiquities, edited by Hilis, Vol. I., p. 415. 

(2) For the significance of the usage of the verb ‘ muse’ in the sense 
of ‘to marvel,’ as bearing upon the problem ot the authorship of the 
Tracts, see the List. Intro. 294, note (2).

INTRODUCTORY NOTE 


Ir has already been stated that the Martinist press and 
the printers, John Hodgkins and his assistants, Valentine 
Simms and Arthur Thomlyn, were seized at Newton Lane, 
Manchester, by the Earl of Derby’s men. ‘The printers 
were busy printing the long-promised Morr Worx ror THE 
Coorpr. ‘The adventurous story of. the removal of the 
press from Wolston, the fatal accident with the type at 
Warrington, and the catastrophe at Manchester are fully 
told in the Historical Introduction, 189 et seq. 

When the news of the misadventure reached Job Throk- 
morton, Penry was with his friends at Wolston, where also 
was Henry Sharpe, the bookbinder, hiding at the house of 


his father-in-law. Throkmorton summoned Penry to. 


Haseley. The result was the issue of this defiant little 
Tract, printed probably at Wolston, where we know from 
the printers’ evidence there was a press still remaining. 
The Historical Introduction, on pp. 191--195, gives some 
account of the difficulties of getting it printed and of the 
pitiful and blundering efforts of some unskilled hands who 
set up and printed off the first sheet. A specimen of their 
work can be scen in the reproduction of the title-page given 
at p. 895. The Tract is a small 8vo, Roman type, of 
thirty-two pages. 

The contents of the Prorusvaryon were determined by the 
Manchester catastrophe. Martin is not to be silenced; his 
chief concern is about the printers, left to the mercy of 
Whitgift and the rack; persecution can but benefit a good 
cause; and Martinism is only to be put down by reason 
and Scripture. This part of the work contains several 
pathetic personal touches: his need of self-examination in 
the face of the calamity that has overtaken his enterprise ;

886 INTRODUCTORY NOTE 


though, as he points out, the goodness of a cause is not to 
be judged outwardly—the lesson eternally taught by the 
tragedy of Calvary. he popularity of the Tracts was 
immense—was there any literary work up to this time ~ 
published in England that had enjoyed anything like the 
Same vogue ?—yet Martin’s end in writing was not to 
amuse. . 

He points to along array of writers and writings which 
he declares are unanswered—the implication being that the’ 
Episcopal controyersialists, notwithstanding their freedom 
to print as they list, are not equal to the task. But the 
harsh measures meted out to the ‘seekers after reformation ’ 
are having their uses. The vindication of liberty and the 
demonstration of the folly, as well as the wrongness, of 
intolerance and persecution are in every generation the 
sacred trust of nonconforming minorities. That is the 
great gain of their suffering. We see how this lesson is 
being gradually learnt by Marprelate. His protest against 
the employment of imprisonment, whipping, torture, instead 
of reason and Scripture, leads him along the direct path to 
toleration and liberty of conscience. 

Among the most interesting features of the Prorustatyon 
is the brief account it gives us of the contents of Mors 
Work For THH CoopErR, the manuscript of which does not 
appear to have survived. It followed, so far as we can 
gather from the bare report before us, the general lines of 
the primary Tracts—the ‘metropoliticall writings’ of 
Marprelate—taking im hand the chief of Episcopal pam- 
phleteers at the moment actively engaged in the controversy. 
A large share of attention is given to Dr. Robert Some, who 
had discharged one ‘ Godly Treatise’ against Robert Browne 
and his revolutionary principle of Church government, and 
another against John Penry. ‘The Prormesratyon also 
supplied some of the lacking proofs of 'Tuusns Marrinrane— 
a point whose significance in regard to the suthorship of 
the last-named Tract has not yet been thoroughly traced out.

THE PROTESTATYON 


oF Marrin Marprenatr. 


5 gee. 
S72 


Wherem, notwithstanding the surprising of the 
Printer, he maketh it known unto the world, 
that he feareth neither Proud Priest, Anti- 
christian Pope, Tyrannous Prelate, nor God- 
less Catercap; but defieth all the race of 
them by these presents; and offereth 
conditionally, as is further expressed 
herein, by open disputation to ap- 
pear in the defence of his cause, 
against them and_ theirs. 


Which challenge if they dare not maintain against 
him, then doth he also publish that he never 
meaneth, by the assistance of God, to leave 
the assailing of them and their genera- 
tion until they be utterly extin- 
guished out of our Church. 


Published 
by the worthy gentleman Doctor Martin Marprelate, 
Doctor in all the faculties, Primate, and Metropolitan.

THov canst not lightly be ignorant, good reader, of that 
which hath lately fallen unto some things of mine, which 
were to be printed, or in printing; the press, letters, 
workmen and all, apprehended and carried as malefactors 
before the magistrate (x); whose authority I reverence, and 
whose sword I would fear (2), were I as wicked as our 
Bishops are. These events I confess do strike me and give 
me just cause to enter more narrowly into myself to see 
whether I be at peace with God, or no. But utterly to 
discourage me from mine enterprise, a greater matter than 
that comes to I hope shall never be able. The state of the 
poor men that are taken I do bewail; not because they 
can (3) hurt me, for [ assure thee, they know not who J am, 
but inasmuch as, I fear, the tyranny of our wicked priests 
will do that against them, which neither the Word of God 
doth warrant, nor law of the land doth permit. | or, as their 4 
hatred unto the cause is without ground, so their cruclty 
to those that profess the same is without measure. There- 
fore, good reader, if thou hear of any mean(4) or com- 
passionable punishment inflicted upon them (who, to say the 
truth, have deserved none at all—I mean the printers) I 
would never have thee stand to expostulate with our Bishops 
for this untimely lenity of theirs (5), for whom I dare take mine 
oath (for I know them so well) that if there fall out any 
good to those poor men through the providence of God, and

(2) Romans 134, 

(3) The print is here imperfect. It reads “not becaus thye au hurt 
mee.’ Before ‘au’ there is a faint suggestion of a letter. 

(4) Moderate. ‘ 


(5) As a matter of fact, Hodekins and his men, Thomlyn and Symms, 
were put upon the rack by Whitgift. See Hist. Intro., 197 ed seq.

the gracious clemency of her Majesty, they, for their parts, 
are no more guilty or accessory unto it, than the Spanish 
inguisitors themselves. For indeed, in this one point they 
are of my mind; viz., that reformation cannot well come to 
our Church without blood; and that no blood can hand- 
somely be spilt in that cause, unless they themselves be the 
butchers and horseleeches to draw it out. Thou seest 
6 evidently, they claim that as a piece | and portion of their 
inheritance (z). But tell them from me, that we fear not 
men, that can but kill the body; because we fear that God, 
who can cast both body and soul into unquenchable fire (2). 
And tell them also this. That the more blood the Church 
loseth, the more life and blood it gets. When the fearful 
sentence pronounced against the persecutors of the truth is 
executed upon them, I would then pladly know, whether, 
they who go about thus to shed our blocd, or we whose blood 
erxieth for vengeance against them, shall have the worst end 
of the staff. We are sure to possess our souls in everlasting - 
peace, whensoever we leave this earthly tabernacle ; and in 
the mean time we know that an hair of our head cannot fall 
to the ground without the will of our heavenly Father (3), 
Who, of His great mercy, loveth us in, and for, our Saviour 
Christ Jesus; and that, with a love as far passing the love 
of a natural father toward his children, as He whe so loveth 


6us, excelleth all earthly parents. This per | suasion being 


steadfastly engrafted in their hearts, who either now or 
hereafter shall be trodled (4) for this cause, will be a com- 
fort to them in the midst of all their distresses. 

And, good reader, whosoever thou art, I would not have 
thee discouraged at this, that is lately fallen out. teason 
not from the success of things unto the goodness of the 
cause. For that savoureth too much of the flesh. If, in

and not violence that must uphold their places? Do they 
not know that the more violence they use the more breath

The whole issues of their force (1) and bloodthirsty 
attempts doth nothing else but witness against them, that 
they are the children of those fathers, who never as yet 
durst abide to have their proceedings examined by the 
Word. And, methinks, they should be ashamed to have it 
recorded unto ages to come that they have ever shunned to 

9 maintain their cause, either by open disputation, | or by 
any other sound conference or writing. Let me be over- 
thrown by any of these ways, and I do here by these my 
writings publicly protest that [£ will never molest lord 
bishop again while I live; but will, with very great 
vehemency, to the uttermost of my endeavour, maintain 
them and their cause, as ever I did oppugn the same. 
Otherwise, I do with the hke constancy and resolution 
protest that, by the aid and assistance of God, I will never 
leave the displaying of them and their proceedings, until 
they be made as odious in our Church and Commonwealth 
as that they be thought of all sorts(2) unworthy to be 
harboured therem. 

And this offer of mine, so reasonable, and in every respect 
so easy to be yielded unto, if they refuse, who seeth not 
therein a secret implying, and a close granting (3), of the

Now, because they would gladly know Martin, I will here 
set them down a way, whereby they may not only know 
him, but (that which is more delightful unto them) they 
may quench their thirst with his blood, if they will; pro- 
vided that they be able to make their cause good against 
him by the Word of God. 

1 do therefore by this my Proresration, make 
it known to the whole Church of England, 
especially unto our magistrates, more especially 
unto our gracious Sovereign, and unto all posteri- 
ties to come; that I, who do now go under the 
name of Martin Marprelate, do offer personally to 
appear, and there to make myself known in open 
disputation, upon the danger, not only of my 
liberty, but also of my life; to maintain, against 


all our bishops, | or any else whosoever that shall 11 


dare in any scholastical manner to take their parts 
the cause of the Church government which is now 
in controversy betwixt me and our prelates; so 
that(z1) I may have this condition following 
inviolably kept and observed ; viz., that for appear- 
ing, or for anything that J have either published or 
ee to be published in this cause, I be not dealt 
with, or molested, except they Leerintes me by 
the Word of God; which if they do, confusion be 
upon me if I donotyield. But if in this encounter

it, if they abide the push) then, they to truss

circumcidet Yimothe, when there was hope to wynne the Jewes ; but 
when they wolde haye it of necessitie, hee wolde not circumcide ‘Titus. 
Therefore compelling wold not be used in things of liberty. .. . Con-

religion, have cast away the Popishe apparel [along] with the Pope, 
and yet we that wold be taken for the best, contend to keep it as a 
holie relique. Merke also, how many Mynisters there be here in al coun- 
tries, that be so zelous, not only to forsake that wicked doctryne of 
Poperie ; but ready to leave the mynisterie and their livings, rather than 
to be like the Popish teachers of such superstitions, auther in apparel 
or behaviour.’ With these frank and commonsense views of the Pro- 
testant position, bishop though he was, it is no wonder that Martin 
placed Pilkington among the supporters of reformation.

writings, together with other learned discourses | more, 
whereby the corruption and the unlawfulness of the places 
and proceedings of lord bishops are shamefully laid open 
unto the world, are as yet unanswered; and likely to be no 
otherwise confuted than with slanders, ribaldry, scurrility, 
reviling, imprisonment and torture; and, inasmuch as they 
dare not maintain their cause against me by open and 
public disputation, that, therefore, they do manifestly 
confess their cause and proceedings to be clean foiled, 
overthrown, and made even with the ground; in such sort 
as, beside whorish impudency, halter, axe, bonds, scourging 
and racking, with such other weapons as were bequeathed 
unto them by their forefathers, the ancient enemies and 
persecutors of the Church, they have not left any instrument 
to defend themselves. 

And let them be sure, seeing they dare come to no lawful 
way of trial with me, that there shall not be a post in any 
great street or place of concourse, almost in the land, but I 


will make an affix (1), and set up this my foresaid de | clara-. 


tion of the victory had over them, to their shame; and I 
will also make foreign nations ring of their villanies and 
ungodliness, if the publishing of their doings in Latin can 


do it.

going Protestant reformers. His Acts and Monuments, the result of years 
of toil and persistent search and inquiry, was regarded as a work of 
national importance ; archbishops and bishops were required by the 
Canons, ed. 1571, to have a copy for the use of their households ; later 
it was ordered, with thé Bible and Jewel’s Apology, to be part of the 
furnishing of all churches. The Acts and Monuments might be regarded 
as a suficicnt exposure of the iniquities of prelates ; yet more than his 
writines, most of which were written in Latin, there was the notorious 
fact that, although held in the highest repute because of his work, his 
sterling honesty of character, and especially because of his magnanimity, 
he lived in comparative poverty, because he could not subscribe to 
the Episcopal articles; in particular he would not promise to wear 
the clerical vestments. All he had was a poor prebend at Salisbury 
Cathedral. Asked to subscribe, he took his Greek Testament out of 
his pocket and declared it was the only book he would subscribe to. 
Threatened with deprivation, he mentioned his small benefice, all he 
bad in the Church, that, he said, they might take, adding, ‘and much 
good may it do you.’ The bishops, however, had not suflicient courage to 
carry out the penalty of deprivation in the case of John Foxe.

I have long ago (x) set up my rest (2); making that account 
of it, as in standing against the enemies of God, and for the 
liberty of His Church, it is no value in my sight. My life in 
this cause shall be a gain to the Church, and no loss to 
myself, J know right well ; and this is all the reckoning which, 
by the assistance of the Lord, I will make as long as I live, 
of all the torments they have devised forme. J am blamed 
of many in this mine attempt, not only for throwing myself 
into great danger; but also for the utter undoing of my 
wife and children (3). I do thank them with all my heart, 
for their care over those poor souls, and commend them for 
their secrecy and wisdom that, in knowing my wife and 
children, they have not by showing their unmeasurable love 
towards them discovered me. | You see what it is when 
wise men have the handling of a matter. I perceive, if 
these men were not very provident and wary, that Martin 
could not be longunknown. For I tell you, if a man’s wife 
and children be once known, it is not possible that he can 
be secret any long time. And yet, methinks, that all their 
wisdom, and all their care over my wife and clildren, when 
the matter is well weighed, is scant worth three straws. 
For what if Martin had neither wife nor child in all his life, 
are they not then something too much overweened (4) in 
their own conceit, who give out that he hath both? Will 


you believe me then, if I tell you the truth? To put you 


therefore out-of all doubt, I may safely protest unto you, 
with a good conscience, that howsoever the speech may 
seem strange unto many, yet the very truth is that hitherto 
f never had wife nor child in all my life. Not that I never

Well, concerning the care that our prelates have in leaving 
of things behooveful for their successors, I may truly say 
that, were it not more for fear of law than for any con- 
science of the maintenance of the ministry, the whole 
bishopric, even to-day before tomorrow, would not yicld a 
lord bishop so much as might purchase him an handsome 
halter to hang himself with, as the poet saith. Therefore 
let them never talk more for shame, as their T’. C. doth, of 
the care they have that the Church’s maintenance should 
not decay. And (x) as herein their spoil and | robbery is 21 
apparent; so, on the other side, their tyranny and blood- 
thirsty proceedings against good men is unexcusable. 

And yet is the manner of their proceedings more intoler- 
able and dangerous to the State than their very practices 
themselves. First, you see, they may examine of what they 
will. For who can let (2) them, when they be both sole judges 
and sole witness themselves ; and none otber by but the poor 
examinate. To which effect, what is the seat of justice 
they commonly use in these cases but only some close 
chamber at Lambeth, or some obscure gallery in London 
Palace? Where according to the true nature of an evil 
conscience, that flieth and feareth the light, they may 
juggle and foist in what they list without controlment ; and

more at large appear in a plain statute of the 25th of 
Henry VIL, in the title of Heresy (3). And therefore men 
may see what account they ought to make of those shameless 
speeches of that worthy greyhead, Mistress Cooper's 
husband; who, as he hath been long since too old to 
blush, so did he not let (4) openly to avouch, that, before

wouldest lay 14 up among other thy honest recreations for

he was never Puritan in his life, but always an orderly man, 
and a maintainer of the state of the clergy. 

And if his Grace did appoint any other to preach at his 
good old mastey’s funeral (£1) but only this quick-witted 
Bridges, he was certainly foully overseen (2). For there 
would have been such a mess and such a match, such a pair 
of saints, the one living and the other dead, as I believe the 
Legenda Aurea (3) | would not yield the like; both old 
standards, both proculstants (4), both catercaps, both 
priests, both deans, both hypocrites, both asses. Why, 
sans mercy, said I, &c.—but, alas, ’chave haulf (5) forgotten 
the rest. 

After this, I had a fling at these Puritans, concerning 
whom my desire is that wherein J am faulty the Puritans 
would set me down the particulars. It is odds I shall some 
way or other hear of it. For albeit there have been some 
jars of unkindness betwixt us; yet I would have you know 
that I take the worst of you, inregard of his calling, to be an 
honester man than the best lord bishop in Christendom. 
The report goeth that some of you have preached against 
me; and I believe it in part. Well, look to it; for I may 
happen to be even with you in this manner—J will not 
rest till I have learned what it is that ye have said of me; 
and if I find it to be a just reproof, I will mend my fault, be 
as angry as ye will; if unjust, trust unto it I will hold on 
my course, and there is one rap more than ye looked for.

goeth without a little saunce bell (1) in his pocket, and that

it Ting? If you give good ear, nothing else, I warrant you, 
but ‘My sermons,’ ‘My writings’ ‘My reasons’ ‘My 
arguments’; and all is ‘My, My, My’; asif the depth of 
all Jearning were included inthe channelof his brain. This 
is even he that, let him write a many books as he will

wooden dish or other.

with them.

Church ; (11) an antithesis between our Saviour Christ and

published so untimely. But as for him and his elder 
brother, together with that blind ass Pasquill (7), I will have

points, with an honourable mention of all noble soldiers, a 
complaint of the loss of my papers, and the misery of sea 
journeys; I ended my ’Pistle, being the first tome of
